item.title: San Francisco Peninsula Coffee Roasters and Cafes
item.description: The Peninsula's coffee reputation is all tech campus cold brew and chains on El Camino. That's a little insulting to the roasters who were here long before
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Peninsula Coffee Roasters and Cafes

The Peninsula's coffee reputation is all tech campus cold brew and chains on El Camino. That's a little insulting to the roasters who were here long before. Plantation has been roasting on the same German machine on a San Carlos side street since 1981, and the smell down Laurel Street gives it away. Eight Peninsula coffee roasters and cafes worth the detour.

Soul Grind Coffee Roasters — 5400 Coast Highway, Pacifica. They roast on site a sand dune away from the Pacifica State Beach surf break, so your latte comes with wetsuits dripping by the door. Dog friendly, fog usually included. Grab a window seat and watch the sets roll in. @soulgrindcoffee

Half Moon Bay Coffee Company — 20 Stone Pine Rd, Half Moon Bay. A family run spot just off Main Street where the all day breakfast is the real reason to linger over a second cup. Come after a walk downtown, settle in, and do not rush the morning. @hmbcoffeeco

Three Bees Coffee House — 224 E 3rd Ave, San Mateo. A genuine mom and pop holding down downtown San Mateo since 2002, walls rotating with local art instead of corporate posters. Order a pastry, settle into the warm room, and remember what a neighborhood cafe felt like. @3beescoffee

Plantation Coffee Roastery — 784 Laurel St, San Carlos. That 1981 roaster from up top runs most mornings. That's why the whole block smells like breakfast. Beans go from drum to cup about as fresh as it gets on the Peninsula. Buy a bag, you will be back. @plantationcoffeeroastery

Connoisseur Coffee Company — 2801 Middlefield Rd, Redwood City. More than 40 years in, they still roast in house from beans across 25 plus countries, an old school roaster hiding in plain sight. Tell them how you brew at home and let them point you somewhere new. @connoisseur_coffee_company

Coffeebar — 1149 Chestnut St, Menlo Park. It started up in Truckee and brought its own roasted beans and a full food menu down to Menlo Park, open early to late seven days a week. Bright and buzzy, it is built for a real work session or a slow catch up. @coffeebar

Cafe Borrone — 1010 El Camino Real, Menlo Park. A Peninsula institution beside Kepler's Books, where people have nursed one cappuccino through a whole afternoon since the late 1980s. Grab a book next door, claim a patio table, and join the long tradition of lingering. @cafeborrone

Coupa Cafe — 538 Ramona St, Palo Alto. The Ramona Street original is a family run Venezuelan cafe pouring organic coffee next to real arepas and tequenos, a downtown Palo Alto fixture for years. Come hungry, order past the latte, and claim a sidewalk table. @coupacafe

Eight for Peninsula coffee: Soul Grind, Half Moon Bay Coffee, Three Bees, Plantation, Connoisseur, Coffeebar, Cafe Borrone, and Coupa. Who is roasting your favorite bag right now?

item.title: San Francisco Cheese Shops
item.description: Say Cheese has held the same Cole Valley corner since 1976, cutting cheese to order and stocking wine while the rest of San Francisco chased the next thing
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Cheese Shops

Say Cheese has held the same Cole Valley corner since 1976, cutting cheese to order and stocking wine while the rest of San Francisco chased the next thing. The city's best cheese is still like that, tucked into the neighborhoods. Eight SF cheese stops worth the trip.

Say Cheese — 856 Cole Street, San Francisco. Neighborhood cheese and wine shop since 1976, where the counter crew will hand you a taste and talk you into the runny one. Grab a sandwich on good bread while you decide. @saycheesesf

Cheese Plus — 2001 Polk Street, San Francisco. A serious cheese case on the sunny corner of Polk and Pacific, with a full deli, wine, and an espresso bar if you want to linger. Tell them what you are cooking and they will match it. @cheeseplus

Little Vine — 1541 Grant Avenue, San Francisco. A tiny North Beach shop stocked with cheese, natural wine, and pantry things you did not know you needed. Come for a wedge, leave with dinner and a bottle. @littlevinesf

Rainbow Grocery — 1745 Folsom Street, San Francisco. The worker cooperative has run since 1975, and its cheese department is huge, deep, and priced better than most specialty shops. Bring a list and leave room in the fridge. @rainbow_grocery

Bi-Rite Market — 3639 18th Street, San Francisco. The Mission classic where the cheese buyer actually trained in Vermont and Europe, so the case runs from comte to a gouda worth the splurge. Ask what is peaking right now. @biritesf

The Epicurean Trader — 465 Hayes Street, San Francisco. A craft grocery in Hayes Valley that treats farmstead cheese and charcuterie like the good stuff it is, right next to small batch chocolate and wine. Build a picnic for the park nearby. @theepicureantrader

Gus's Community Market — 1530 Haight Street, San Francisco. A neighborhood grocer since 1981 with a cheese counter locals actually shop, planted in the middle of Haight Street. Handy when you want good cheese without a special trip. @gussmarket

The Cheese School of San Francisco — 2535 3rd Street, San Francisco. Not a grab a wedge shop but the city's cheese classroom, running tastings and classes inside Daily Driver, home to the only creamery in town. Book a class and learn why your board never looks right. @thecheeseschool

Eight for a San Francisco cheese run: Say Cheese, Cheese Plus, Little Vine, Rainbow, Bi-Rite, Epicurean Trader, Gus's, and the Cheese School. Which counter has your loyalty, and what belongs on this list?

item.title: San Francisco Butcher Shops
item.description: Guerra Quality Meats has been breaking down whole animals on Taraval since 1954, back when every San Francisco neighborhood kept its own butcher. A surpris
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Butcher Shops

Guerra Quality Meats has been breaking down whole animals on Taraval since 1954, back when every San Francisco neighborhood kept its own butcher. A surprising number of them still do. Eight SF butcher shops worth the trip across town.

Guerra Quality Meats — 490 Taraval Street, San Francisco. A family butcher and Italian deli since 1954, custom cuts up front and housemade lasagna and sausages in the case. Go for the meat, walk out with dinner already half made. @guerrameatssf

Avedano's Holly Park Market — 235 Cortland Avenue, San Francisco. A Bernal Heights butcher in a storefront that has sold meat for close to a century, breaking down whole animals from small farms. It nearly closed in 2025 before a backer stepped in, so go give it a reason to stay. @avedanos

Marina Meats — 2395 Chestnut Street, San Francisco. The Marina's neighborhood butcher, stocking sustainable meat, poultry, and fish cut at a real counter instead of a supermarket foam tray. Tell them your plan and they will steer you right. @marinameats

Bryan's Quality Meats — 3445 California Street, San Francisco. On the same Laurel Village block since 1963, with roots in the Flannery beef family and a meat case regulars plan their menus around. This is the splurge butcher for the holiday roast. @bryansmarket

Olivier's Butchery — 1192 Illinois Street, San Francisco. A French butcher in Dogpatch since 2011, turning out European style cuts and charcuterie you will not find at the chain store. Closed Monday and Tuesday, so plan the visit. @oliviersbutchery

Fatted Calf — 1 Ferry Building, San Francisco. The whole animal butcher and salumi maker that settled into the Ferry Building, where the salami, pate, and terrines are the reason to come. Grab a sandwich and eat it by the water. @fattedcalf

Le Beau Nob Hill Market — 1263 Leavenworth Street, San Francisco. A family run corner market since 1984 with a real butcher case hiding inside, the kind of place Nob Hill locals rely on for a good steak on a Tuesday. Small store, better meat than it lets on. @lebeaumarketsf

Antonelli Brothers — 3585 California Street, San Francisco. Third generation butchers working the counter inside Cal-Mart since 1956, a block from Bryan's, so Laurel Village quietly has two of the city's best. Old school service, custom cuts, no attitude. @antonellibros

Eight for a San Francisco butcher run: Guerra, Avedano's, Marina Meats, Bryan's, Olivier's, Fatted Calf, Le Beau, and Antonelli Brothers. Who is your neighborhood butcher, and which one belongs here?

item.title: San Francisco Wine Bars
item.description: Eight San Francisco wine bars worth crossing town for, and the Dogpatch one is run by a Master Sommelier, among only about two dozen women in the whole cou
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Wine Bars

Eight San Francisco wine bars worth crossing town for, and the Dogpatch one is run by a Master Sommelier, among only about two dozen women in the whole country to earn that title. The best glass in SF is not behind a white tablecloth downtown, it is spread across eight neighborhoods. Start here.

Amelie — 1754 Polk Street, San Francisco. A cozy French wine bar in Polk Gulch known for flights, three pours built around a theme, plus live music some nights and a genuinely good happy hour. Low lighting, easy dates, no wine snobbery. @ameliesanfrancisco

Verjus — 550 Washington Street, San Francisco. The candlelit Jackson Square wine bar from the Quince and Cotogna team, no reservations, walk in and graze charcuterie and cheese with an ever changing pour list. On the Chronicle Top 100 and the Michelin guide for 2026. @verjus_sf

Ungrafted — 2419 3rd Street, San Francisco. The Dogpatch wine bar run by Master Sommeliers Rebecca Fineman and Chris Gaither, with a nearly 1,000 bottle list and a front of house that is all somms. Order the smash burger with something rare by the glass. @ungraftedsf

Bar Part Time — 496 14th Street, San Francisco. Part natural wine bar, part dance floor in the Mission, complete with a disco ball and a record driven crowd that stays late. Living wines from small producers, then the DJ turns it into a party. @barparttime

High Treason — 443 Clement Street, San Francisco. A sommelier run wine bar and bottle shop in the Inner Richmond where you can wear a hoodie, hear punk and hip hop on the speakers, and still drink grand cru Burgundy. Up to 45 wines by the glass. @hightreasonsf

Birba — 458 Grove Street, San Francisco. A tiny 16 seat Hayes Valley wine bar with a back garden that feels hidden from the city. Classic and natural bottles from a sommelier owner, no reservations, so slip in early. @birbawine

Palm City Wines — 4055 Irving Street, San Francisco. The Outer Sunset corner spot for natural wine and arm length hoagies, with a list built by a former Nopa wine director. Grab a glass and an Italian American hoagie, or a bottle to take to the beach. @palmcitywines

Scopo Divino — 2800 California Street, San Francisco. A Pacific Heights wine bar with live music five nights a week, a wine shop up front, and weekend brunch. Come for a glass, stay for the set. @scopodivino

Eight for the San Francisco wine bar crawl: Amelie, Verjus, Ungrafted, Bar Part Time, High Treason, Birba, Palm City, and Scopo Divino. Which neighborhood pour is your regular, and which SF wine bar should be on this list?

item.title: San Francisco Chocolate Shops and Makers
item.description: San Francisco's bean to bar movement basically started at a Valencia Street shop that still roasts its own cocoa beans on site, no trip to Ghirardelli Squa
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Chocolate Shops and Makers

San Francisco's bean to bar movement basically started at a Valencia Street shop that still roasts its own cocoa beans on site, no trip to Ghirardelli Square required. The city is quietly stacked with real makers. Eight San Francisco chocolate shops and makers worth the detour.

Dandelion Chocolate — 740 Valencia Street, San Francisco. The Mission shop that kicked off the city's bean to bar craze back in 2012, roasting single origin beans right there while you sip a house hot chocolate. Sit at the bar and taste what origin actually does. @dandelionchocolate

Recchiuti Confections — 1 Ferry Building, San Francisco. The Ferry Building flagship whose fleur de sel caramels turned a lot of skeptics into believers. Grab the s'mores kit or the burnt caramel bar and thank yourself later. @recchiuticonfections

Christopher Elbow — 401 Hayes Street, San Francisco. In Hayes Valley the bonbons look like tiny hand painted art pieces, almost too pretty to bite. The salted caramel and the fig are the gateway. Go before a show at the symphony. @elbowchocolates

Z — Cioccolato. 474 Columbus Avenue, San Francisco. North Beach fudge shop with more than 50 rotating flavors and a wall of nostalgic candy you forgot existed. The layered fudge got ranked among the best in the country. Free samples, obviously. @z.cioccolato

Socola Chocolatier — 535 Folsom Street, San Francisco. A SoMa chocolatier run by two sisters whose Vietnamese inspired bonbons lean salty, spicy, and a little unexpected. The salted butter caramels move fast. Weekday afternoons are the window, they keep short hours. @socolachocs

XOX Truffles — 754 Columbus Avenue, San Francisco. A tiny North Beach cafe making French style truffles by hand since 1997, 26 flavors from cognac to matcha. Order any coffee and they hand you a free truffle, every single time. Closed Thursdays.

Chocolate Covered — 4069 24th Street, San Francisco. This narrow Noe Valley shop has stocked over 900 chocolate bars from more than 30 countries since 1994. The other draw is the hand decorated tins printed with San Francisco street signs, nearly every street in the city. @chocolatecoveredsf

Feve Artisan Chocolatier — 2222 Palou Avenue, San Francisco. Out in the Bayview, this four time Good Food Award winner runs its factory and shop in one, so you can watch bonbons being made on a weekday. Small batch, seriously good, worth going off the tourist path. @fevechocolates

Eight for San Francisco chocolate: Dandelion, Recchiuti, Christopher Elbow, Z. Cioccolato, Socola, XOX Truffles, Chocolate Covered, and Feve. Which one are you gifting this year?

item.title: San Francisco Peninsula Taquerias
item.description: La Tapatia in South San Francisco opened in 1976 as a working tortilla factory, years before it ever sold a taco. That is the Peninsula in a nutshell, wher
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Peninsula Taquerias

La Tapatia in South San Francisco opened in 1976 as a working tortilla factory, years before it ever sold a taco. That is the Peninsula in a nutshell, where the best Mexican food sits nowhere near a tourist map and never needs a bridge. Eight taquerias worth the drive, one town at a time.

El Grullense Grill — 768 Woodside Rd, Redwood City. The Grullense name is all over Redwood City, and this is the sit down one where the al pastor comes off the trompo with real char. Order it con todo, grab a Jarritos, and know they stay open late. @elgrullensegrill

Taqueria La Cumbre — 28 N B St, San Mateo. The San Mateo cousin of the SF spot that helped put the Mission style burrito on the map. Come for the carne asada and the refried beans people genuinely rave about. Downtown, no frills, all substance. @tlctaco

La Corneta Taqueria — 1123 Burlingame Ave, Burlingame. Right on Burlingame Ave, this is the one where the burrito lands the size of your forearm and both the al pastor and the shrimp hold their own. Order at the counter, watch them build it, regret nothing. @lacorneta_burlingame

La Tapatia Mexicatessen — 411 Grand Ave, South San Francisco. Half Mexican market, half taqueria, open since 1976 and once a real tortilla factory. Walk past the pan dulce to the counter in back for tacos on tortillas made the right way. A Grand Ave institution. @latapatia.southcity

Taqueria La Cazuela — 2390 Clarke Ave, East Palo Alto. Family run since 2011 and everything is made to order. That's exactly why the line is worth it. Get the al pastor or the carnitas, and do not sleep on the free chips and salsa. Closed Sundays, so plan around it.

Taqueria Tres Amigos — 270 Cabrillo Hwy S, Half Moon Bay. The coastside taqueria since 1985, started by three friends from Jalisco who brought their hometown taco recipes north. This is the grab a burrito before the beach move, and the carne asada delivers. Cash saves you the card fee.

Taqueria Los Cuernos — 6286 Mission St, Daly City. A Top of the Hill favorite that only opens Wednesday through Saturday, so treat it as a weekend plan, not a Monday craving. The regulars line up early and it moves fast. Do as they do and get there before the rush. @taqueria.los.cuernos

Taqueria San Bruno — 1045 San Mateo Ave, San Bruno. Two thousand plus reviews and still the first name locals drop when you ask where to eat. The carnitas burrito is the order, crispy edges and all, and it is massive. On San Mateo Ave, closed Mondays. @taqueriasanbruno

Eight for the Peninsula taco run: El Grullense, La Cumbre, La Corneta, La Tapatia, La Cazuela, Tres Amigos, Los Cuernos, and Taqueria San Bruno. Which town wins the burrito crawl?

item.title: San Francisco Tea Houses
item.description: Imperial Tea Court opened in 1993 as the first traditional Chinese teahouse in America, and it still pours in San Francisco's Ferry Building. Skip the souv
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Tea Houses

Imperial Tea Court opened in 1993 as the first traditional Chinese teahouse in America, and it still pours in San Francisco's Ferry Building. Skip the souvenir tins stacked in the Grant Avenue windows. These are the counters where the tasting is free and the leaf is single origin. Eight tea houses worth slowing down for.

Red Blossom Tea Company — 831 Grant Ave, San Francisco. The Luong family flies to China and Taiwan every year to buy direct, so the hundred plus teas on the wall are sorted by harvest and varietal like a wine list. Ask for a sample size before you commit to a whole tin. @redblossomteacompany

Vital Tea Leaf — 1044 Grant Ave, San Francisco. The Chinatown shop that runs on the hard sell of hospitality, steeping you cup after cup for free until an oolong or an aged pu erh finally clicks. Go with time and an open mind, not a shopping list.

Imperial Tea Court — 1 Ferry Building, San Francisco. The Fongs' teahouse still runs full gongfu service at a table in the Ferry Building, tiny clay pots, many short steeps, no rushing. Sit down, watch the water hit the leaf, and taste why the ritual beats a paper cup. @imperialteacourt

Song Tea and Ceramics — 2120 Sutter St, San Francisco. A hushed Lower Pacific Heights room where the tea is small batch and often exclusive to the shop, poured next to handmade cups you will want to take home. Book a tasting flight and leave with a leaf you cannot find anywhere else. @hellosongtea

Aroma Tea Shop — 302 6th Ave, San Francisco. An Inner Richmond wall of canisters holding more than 150 loose leaf teas, from roasted oolong to blooming jasmine, with staff who will walk you through every one. You come in for a single tea and leave with five. @aromateashop

Stonemill Matcha — 561 Valencia St, San Francisco. A calm Valencia Street cafe built around stone milled Japanese matcha whisked to order, served with a full Japanese breakfast on weekends. Come for the ceremonial grade, stay for the miso, rice, and grilled fish. @stonemillmatcha

Dartealing Lounge — 470 3rd St, San Francisco. A Victorian styled lounge near South Beach pouring around 40 loose leaf teas with a proper tiered afternoon tea. Weekends only, so plan it, then settle in and let the second pot go long. @dartealinglounge

Lovejoy's Tea Room — 1351 Church St, San Francisco. Noe Valley afternoon tea in a mismatched parlor that feels like an English cottage wandered off and settled in California. Reserve ahead, get the full service with scones and clotted cream, and give it a slow two hours. @lovejoys_tearoom

Eight for San Francisco tea: Imperial Tea Court, Red Blossom, Song Tea, Vital Tea Leaf, Aroma, Stonemill Matcha, Lovejoy's, and Dartealing. Grant Avenue gongfu or a Noe Valley scone, which one are you booking first?

item.title: San Francisco Wine Shops
item.description: D&M Wines has sold Champagne from the same Fillmore Street corner since 1935, older than almost everything around it. San Francisco quietly runs on indepen
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Wine Shops

D&M Wines has sold Champagne from the same Fillmore Street corner since 1935, older than almost everything around it. San Francisco quietly runs on independent bottle shops like that, so here are Eight worth a detour, not a grocery aisle among them.

Ferry Plaza Wine Merchant — 1 Ferry Building, San Francisco. Tucked in the Ferry Building with a curated global list and a bar counter, so you can taste a glass before you commit to the bottle. A cheese shop from the same crew opens next door in summer 2026. Grab one before the ferry. @ferryplazawine

K&L Wine Merchants — 855 Harrison Street, San Francisco. The big one in SoMa, a famously deep list running from twelve dollar weeknight reds to rare and collectable trophies. The staff notes taped to the shelves are actually worth reading. Go in with a budget and a plan. @klwines

Biondivino — 1415 Green Street, San Francisco. A jewel box of a shop on Russian Hill that has beaten the drum for Italian wine since 2006, twenty regions deep, from Barolo you know to grapes you cannot pronounce yet. Tell them what you like and trust the handsell. @biondivino

Arlequin Wine Merchant — 384 Hayes Street, San Francisco. Family run in Hayes Valley since 1998, the pre show stop for something fun, fine, and a little interesting without needing a sommelier degree. Prices are friendlier than the block suggests. Perfect before the symphony. @arlequinwine

D&M Wines and Liquors — 2200 Fillmore Street, San Francisco. The Champagne temple, in the family and the same spot since 1935. Also the place for the three great French brandies, Armagnac, Calvados, Cognac, plus a wall of single malt. Come for bubbles, stay for the education. @dandmwineandliquors

Plumpjack Wine and Spirits — 3201 Fillmore Street, San Francisco. A Cow Hollow fixture since 1992 that keeps rare library bottles for collectors and easy everyday wine for the rest of us on the same shelves. No attitude, real range. Ask what is drinking well right now. @plumpjackwineandspirits

William Cross Wine Merchants — 2253 Polk Street, San Francisco. Everything on the shelves is hand picked, small production, and a little opinionated. There is a tasting bar in back and a serious cheese case up front, and the Wednesday tastings are the neighborhood move. @wmcrosswine

Verve Wine — 2358 Fillmore Street, San Francisco. Co founded by a Master Sommelier from the Somm films, so the geekery runs deep, but the room is friendly, not fussy. Strong on Champagne and off the beaten path bottles. Say your price and let them run with it. @vervewinesf

Eight for the San Francisco wine run: Ferry Plaza, K&L, Biondivino, Arlequin, D&M, Plumpjack, William Cross, and Verve. Which one is closest to your front door?

item.title: San Francisco Peninsula Wine Bars
item.description: Eight Peninsula wine bars where the person pouring knows the vineyard, not just the register. A Burlingame room keeps 1,100 bottles on the list. A Half Moo
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Peninsula Wine Bars

Eight Peninsula wine bars where the person pouring knows the vineyard, not just the register. A Burlingame room keeps 1,100 bottles on the list. A Half Moon Bay winery pours what it makes out back. Skip the grocery aisle.

Vin Vino Wine — 437 California Avenue, Palo Alto. Half bottle shop, half tasting bar, and the California Avenue regulars treat it like a second kitchen. Tell them what you are cooking and they will hand you the glass that fixes it. Grab a bottle for the road on the way out. @vinvinopaloalto

Vino Locale — 431 Kipling Street, Palo Alto. Tucked in a downtown Victorian since 2005, with a back garden that runs live music most nights. Order a flight with the cheese board and let the set list do the talking. Best seat is outside once the fog burns off. @vinolocalepaloalto

The Cask — 782 Laurel Street, San Carlos. Exposed brick, candlelight, and a Laurel Street crowd that lingers past closing. It reads date night but works just as well solo at the bar with a cheese plate. Weekends fill fast, so put your name in early. @thecaskwinebar

CRU Wine Bar and Merchant — 900B Middlefield Road, Redwood City. The little sibling of Donato Enoteca, so the Italian list runs deep and the staff actually want to nerd out about it. Buy a bottle off the shelf at retail and drink it right there. Trivia nights pull a fun crowd. @cruredwoodcity

B Street and Vine — 320 South B Street, San Mateo. Downtown San Mateo's cozy corner for a glass and a bruschetta plate, with live jazz warming up the weekend. The heated patio means you are never chased inside by the evening chill. Happy hour is the local move. @b_street_and_vine_official

Velvet 48 — 310 Lorton Avenue, Burlingame. Forty plus wines by the glass and over 1,100 on the full list, run by a guy who spent 20 years in the trade. Come in without a plan and let them pour you something you cannot pronounce. Small plates keep you honest. @velvet48winebar

Half Moon Bay Wine and Cheese Company — 421 Main Street, Half Moon Bay. Part shop, part bar, right on Main Street for the post beach reset. Build a cheese flight, pull a coastal bottle, and settle in while the fog rolls back over the hills. Grab picnic supplies before you leave town. @hmbwineandcheese

Barterra Winery — 151 Harvard Avenue, Half Moon Bay. A rare thing on the coast, a tasting room pouring wine it actually makes, a short walk from Pillar Point Harbor. Weekends only, so time it with the harbor and a plate of oysters nearby. Ask what just came off the barrel. @barterrawinery

Eight for a Peninsula wine crawl: Vin Vino, Vino Locale, The Cask, CRU, B Street and Vine, Velvet 48, Half Moon Bay Wine and Cheese, and Barterra. Which stretch of the Peninsula gets your first pour?

item.title: San Francisco Peninsula Ice Cream and Gelato Shops
item.description: Eight Peninsula ice cream and gelato shops that put the chains to shame. A Palo Alto counter has scooped since 1956. A Redwood City spot spikes its signatu
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Peninsula Ice Cream and Gelato Shops

Eight Peninsula ice cream and gelato shops that put the chains to shame. A Palo Alto counter has scooped since 1956. A Redwood City spot spikes its signature scoop with bourbon. Bay Area summer, sorted.

Rick's Ice Cream — 3946 Middlefield Road, Palo Alto. A neighborhood fixture since 1956 that changed hands in 2026, so the 48 flavors now run from old school mint chip to black sesame crunch and Alphonso mango. Still small batch, still Guittard chocolate. Get the sampler spoons. @ricksicecream

The Penny Ice Creamery — 170 State Street, Los Altos. The Santa Cruz favorite made the trip over the hill, and everything is still built from scratch with local organic milk. Flavors change with the season, so the board is never quite the same twice. Ask what just went in fresh. @thepennyicecreamery

Gelataio — 644 Laurel Street, San Carlos. A tiny modern nook turning California seasonal fruit into Italian style gelato and sorbetto made in house. The fruit flavors taste like whatever is ripe that week. A cone here is the reason to wander Laurel Street after dinner. @gelataiosancarlos

Humphry Slocombe — 2077 Broadway, Redwood City. The San Francisco cult brand finally planted a scoop shop downtown, and yes, Secret Breakfast (bourbon and cornflake cookies) is the one to order. Adventurous flavors, zero apology. Open late enough for a post dinner detour. @humphryslocombe

SF Gelateria — 2621 Broadway, Redwood City. The owner went all the way to Gelato University in Italy, then came home to make farm to cone gelato with California fruit. Classics like stracciatella share the case with vegan sorbetti. A few doors from the late night crowd. @sfgelateria

Romolo's Cannoli and Spumoni — 81 37th Avenue, San Mateo. Three generations deep since 1968, and the cannoli are filled to order so the shell never goes soft. The gelato and spumoni case is the sleeper hit most people miss. Old San Mateo, no frills, all heart. @romoloscannoli

Preston's Candy and Ice Cream — 1170 Broadway, Burlingame. Scooping and hand dipping chocolates on Broadway since 1946, with the current owner still making the candy by hand. Get a scoop, then let them talk you into a box of buttercreams. The kind of counter that raised a few generations. @prestonscandy

Gulino Gelato — 330 Main Street, Half Moon Bay. The reward at the end of a foggy coast day, a proper gelato window right on Main Street. Dense, slow churned scoops that hit different after a walk on the beach. Two flavors in a cup beats one every time. @gulinogelato

Eight for a Peninsula sugar run: Rick's, The Penny, Gelataio, Humphry Slocombe, SF Gelateria, Romolo's, Preston's, and Gulino Gelato. Cone or cup, and which town are you starting in?

item.title: San Francisco Classic Diners
item.description: Six San Francisco diners that outlasted the trend cycle. Everyone lines up at one for the Swedish pancakes and skips the rest: a 1927 railroad dining car f
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Classic Diners

Six San Francisco diners that outlasted the trend cycle. Everyone lines up at one for the Swedish pancakes and skips the rest: a 1927 railroad dining car flipping burgers till 4am, a 24 hour counter a block off Union Square, a Dogpatch cafe baking its own beignets. Vinyl booths, flat top griddles, zero irony. The classics still standing.

Sears Fine Food — 439 Powell Street, San Francisco. Since 1938, right where the Powell Street cable car clangs past Union Square. The move is the world famous order of 18 little Swedish pancakes, still made from the original family recipe. Old school sit down service, zero pretension, a proper downtown anchor.

Pinecrest Diner — 401 Geary Street, San Francisco. A proper chrome and vinyl diner that has held this Union Square corner since 1969, open 24 hours Wednesday through Saturday. Come after the show for a fluffy omelet, a burger, or a milkshake at midnight when half the city is asleep. Steps from the theaters, no reservations. @pinecrestdiner

Grubstake — 1525 Pine Street, San Francisco. The whole diner is built inside a 1927 railroad dining car wedged into Lower Nob Hill, and it runs till 3am on weeknights, 4am Thursday through Saturday. Order off the Portuguese menu or grab a late burger with the after hours crowd. Guy Fieri put it on the map, but locals never left. @grubstakesf

Mel's Drive-In — 3355 Geary Boulevard, San Francisco. This Richmond District classic has been serving burgers, malts and all day breakfast since 1947, and yes, this is the American Graffiti one. Chrome, red booths and neon, the retro diner every generation of the family knows. A local institution you can just walk into. @melsdrivein

Lori's Diner — 500 Sutter Street, San Francisco. A full 1950s throwback a block up from Union Square, open every day with counter service and all day breakfast. Sparkling red booths, rock and roll on the speakers, Elvis and Marilyn on the walls. Around since 1986, an easy downtown pick when you just need a diner.

Just For You Cafe — 732 22nd Street, San Francisco. A Dogpatch neighborhood cafe since 1990, where the kitchen bakes everything on site and fries New Orleans style beignets to order under a snowstorm of powdered sugar. Big breakfasts, pancakes, house made breads, plus a counter and a parklet out front. The tucked away local favorite. @justforyoucafe

Six for a real San Francisco diner day: Sears, Pinecrest, Grubstake, Mel's, Lori's, and Just For You. Every one still open, still griddling. Which counter stool are you claiming first?

item.title: San Francisco Salvadoran Restaurants and Pupuserias
item.description: Six San Francisco pupuserias where the comal never really cools off. Everyone crowds the taqueria line and walks right past the Salvadoran counter next doo
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Salvadoran Restaurants and Pupuserias

Six San Francisco pupuserias where the comal never really cools off. Everyone crowds the taqueria line and walks right past the Salvadoran counter next door. That's where the loroco, curtido and revueltas actually live. A mostly walkable Mission to Excelsior crawl.

Balompie Cafe — 3349 18th St, San Francisco. The soccer jersey pupuseria locals defend like a home team, handmaking revueltas and chicharron since the neighborhood rent was cheaper. Come hungry, get the pupusa platter, add platanos with crema. Closed Monday and Tuesday, so plan around it. @balompiecafe.1

Panchita's — 3091 16th St, San Francisco. Family run since 1989 and open stupid late, till 2:30am on weekends. That makes it the move after a show. Pupusas fresh off the comal, curtido with real bite, zero frills. A true Mission pocket institution. @panchitaspupuseria

Sarita's Grill and Beer — 995 Valencia St, San Francisco. The Valencia anchor that pairs handmade pupusas with pinchos, cebiches and a cold beer, which the pupusa only counters cannot touch. Order a carne asada pupusa and the crazy corn. Open till 11 on weekends.

D'maize — 2778 24th St, San Francisco. A tucked away 24th St counter that does genuinely vegan friendly pupusas without losing the plot, masa taken seriously and catering on lock. Family run. Tuesday to Saturday, 9 to 3 only, so treat it as a breakfast and lunch move. @dmaizerestaurant

Reina's Restaurant — 5479 Mission St, San Francisco. Reina opened this Crocker Amazon room in 1991 and SFGate once called it the best pupusas around. Salvadoran and Mexican, breakfast through dinner, the established kind of place where regulars get greeted by name. @reinas_sf

Pupuseria Metapan — 4769 Mission St, San Francisco. Named for Lilian's hometown in El Salvador, this family kitchen reaches past pupusas into sopa de gallina india and sopa mariscada that outer Mission St regulars swear by. Open daily till 10:30, a proper sit down.

Six for the pupusa crawl: Balompie on 18th, Panchita's on 16th, Sarita's on Valencia, D'maize on 24th, then Reina's and Metapan down Mission St. Which one is your ride or die?

item.title: San Francisco Peninsula Diners and Breakfast Spots
item.description: Seven Peninsula breakfast spots that beat the chains on El Camino. The good stuff is older than the tech here: a 1923 creamery counter, a 1974 blueberry co
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Peninsula Diners and Breakfast Spots

Seven Peninsula breakfast spots that beat the chains on El Camino. The good stuff is older than the tech here: a 1923 creamery counter, a 1974 blueberry coffee cake, pancakes people cross town for. From Burlingame to Redwood City, this is where locals actually eat.

Stacks — 361 California Dr, Burlingame. The California Drive anchor for people who take pancakes seriously, farm eggs, real butter, portions built to share. Open 7 days from 8am, and the line moves faster than it looks. Walkable to the Avenue after.

Peninsula Creamery — 900 High St, Palo Alto. A dairy store and grill since 1923. That makes it older than most of the Peninsula's zip codes. Come for the thick milkshakes and a griddle breakfast at the counter. Locals just call it the Pen.

Cafe Borrone — 1010 El Camino Real, Menlo Park. Family run since 1979 with a tagline that says it all, because Europe is too far. The courtyard tables are where Menlo Park lingers over coffee and a fresh pastry. Breakfast and brunch daily except Tuesdays. @cafeborrone

Hobee's — 4224 El Camino Real, Palo Alto. A Silicon Valley institution since 1974, famous for a blueberry coffee cake so good they ship it nationwide, plus the cinnamon orange tea regulars swear by. Healthy leaning breakfasts, closed Mondays. @hobeesrestaurants

Coupa Cafe — 4748 El Camino Real, Los Altos. Family owned since 2004 and roasting its own beans, this is the Los Altos pick for a proper breakfast that comes with a serious cup of coffee. They lean on local farms, so the plate changes with the season. @coupacafe

Sweet Maple — 150 University Ave, Palo Alto. The downtown University Ave move when you want brunch that earns the hype, this is the home of Millionaire's Bacon, thick candied strips worth the walk. First come first served, open every day till 2:30. No reservations, so go early.

Mademoiselle Colette — 2401 Broadway, Redwood City. A little pocket of Paris on Broadway, the French bakery for a flaky croissant and a proper espresso before the day starts. Organic and seasonal, breakfast and lunch till 4pm. Save room for a tart. @mademoiselle_colette

Seven Peninsula breakfast tables worth setting an alarm for: Stacks in Burlingame, Peninsula Creamery, Hobee's and Sweet Maple in Palo Alto, Cafe Borrone in Menlo Park, Coupa in Los Altos, Mademoiselle Colette in Redwood City. Which counter gets your first weekend?

item.title: San Francisco Peninsula Italian Restaurants
item.description: Seven Peninsula Italian spots that go way past red sauce and a chain menu. We are talking Naples certified pizza, a Michelin Bib Gourmand pasta counter, an
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Peninsula Italian Restaurants

Seven Peninsula Italian spots that go way past red sauce and a chain menu. We are talking Naples certified pizza, a Michelin Bib Gourmand pasta counter, and a coastal room pouring Italian wine since 1993. From Redwood City to Half Moon Bay, this is the real list.

Donato Enoteca — 1041 Middlefield Road, Redwood City. The downtown Redwood City wine and pasta hub, contemporary Italian built around housemade pasta and one of the deepest Italian wine lists on the Peninsula. Shareable plates, happy hour on the patio, closed Mondays. @donatoenoteca

Terun — 448 California Ave, Palo Alto. Certified Verace Pizza Napoletana, meaning the wood fired pies follow the actual Naples rulebook, Italian tomatoes, naturally leavened dough, fresh mozzarella. Food Network ranked it among America's most authentic Neapolitan pizzerias. Patio on California Ave, open 7 days. @terunpizza

Pausa — 223 E 4th Ave, San Mateo. Downtown San Mateo's Michelin Bib Gourmand Italian, where chef Andrea Giuliani makes the pasta, bread, mozzarella and salumi in house. An all Italian wine list and a Spritz Hour in the parklet that locals guard like a secret. @pausasanmateo

Impasto — 661 El Camino Real, San Carlos. The San Carlos sister to Terun, another AVPN trained kitchen turning out Neapolitan pizza and fresh handmade pasta, with a few grains milled differently just to play. Family friendly, dinner nightly from 5. @impastosancarlos

Vina Enoteca — 700 Welch Road, Palo Alto. Tucked by Stanford, this is the special occasion Italian, house made pasta and a wine program deep enough to have its own club. There is even an attached Italian market, Vina Mercato, for the pasta and sauce to take home. Dinner Tuesday to Saturday. @vina_enoteca

Mezza Luna — 459 Prospect Way, Half Moon Bay. Worth the coast drive, southern Italian by the harbor since 1993, set in the historic 1906 Princeton Inn with a fireplace going. Housemade pasta and fresh local seafood, then a walk along the shore. Reserve on weekends. @mezzalunarestauranthmb

Italico — 341 California Ave, Palo Alto. A block down from Terun and a notch more grown up, elevated Italian and a serious wine bar on California Ave. Recognized by Michelin and Wine Spectator, and yes, there is a Cacio e Pepe Day every Wednesday and Sunday. @italico341

Seven Peninsula Italian rooms doing it right: Donato Enoteca in Redwood City, Terun and Vina Enoteca and Italico in Palo Alto, Pausa in San Mateo, Impasto in San Carlos, Mezza Luna in Half Moon Bay. Pizza night, pasta night, or a coast drive, which are you booking first?

item.title: San Francisco Marin Coffee Roasters and Cafes
item.description: Six Marin coffee stops worth planning a morning around, and the best part is the county roasts its own. Everyone grabs a freeway chain cup and misses the c
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Marin Coffee Roasters and Cafes

Six Marin coffee stops worth planning a morning around, and the best part is the county roasts its own. Everyone grabs a freeway chain cup and misses the cafes locals actually linger in, from a San Rafael roastery to a Tiburon espresso bar steps off the ferry. Here is a walkable pocket of the North Bay, a cortado at a time.

Equator Coffees — 115 Jordan Street, San Rafael. The certified B Corp roaster behind a lot of the good cups poured across Marin, based right here in San Rafael. Order their beans at a cafe anywhere in the county and this Jordan Street roastery is where they were actually roasted. Local coffee, roasted local. @equatorcoffees

M.H — Bread and Butter. 101 San Anselmo Avenue, San Anselmo. A small, established San Anselmo bakery cafe turning organic flour and local farm ingredients into some of the best morning pastry in Marin. Order a coffee and a warm bun, grab a sidewalk seat, and watch the avenue wake up. This corner is the walkable heart of town. @mhbreadbutter

Emporio Rulli — 464 Magnolia Ave, Larkspur. Gary and Jeannie Rulli have run this old world Italian pasticceria and caffe in downtown Larkspur since 1988. Order an espresso and a real Milanese pastry at the counter and you could be in Turin, not twenty minutes off the Golden Gate Bridge. A proper Larkspur institution. @emporiorulli

Caffe Acri — 1 Main Street, Tiburon. Italian inspired cafe on the corner of Main Street and Tiburon Boulevard, steps from the ferry landing, pouring elevated coffee since 2003. Grab a cappuccino and a pastry, take a seat by the water, and watch the boats come in off the bay. There is live piano on weekend nights if you linger. @caffe_acri

Comforts — 335 San Anselmo Ave, San Anselmo. The Miwa family opened this cafe and marketplace in 1986, and the second generation runs it now. That's why it still feels like the whole town's kitchen. Sit down for weekend brunch or grab a coffee and something from the deli case on your way through. A San Anselmo anchor, generations deep. @comfortscafe

Cafe del Soul — 247 Shoreline Highway, Mill Valley. A counter service organic cafe out at Tam Junction where everything is made to order and, they will tell you, made with love. Order a coffee and a bowl, and you have found the mellow, local Mill Valley the guidebooks skip. Easy, tucked away, no fuss. @cafedelsoul

Six for your Marin coffee run: Equator Coffees, M.H. Bread and Butter, Emporio Rulli, Caffe Acri, Comforts, and Cafe del Soul. From a San Rafael roastery to a Tiburon espresso steps off the ferry, that is the whole county in a cup. Which one are you starting with?

item.title: San Francisco Peninsula Sushi Restaurants
item.description: Five Peninsula sushi spots worth crossing town for, and the best ones are not chasing a scene. A tiny omakase counter in San Mateo, a bar that has been sli
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Peninsula Sushi Restaurants

Five Peninsula sushi spots worth crossing town for, and the best ones are not chasing a scene. A tiny omakase counter in San Mateo, a bar that has been slicing since 1988, a Palo Alto institution with real tatami rooms. Skip the mall conveyor belts. The Peninsula sushi run the locals keep quiet.

Sushi Edomata — 38 E 25th Ave, San Mateo. The old Sushi Sam's crew carrying a San Mateo counter that has been going since 1988. Blackboard specials change with whatever came in fresh that morning, so trust the chef and order what he points at. Get there early, this stretch fills up and they do not rush the rice.

Wakuriya — 115 De Anza Blvd, San Mateo. A tiny De Anza strip mall hides one of the Bay's most quietly serious Japanese counters, a single chef and a seasonal menu worth the ceremony. Reservations open a month ahead to the day and vanish fast, so set a reminder and call the second the window opens. A special occasion anchor.

Sakae Sushi — 243 California Dr, Burlingame. A Burlingame fixture since 1995, right in the walkable California Drive pocket, now under new ownership with the original head chef still on the rice. Come for the Hokkaido uni and the izakaya plates you will not find on the sushi menu. Sit at the bar and let them steer. @sakaesushi_burlingame

Sushi Tomo — 201 University Ave, Palo Alto. The value pick, and a genuinely fun one, parked on downtown University Avenue with little sushi boats floating the counter. Regulars swear by the Crazy Horse roll and the oversized hand rolls for the price. Grab a walkable lunch, then work it off window shopping.

Fuki Sushi — 4119 El Camino Real, Palo Alto. A Palo Alto institution with private tatami rooms, the kind of established spot families book for the big birthdays. Kick off your shoes, order the sushi and a round from the deep sake list, and settle in. Reservations are the move on weekends, the tatami rooms go first.

Five for your Peninsula sushi list: Edomata and Wakuriya in San Mateo, Sakae in Burlingame, Sushi Tomo and Fuki in Palo Alto. Omakase splurge or downtown sushi boats, which way are you leaning first?

item.title: San Francisco Marin Italian Restaurants
item.description: Six Marin Italian kitchens worth crossing the bridge for, where the pasta is still rolled by hand and most of the room is regulars, not tourists. Everyone
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Marin Italian Restaurants

Six Marin Italian kitchens worth crossing the bridge for, where the pasta is still rolled by hand and most of the room is regulars, not tourists. Everyone lines up in North Beach and drives right past the North Bay. From a Sausalito harbor patio to Fairfax wine poured straight from the barrel, here is the lineup locals actually book.

Poggio Trattoria — 777 Bridgeway, Sausalito. The harbor view patio gets the postcard, but the housemade pasta and wood fired everything are why it has held down this Bridgeway corner since 2003. Northern Italian, and one of the few spots doing a real sit down breakfast on the water. Come hungry, stay a while. @poggiotrattoria

Piazza D'Angelo — 22 Miller Avenue, Mill Valley. It anchors the downtown plaza, so grab a bar seat and watch the regulars roll in by name. Southern Italian, wood fired pizzas and fresh pasta, but the tiramisu is the one people quietly drive over for. Walkable to the whole village after. @piazzadangelo

Il Davide — 901 A Street, San Rafael. Downtown San Rafael's established Italian since 1995, the kind of room families book for weddings and weeknights alike. Order the truffle ravioli and grab the patio on a cool Marin night. Closed Mondays, so plan around it. @ildavidesanrafaelca

Piatti — 625 Redwood Highway, Mill Valley. The pasta is rolled and cut by hand every morning, and the patio looks straight at Mt. Tamalpais. A neighborhood trattoria since 1987 that just took Best Happy Hour in Marin, so come at 3 for the bar menu and the view. @piattimillvalley

Servino — 114 Main Street, Tiburon. Back on Tiburon's historic Ark Row where the family started in 1977, now with an Enoteca wine bar next door in the old Yellow Ark and a garden patio out back. Southern Italian plates and an all Italian wine list worth getting lost in. Walk it off along Main after. @servino_tiburon

Fradelizio's — 35 Broadway Blvd, Fairfax. Funky, friendly, and unmistakably Fairfax, with homemade organic pasta and gnocchi and six wines poured straight from the barrel, not the bottle. A downtown fixture for 20 plus years. Closed Tuesday and Wednesday, so aim for a weekend table. @fradeliziosinfairfax

Six for the Marin Italian shortlist: Poggio on the Sausalito water, Piazza D'Angelo and Piatti in Mill Valley, Il Davide in San Rafael, Servino in Tiburon, Fradelizio's in Fairfax. Handmade pasta, harbor patios, wine from the barrel. Which North Bay table are you booking first?

item.title: San Francisco Marin Pizza
item.description: Five Marin pizzas that hold their own against any slice in the city, most of them wood fired with the mozzarella pulled in house that morning. From a Sausa
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Marin Pizza

Five Marin pizzas that hold their own against any slice in the city, most of them wood fired with the mozzarella pulled in house that morning. From a Sausalito fire pit on the water to a Mill Valley counter slinging pies since 1972, this is the North Bay pizza run locals keep on rotation.

Pizzalina — 914 Sir Francis Drake Boulevard, San Anselmo. Tucked into the Red Hill center, this is the neighborhood wood fired spot locals default to, hand stretched dough, Bianco di Napoli tomatoes, and mozzarella made in house. It lands on Bay Area best pizza lists for a reason. Ask about the pie of the month. @eatpizzalina

Bar Bocce — 1250 Bridgeway, Sausalito. Wood fired pies on a little back patio right on the water, with a fire pit and some of the best sunset seats in town. It runs first come with a waitlist, so put your name in and grab a drink while the harbor does its thing. Pure Sausalito hang.

Pizzeria Picco — 316 Magnolia Ave, Larkspur. A downtown Larkspur favorite doing traditional Neapolitan thin crust in a wood burning oven, mozzarella pulled fresh every day. Get the Marin pizza, then close it out with Double 8 Dairy soft serve. Small spot, big following, so time it. @restaurantpicco

Boca Pizzeria — 1544 Redwood Highway, Corte Madera. Rome meets Emilia Romagna pizzeria firing 12 inch Neapolitan pies in a 900 degree oven, two minutes flat, on long fermented Caputo dough with San Marzano tomatoes. Indoor or patio, seven days a week, and an easy family move on a weeknight. @bocapizzeria

Stefano's Pizza — 11 East Blithedale Ave, Mill Valley. The local classic since 1972, the solar powered corner that has slung something like ten million pies to Marin kids, teams, and late Friday nights. Not fancy, just the hometown standard for delivery and takeout. Grab a pie for the couch. @stefanos.pizza

Five for the Marin pizza rotation: Pizzalina in San Anselmo, Bar Bocce on the Sausalito water, Pizzeria Picco in Larkspur, Boca in Corte Madera, Stefano's in Mill Valley. Wood fired, harbor side, or straight to the couch. Which one is tonight?

item.title: San Francisco Peninsula Indian Restaurants
item.description: Eight Peninsula Indian restaurants worth crossing town for, and four have Michelin recognition. Most people default to the nearest strip mall tikka masala
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Peninsula Indian Restaurants

Eight Peninsula Indian restaurants worth crossing town for, and four have Michelin recognition. Most people default to the nearest strip mall tikka masala and miss the coastal South Indian cooking, the daal simmered overnight, the halal Memoni samosa a town over. Burlingame down to Los Altos, here is the run locals keep quiet.

Rasa — 209 Park Rd, Burlingame. The Peninsula's Michelin rated South Indian room, where dosa comes butter paper crisp and seafood steams in banana leaf. Coastal Kerala cooking that regulars will tell you is worth the reservation. Order the vada pav sliders to start. @rasa_indian

Rasoi — 1425 Burlingame Ave, Burlingame. The Aslam family cooks Northern Indian and Pakistani off a lounge menu right on Burlingame Ave, so the tandoor and the cocktails share a room. Chef Asif's kebabs are the anchor here. Come hungry and let the table order for you. @rasoiburlingame

Curry and Kabab — 1923 S El Camino Real, San Mateo. Chef Mandy's North Indian curries and tandoori are the draw, but the sleeper order is the Indian pizza, naan dough under spiced toppings. Casual, quick, open till 10 daily. Grab the soya chaap if you see it. @eatcurrykabab

Tabla — 450 S Norfolk St, San Mateo. A neighborhood standby for Hyderabadi biryani and dosa, tucked off Norfolk in a room that fills up fast at lunch. The kitchen came up through bigger houses and it shows in the rice. Go for the biryani and a paneer butter masala. @tablaindiansm

Saffron — 1143 San Carlos Ave, San Carlos. A Michelin listed kitchen giving San Carlos daal makhani cooked low for a full day and butter chicken done Old Delhi style. There is a 100 year communal table built for long dinners. Bring people and share the chef's platters. @saffron_restaurants

Dosa Point — 840 Willow Rd, Menlo Park. A North and South Indian spot on Willow that runs live dosa parties, the batter crisping to order in front of you. This is the move when you want a dosa fix without the Palo Alto wait. Bring a group and try the specialty dosas.

Zareen's — 365 S California Ave, Palo Alto. The Michelin Guide Pakistani Indian counter just off the California Ave scene, famous for chicken Memoni samosas and shami kebabs from a recipe only a handful of grandmothers know. Halal, always packed, worth the line. Get the samosas first. @zareensrestaurant

Aurum — 132 State St, Los Altos. Downtown Los Altos' contemporary Indian room, Michelin recommended five years running, plating lamb chops and gulab jamun cheesecake under a hand painted mural. This is the special occasion end of the list. Book ahead and order the tasting. @aurumlosaltos

Eight for the Peninsula Indian short list: Rasa and Rasoi in Burlingame, Curry and Kabab and Tabla in San Mateo, Saffron in San Carlos, Dosa Point in Menlo Park, Zareen's in Palo Alto, Aurum in Los Altos. Which one are you booking first?

item.title: San Francisco Peninsula Thai Restaurants
item.description: Eight Peninsula Thai kitchens that go past pad thai, strung down El Camino from South San Francisco to Mountain View. Most people reorder the same noodle p
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Peninsula Thai Restaurants

Eight Peninsula Thai kitchens that go past pad thai, strung down El Camino from South San Francisco to Mountain View. Most people reorder the same noodle plate and never reach the Isan larb, the pumpkin curry, the crispy pork belly krapow. One just took Best Thai in Palo Alto again this year. Here is the run locals actually save.

Thai Satay — 265 Grand Ave, South San Francisco. On the corner of Grand and Linden, this is the South City Thai anchor the Genentech crowd runs on, open daily till 9. The pad kee mao and tom yum goong carry real heat, not the dialed back kind. Start with the namesake satay. @thaisatayssf

New Thai Elephant — 200 S B St, San Mateo. A small family run room downtown where regulars swear by the kao gra prow, holy basil over rice with a fried egg on top. Nothing fancy here, just steady honest Thai cooking off B Street. Order it spicy and add the egg.

Chai Yo Thai — 2116 S El Camino Real, San Mateo. Corner spot near Highway 92 that leans vegetarian friendly and turns out a tom kha soup people cross town for. Casual, family run, easy takeout on a weeknight. Ask about the ginger noodles if you like it mild.

Spoon and Fork — 1480 El Camino Real, Belmont. A warm little Belmont room that recently added Thai brunch, so it is holy basil pork belly at lunch and Monkey Morning pancakes earlier. Closed Tuesdays. The crispy pork belly pad krapow is the one to beat. @spoonandforkbelmont

Isarn Garden — 1050 El Camino Real, San Carlos. Named for Thailand's northeast, so this is your Peninsula stop for real Isan cooking, som tum and larb and sticky rice done properly. A quiet San Carlos storefront that overdelivers. Get the papaya salad Thai spicy.

Bangkok Bay — 825 El Camino Real, Redwood City. A Redwood City neighborhood favorite for pumpkin curry and drunken noodles, the kind of place picky kids and heat seekers both leave happy. Order direct, they would rather skip the delivery apps. Try the pumpkin curry.

Lotus Thai Bistro — 425 California Ave, Palo Alto. Family run on the California Ave stretch and voted Palo Alto Weekly's Best Thai in 2025 and 2026, so the locals have settled that debate. The weekday lunch specials are the smart move. Order online direct and skip the wait. @lotusthaibistro

Amarin Thai — 147 Castro St, Mountain View. A downtown Castro Street mainstay voted the Mountain View Voice's Best Thai just about every year since 1999, with generations of family recipes from curry to BBQ pork shoulder. An easy anchor on the south end of this list. Grab a table and share family style. @amarin_thai_cuisine

Eight for the Peninsula Thai short list: Thai Satay in South City, New Thai Elephant and Chai Yo in San Mateo, Spoon and Fork in Belmont, Isarn Garden in San Carlos, Bangkok Bay in Redwood City, Lotus in Palo Alto, Amarin in Mountain View. Which one is dinner tonight?

item.title: San Francisco Peninsula Burger Joints
item.description: Five Peninsula burgers worth crossing town for, picked by locals not apps. From a 1923 Palo Alto soda fountain to a redwood roadhouse above Woodside, these
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Peninsula Burger Joints

Five Peninsula burgers worth crossing town for, picked by locals not apps. From a 1923 Palo Alto soda fountain to a redwood roadhouse above Woodside, these are the keepers, zero chains. The next slow Peninsula Saturday, this is the run.

Peninsula Creamery — 900 High Street, Palo Alto. Same family since 1923, and the cheeseburger with a hand spun malt still tastes like the Palo Alto that existed before the venture money moved in. Grab a stool at the counter, watch downtown stroll past, and you will see why locals call it the Pen. An established landmark that never chased a trend.

Dutch Goose — 3567 Alameda de las Pulgas, Menlo Park. Peanut shells underfoot, decades of community photos on the walls, an arcade in the corner, and burgers and brews since 1966. This is the unfussy Menlo Park locals quietly guard, tucked on the Alameda away from the Sand Hill polish. Bring quarters, bring a crew, skip the white tablecloth.

Half Moon Bay Brewing Company — 390 Capistrano Road, Half Moon Bay. Order a creative burger and a beer brewed steps from Pillar Point Harbor, then take the patio while the fog rolls over the boats. It has anchored this stretch of coast since 2000, equal parts local hangout and traveler find. Worth the drive over the hill when the city gets loud. @hmbbrewingco

Town — 716 Laurel Street, San Carlos. Yes it is a proper steakhouse in the historic Tivoli building, but the sleeper order is the Filet Smash Burger, crusty edged and easy to miss on a menu full of hand cut steaks. Walkable Laurel Street is the heart of San Carlos, so park once and make a night of it. No reservations, so go early. @townsancarlos

Alice's Restaurant — 17288 Skyline Boulevard, Woodside. Where Skyline meets Woodside Road up in the redwoods, bikers and Ferraris and hikers all pull in for a gourmet burger and sweet potato fries. Grab a seat on the patio, split a slice of homemade pie, and take in the best people watching on the Peninsula. A true crossroads with real character. @aliceswoodside

Five for your next Peninsula burger run: Peninsula Creamery in Palo Alto, Dutch Goose in Menlo Park, Half Moon Bay Brewing on the coast, Town in San Carlos, and Alice's above Woodside. Which is your Peninsula move?

item.title: San Francisco Peninsula Bakeries
item.description: Six Peninsula bakeries worth setting an alarm for, from a 1977 Danish institution to a naturally leavened newcomer with a weekend line out the door. No gro
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Peninsula Bakeries

Six Peninsula bakeries worth setting an alarm for, from a 1977 Danish institution to a naturally leavened newcomer with a weekend line out the door. No grocery store croissants here, just the real local spots that make the Peninsula smell like butter on a Saturday.

Copenhagen Bakery and Cafe — 1216 Burlingame Avenue, Burlingame. A Danish anchor on the Avenue since 1977, famous for the Princess Cake, a dome of marzipan and cream people cross the county to fetch. Slide in for a pastry and coffee, then walk it off on Burlingame Ave. The kind of established spot a neighborhood is lucky to keep. @copenhagen_bakery_and_cafe

Backhaus — 32 3rd Avenue, San Mateo. The naturally leavened darling of downtown San Mateo, where the weekend line forms early for mini chocolate sourdough and a Speck and Egg breakfast bowl baked right inside croissant dough. Go early, then wander the walkable 3rd Avenue pocket with a coffee in hand. @backhausbread

Woodside Bakery and Cafe — 325 Sharon Park Drive, Menlo Park. One of the last true European bakeries around, family run since 1981 and tucked into Sharon Heights off Sand Hill Road. This is old school done right, napoleons, fresh fruit tarts, cannoli, and a mile high apple pie. Post up with a cappuccino and a slice and settle in.

La Biscotteria — 2747 El Camino Real, Redwood City. A family run Italian bakery baking biscotti by hand since 1989, from anise to chocolate hazelnut, plus amaretti, panettone, and a Neapolitan Easter pie worth planning around. A genuine Peninsula hidden gem just minutes from campus. Grab a box, dip one in coffee, thank me later. @labiscotteria2747

Manresa Bread — 271 State Street, Los Altos. The levain, the kouign amann, the pain au chocolat, all so good they will quietly ruin grocery store bread for you. The shop sits right in walkable downtown Los Altos, so pair a warm croissant with a slow stroll down State Street. Come before noon, the good stuff goes fast. @manresabread

Mademoiselle Colette — 499 Lytton Avenue, Palo Alto. A little slice of Paris a block off University, all buttery croissants, glossy fruit tarts, and jewel box entremets in a cozy cafe built for lingering. Come for breakfast, stay through an afternoon coffee, and let downtown Palo Alto drift past the window. A polished community favorite. @mademoiselle_colette

Six for your Peninsula sweet tooth: Copenhagen in Burlingame, Backhaus in San Mateo, Woodside Bakery in Menlo Park, La Biscotteria in Redwood City, Manresa Bread in Los Altos, and Mademoiselle Colette in Palo Alto. Which local bakery do I have to add next?

item.title: San Francisco German and Central European Restaurants
item.description: Eight German and Central European tables worth staying in San Francisco for. Everyone assumes you leave the city for a real schnitzel or a proper boot of p
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco German and Central European Restaurants

Eight German and Central European tables worth staying in San Francisco for. Everyone assumes you leave the city for a real schnitzel or a proper boot of pilsner. You do not. From a Bavarian beer hall that outlived the 1906 quake to a Swiss chalet on Van Ness, the whole spread is here, FiDi to Fort Mason to the Mission. Where to start.

Suppenkuche — 525 Laguna St, San Francisco. The Hayes Valley anchor that opened in 1993 when nobody wanted the block, and still packs long communal tables for spaetzle, schnitzel and a wall of German taps. Go with a group, order the potato pancakes, make friends with strangers. @suppenkuchesf

Schroeder's — 240 Front St, San Francisco. Founded 1893, rebuilt after the 1906 fire, and still the Financial District's Bavarian beer hall, all dark wood, communal benches and liter steins. Duck in for the pork schnitzel and a cold German lager when downtown empties out. It has more character than anything on the block.

Biergarten — 424 Octavia St, San Francisco. Suppenkuche's little outdoor sibling, a gravel pocket in Hayes Valley with picnic tables, pretzels the size of your head and German beer poured till the fog rolls in. Grab a bratwurst, claim a bench, stay for one more. It is the move on a rare sunny afternoon. @biergarten_sf

Radhaus — 2 Marina Blvd, Building A, San Francisco. Tucked inside Fort Mason with a 30 foot bar and Golden Gate views, this Alpine beer hall does doppelbock, giant pretzels and proper bratwurst under one very handsome roof. Come at golden hour, get the sausage sampler, watch the bridge light up. @radhaus_sf

Rosamunde Sausage Grill — 2832 Mission St, San Francisco. A Mission fixture since 1998, this tiny German grill turns out currywurst, bratwurst and a rotating vegan sausage next to a serious craft beer list. Tuesday trivia gets loud and local. Grab a duck sausage and a Schneider Weisse and post up.

Paprika — 3324 24th St, San Francisco. The Mission's little taste of Prague and Budapest, family run since 2013, with a two time Michelin recommended pork goulash and Czech pilsner served in glass boots. Vegan options too. Bring people, order the goulash and a boot, stay for the live Balkan nights. @paprika_sf_restaurant

Matterhorn — 2323 Van Ness Ave, San Francisco. A full Swiss chalet hiding on Van Ness, wood beams and all, built around bubbling pots of cheese and chocolate fondue. This is a cold foggy night in edible form. Bring your person, order the Emmentaler fondue, take your time with the long forks. @matterhornsf

Europa Wine Bar and Kitchen — 4318 California St, San Francisco. A cozy Inner Richmond corner doing Eastern and Central European comfort food, schnitzel, pierogi and goulash, paired with rare Old World wines you will not find elsewhere. Low light, small room, great for a date. Go early, order the pierogi, let them pick the wine.

Eight for a German and Central European crawl across San Francisco: Suppenkuche, Schroeder's, Biergarten, Radhaus, Rosamunde, Paprika, Matterhorn, Europa. Beer halls, sausage grills, fondue and goulash, no bridge required. Which one are you starting on?

item.title: San Francisco Himalayan and Nepalese Restaurants
item.description: Five Himalayan and Nepalese tables that prove San Francisco does momos as well as any city. Everyone races to the same Indian spots and walks right past th
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Himalayan and Nepalese Restaurants

Five Himalayan and Nepalese tables that prove San Francisco does momos as well as any city. Everyone races to the same Indian spots and walks right past the Nepali kitchens quietly steaming dumplings a few doors down. The city's first Nepalese restaurant opened here back in 2003, and the scene only got better. Start here.

Little Nepal — 925 Cortland Ave, San Francisco. The one that started it all, San Francisco's first Nepalese restaurant, anchoring Bernal's walkable Cortland strip since 2003. White tablecloths, warm welcome, momos and clay oven kukhura that regulars have loved for two decades. Book ahead on weekends, it is small.

Bini's Kitchen — 1001 Howard St, San Francisco. Chef Binita Pradhan came up through La Cocina and became the city's unofficial queen of momos, hand folding thousands of turkey and lamb dumplings a week in this bright SoMa room. Get the Khana plate and the famous tomato timur sauce. Lunch is the move. @bini_kitchen

Dancing Yak — 280 Valencia St, San Francisco. Nepali comfort food meets a real cocktail bar on lower Valencia, open since 2018 and built for a night out. Momos, sizzling platters and craft drinks under one roof in one of the city's most walkable pockets. Come hungry, share the momo sampler, stay for happy hour. @dancingyaksf_

Cuisine of Nepal — 3486 Mission St, San Francisco. A warm little room on the Mission stretch below Bernal, bringing Himalayan comfort to the table, momos, dal bhat and steaming bowls of thukpa built for a cold night. Featured on Check, Please Bay Area, and vegan friendly. Open evenings Tuesday through Sunday, so plan dinner and get the jhol momo. @cuisineofnepal

Sunset Indian Cuisine — 642 Irving St, San Francisco. Where the Inner Sunset goes for Himalayan and Indian comfort near Golden Gate Park, momos and tandoori and curry served generously and late. A dependable neighborhood table when the fog settles in over Irving. Go with a crew, order across the menu, take the leftovers home.

Five for a Himalayan and Nepalese run through San Francisco: Little Nepal, Bini's Kitchen, Dancing Yak, Cuisine of Nepal, Sunset Indian Cuisine. From the city's first Nepali dining room to late night momos in the Sunset, the dumplings travel well. Who makes your favorite momo?

item.title: San Francisco Marin Taquerias and Mexican
item.description: Eight Marin taquerias and Mexican kitchens locals keep in rotation, from a Sausalito waterfront table to a Novato cantina running to 2am on weekends. Most
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Marin Taquerias and Mexican

Eight Marin taquerias and Mexican kitchens locals keep in rotation, from a Sausalito waterfront table to a Novato cantina running to 2am on weekends. Most visitors grab a taco and call it. You want the whole map.

Los Moles — 912 Lincoln Ave, San Rafael. Chef Lito Saldana makes eight different moles here, poblano to a pineapple one, each built on family recipes and thirty plus ingredients. The weekend buffet is the local move, and the beer list leans on breweries a few blocks away. Come hungry, wear the forgiving pants. @losmoles

Playa — 41 Throckmorton Ave, Mill Valley. Contemporary Mexican that pulled a Michelin Bib Gourmand, sitting a few doors from the Sequoia theater. Club Cuatro happy hour runs Tuesday through Friday from 4, and Taco Tuesday drops street tacos to a few bucks a piece. Angle for the back deck if the fog lifts. @playamillvalley

Mas Masa — 31 Bolinas Road, Fairfax. They nixtamalize corn and press masa fresh daily, so the tortillas taste like their own food group. Cali Mexican, plenty for vegans, no reservations, first come first served on the little indoor outdoor patio. Downtown Fairfax parking is a rumor, so walk over if you can. @eatmasmasa

Marinitas — 218 Sir Francis Drake Blvd, San Anselmo. Guacamole mashed to order, tacos on house made corn tortillas, and a tequila and mezcal list that goes deep. It anchors downtown San Anselmo, half restaurant and half cantina, the back end turning into music and dancing as the night runs on. Post up at the bar for a Casa Margarita. @marinitas_marin

Flores — 301 Corte Madera Town Center, Corte Madera. The San Francisco favorite carried its traditional plates north, mole poblano, birria enchiladas, and a tequila and mezcal flight menu that reads like a novel. Tucked into the shopping center and far better than that address suggests. Happy hour starts at 3. @flores_sf

Joe's Taco Lounge and Salsaria — 382 Miller Ave, Mill Valley. The scrappy Mill Valley classic, all Mexican comfort food and street cart favorites, the kind of counter regulars keep on speed dial. Snag a seat on the front deck and work through a plate of tacos. Kitchen tends to close around nine, so do not dawdle.

Copita — 739 Bridgeway, Sausalito. Upscale, agave forward Mexican right on the Sausalito waterfront, a tequileria where the cocktail list runs as long as the food menu. Weekend brunch goes 11 to 2, prime real estate for watching the ferry crowd spill off Bridgeway. Grab a table and order a mezcal you cannot pronounce. @copitasausalito

Maya Palenque — 349 Enfrente Road, Novato. The Novato cantina that refuses to call it a night, kitchen and bar open to midnight most nights and 2am Thursday through Saturday. A DJ takes Saturdays, karaoke lands on Thursdays, happy hour weekdays from 2. When the rest of Marin rolls up the sidewalks, this is where you land.

Eight for the Marin Mexican rotation: Los Moles, Playa, Mas Masa, Marinitas, Flores, Joe's Taco Lounge, Copita, and Maya Palenque. Which Marin spot got left off that you would go to bat for?

item.title: San Francisco Marin Seafood On the Water
item.description: Seven Marin seafood spots right on the water, the ones locals drive to instead of fighting the crowds at Fisherman's Wharf. Think Sausalito decks over the
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Marin Seafood On the Water

Seven Marin seafood spots right on the water, the ones locals drive to instead of fighting the crowds at Fisherman's Wharf. Think Sausalito decks over the bay, Tomales oyster shacks, and a Tiburon classic worth the wait. Every stop comes with a view and a jacket worthy breeze off the water. Go on the next clear Saturday.

Sam's Anchor Cafe — 27 Main Street, Tiburon. The waterfront deck is the whole point, on a clear day you are staring straight at Angel Island, Alcatraz and the city skyline. They take reservations inside but never on the deck, so the move is to show up early and dig in. Weekend brunch here is a proper Bay Area institution. Take the ferry over from the city and skip the parking hunt. @sams_cafe

Fish — 350 Harbor Drive, Sausalito. A no frills waterfront spot on the harbor, order at the counter and grab a picnic bench right by the boats. The whole operation is dead serious about sustainable, local catch, and yes, the pup is welcome on the patio. It sits past the ferry landing, so it stays a locals find instead of a tourist stop. Come hungry and come early. @fishrestaurantsausalito

Scoma's of Sausalito — 588 Bridgeway, Sausalito. The dressier pick, a longtime waterfront landmark sitting right over the bay with unobstructed views back at the city. This is the spot for taking the parents or marking an occasion, think whole Dungeness crab, wild king salmon, and petrale sole done right. Book ahead and ask for a window table, it is worth the call. @scomassausalito

Barrel House Tavern — 660 Bridgeway, Sausalito. Built inside the old ferry terminal that carried folks to the city before the Golden Gate existed, so the character comes free. The back patio opens right onto the bay with the skyline dead ahead. Half a dozen oysters run twelve bucks at happy hour. That's the smart way in. Time your table for sunset and do not rush it. @barrelhousetavern

Hog Island, The Boat Oyster Bar — 20215 Shoreline Highway, Marshall. This is oyster country, a working farm on Tomales Bay where the outdoor tables sit feet from the water the oysters are grown in. Reserve Friday through Monday for the full cafe, or roll up Thursday to shuck your own by the dozen. Bring layers and something cold to drink. Summer reservations vanish fast, plan ahead. @hogislandoysterco

Nick's Cove — 23240 Highway One, Marshall. Further up the shoreline, all weathered wood charm with decks built right over Tomales Bay. The BBQ oysters are the order here, SFGate named them one of the best things they ate back in 2023. There are twelve cottages too, handy when the drive home feels long. Post oyster naps are undefeated. @nickscove

Saltwater Oyster Depot — 12781 Sir Francis Drake Boulevard, Inverness. The one that is a block off the bay, not over it, and it still earns a spot, a tiny Inverness oyster bar and wine shop out toward Point Reyes. They shuck oysters minutes after they leave Tomales Bay and pour regional wine straight from the tap. Weekends run a la carte, weeknights a prix fixe. Make it the reward at the end of the drive.

Seven for Marin seafood on the water: Sam's Anchor in Tiburon, Fish, Scoma's and Barrel House on the Sausalito waterfront, then Hog Island, Nick's Cove and Saltwater out on Tomales Bay. White tablecloths or a paper tray of oysters, the whole coastline delivers. Which end are you starting from, Sausalito or the oyster shacks?

item.title: San Francisco Marin Breakfast and Brunch
item.description: Seven Marin breakfast and brunch spots the locals drive to, from a 100 year old Tiburon deck on the bay to a Point Reyes room that has been flipping eggs s
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Marin Breakfast and Brunch

Seven Marin breakfast and brunch spots the locals drive to, from a 100 year old Tiburon deck on the bay to a Point Reyes room that has been flipping eggs since 1964. Tourists idle on the Sausalito boardwalk. You are going to eat better. Weekends fill fast, so go early.

Sam's Anchor Cafe — 27 Main St, Tiburon. The waterfront deck stares straight at Angel Island, Alcatraz and the city skyline, and weekend brunch here has been a Bay Area ritual for a century. They do not take reservations for the deck, so the wait is the cover charge for that view. Get there before the ferry crowd, put your name in, and settle in with something cold. @sams_cafe

Le Garage Bistro — 85 Liberty Ship Way, Sausalito. A little French place tucked into a literal old garage down by the Schoonmaker boats, roll up door thrown open to the water. Weekend brunch runs 10 to 2:30, and on weekday mornings it is coffee and croissants. It is tiny, so book ahead or plan to circle the lot a few times. The waterfront corner people picture when they say they want to move to Marin. @le_garage_bistro

Copita — 739 Bridgeway, Sausalito. Right on the main drag, a bright Mexican tequileria where weekend brunch runs 11 to 2 and the agave list is longer than most wine menus in town. Handmade tortillas, fresh ceviche, a margarita that makes the walk back uphill feel optional. Snag a sidewalk table and watch Bridgeway do its Sunday parade. @copitasausalito

Flour Craft Bakery — 702 San Anselmo Ave, San Anselmo. An all gluten free bakery and cafe that converts skeptics daily, nobody at the table will guess the scones and focaccia skip the wheat. Come for weekend brunch and plant forward plates, stay for a loaf to take home. Open Tuesday through Sunday till 3, with a second shop in the Mill Valley Lumber Yard if you are on the other side of the hill. @flourcraft

Toast — 5800 Nave Dr, Novato. North Marin's reliable all day brunch, an airy 200 seat room at Hamilton with a brick pizza oven, ponds out front and, the real North Bay luxury, a parking lot that is not a bloodsport. Order the eggs Benedict, split a mimosa flight, and let the kids wander by the water. Weekends it opens at 8, and yes, there is a wait by 9:30.

Parkside Cafe — 43 Arenal Ave, Stinson Beach. A block from the sand, this is the West Marin breakfast that makes the winding drive over the hill worth it. The espresso cart opens at 6 for the surf and hike crowd, the cafe does real breakfast from 7:30, and the onsite bakery means the pastries are still warm. Fuel up here before Mount Tam, or limp in after for the 1949 snack bar burger. @parksidecafestinsonbeach

Station House Cafe — 11285 Highway 1, Point Reyes Station. The West Marin classic since 1964, now back on its original Main and 3rd corner after a move, doing farm to table brunch weekends from 10 to 3. This is the fuel stop before the Point Reyes lighthouse, the oyster farms and the elk, so eat well. One warning worth its own post, they are closed Wednesdays, so plan the drive around it. @stationhousecafe

Seven for a Marin brunch that beats the SF wait: Sam's deck in Tiburon, Le Garage and Copita on the Sausalito water, Flour Craft in San Anselmo, Toast in Novato, Parkside at Stinson, Station House in Point Reyes. Which one is your Sunday, and what did I leave off?
