item.title: San Francisco Peninsula Vietnamese and Pho
item.description: Six Peninsula Vietnamese and pho spots where the broth earns the drive, Daly City down to Redwood City. None of them need a bridge, a reservation, or a tre
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Peninsula Vietnamese and Pho

Six Peninsula Vietnamese and pho spots where the broth earns the drive, Daly City down to Redwood City. None of them need a bridge, a reservation, or a trendy zip code, a spoon and an appetite. Tourists chase the SF names while the Peninsula quietly wins the broth. Going north to south.

Kevin's Noodle House — 85 Southgate Ave, Daly City. Still flying under its old name Pho Huynh Hiep, this is the number three in a family that has fed foggy Daly City for years. Come for the beef pho, stay because the broth tastes like somebody's grandmother is watching the pot. The Southgate strip will not win design awards, but parking is free and the bowls are enormous.

Ben Tre Vietnamese Homestyle Cuisine — 398 Grand Ave, South San Francisco. Grand Ave is having a quiet restaurant renaissance, and Ben Tre is the anchor everyone forgets to name. Homestyle is the operative word here, clay pot, lemongrass, the kind of shaking beef you plan a Tuesday around. Bright, unfussy room right on the main drag. @bentrerestaurant

Pho de Nguyen — 586A San Mateo Ave, San Bruno. Chef Phong's oxtail pho is the reason San Bruno's old downtown strip smells like star anise by 11am. Order the bun bo hue if you like a little lemongrass fire with lunch. They will cater a party of seventy, though you will want that first bowl entirely to yourself. Closed Mondays, so plan accordingly.

PPQ Dungeness Island — 195 El Camino Real, Millbrae. The splurge stop, whole roasted Dungeness crab over a mountain of garlic noodles, best eaten with sleeves rolled and dignity checked at the door. It is the Vietnamese seafood San Francisco's PPQ made famous, minus the city parking nightmare. Bibs on. Closed Tuesdays.

Asian Box — 1401 Burlingame Ave, Burlingame. Right on Burlingame's tree lined shopping stretch, this is the fast, fresh end of the spectrum, build a box of grilled lemongrass chicken or pork over rice or noodles, then hit it with the tamarind sauce. Not a sit down pho night, more a between errands refuel that never tastes like a compromise. @asianbox

Pho Dong — 2610 Broadway St, Redwood City. Downtown Redwood City poured real energy into its restaurant row, and Pho Dong quietly took the best pho crown while the newer spots were still hanging their neon. Clean, deep beef broth, the kind that fixes a gray afternoon. Walkable from Caltrain and the movie theater, so make an evening of it.

Six for a Peninsula pho crawl, El Camino to Broadway: Kevin's in Daly City, Ben Tre in South City, Pho de Nguyen in San Bruno, PPQ in Millbrae, Asian Box in Burlingame, Pho Dong in Redwood City. Bibs optional, appetite mandatory. Which bowl gets your rainy Tuesday vote?

item.title: San Francisco Peninsula Korean Restaurants and BBQ
item.description: Five Peninsula Korean spots worth crossing a bridge for, from a brand new Daly City megamart to a downtown San Mateo kalbijjim counter that runs a line out
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Peninsula Korean Restaurants and BBQ

Five Peninsula Korean spots worth crossing a bridge for, from a brand new Daly City megamart to a downtown San Mateo kalbijjim counter that runs a line out the door. Skip the chain court at the mall this time.

Jagalchi — 63 Serramonte Center, Daly City. The Korean megamart that turned a dead mall anchor into a weekend destination, live seafood tanks, a real butcher, and Basquia's gluten free rice bread up front. Come hungry and you leave with banchan and a full trunk. Weekend lots fill fast, so go before noon. @jagalchi_official

Pogu — 63 Serramonte Center, Daly City. Inside the same complex, a Michelin starred chef runs a 160 seat room built around hansang charim, the full table spread of premium meats and seafood at a low Korean table. This is your anniversary reservation, not your Tuesday. Book ahead and bring the makgeolli crowd. @jagalchi_official

Mom's Tofu House — 133 El Camino Real, Millbrae. The soondubu specialist where the soft tofu stew lands still bubbling like lava and the banchan keeps refilling. Get the combination tofu soup with a side of yang nyum wings, and crack the egg in while it is still roaring. No frills, cash friendly, exactly the point.

Whisper Fusion — 310 Baldwin Ave, San Mateo. Chef Nick Yoon's brunch room where Korean flavor goes fine dining, gochujang fried chicken, truffle wagyu yukke, a seafood jjambbong pasta that has no business working this well. It opened early 2026 and downtown San Mateo has not stopped talking. Budget a wait on weekends. @whisper.sanmateo

Daeho Kalbijjim and Beef Soup — 213 2nd Ave, San Mateo. The kalbijjim locals cross town for, braised short ribs so tender they slide off the bone, with the cheese pull option that made it a Goldbelly star. The seolleongtang is the quiet cure for a cold morning. Order it with cheese once and skip the debate. @daeho_official

Five for your Peninsula Korean rotation: Jagalchi to shop, Pogu to celebrate, Mom's for the soondubu, Whisper for brunch, Daeho for the short ribs. Which counter earns your first drive, and who did I miss between Burlingame and Redwood City?

item.title: San Francisco Peninsula and Coastside Seafood
item.description: Seven Peninsula and coastside seafood spots worth skipping the Wharf for. From Pillar Point Harbor fry shacks to a Burlingame tank holding ten pound Maine
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Peninsula and Coastside Seafood

Seven Peninsula and coastside seafood spots worth skipping the Wharf for. From Pillar Point Harbor fry shacks to a Burlingame tank holding ten pound Maine lobsters, this is where locals eat crab, ceviche, and lobster rolls, coast to bayfront. Realtors call it location. You will call it lunch with a view.

Sam's Chowder House — 4210 N. Cabrillo Hwy, Half Moon Bay. The lobster roll here got named one of America's five best sandwiches on national TV, and the oceanfront deck backs up the hype. Order it hot with butter, add a bowl of clam chowder, and settle onto the patio while the fog burns off. Weekends fill fast, so go early or reserve a table. @samschowderhouse

Barbara's Fishtrap — 281 Capistrano Rd, Half Moon Bay. Frying since 1971, this Pillar Point Harbor shack does the fish and chips and homemade clam chowder you drove out here for, boats bobbing right past the patio. The hours bend to the weather, but they swear they will not close if there is a line. Come hungry, come casual, and time it for a clear day outside.

La Costanera — 260 Capistrano Rd, Half Moon Bay. Same harbor, dressier end. Chef Carlos Altamirano's Peruvian kitchen sends out ceviche and handcrafted cocktails while 180 degree windows put the whole Pacific on your table. It is the special occasion pick of the coast, so save it for the anniversary, not the post hike hoodie run. Sunset reservations go first. @lacostanerarestaurant

Moss Beach Distillery — 140 Beach Way, Moss Beach. Perched on a cliff with an ocean view from every table, this is where you take out of towners for crab cakes, cioppino, and a firepit on the dog friendly Seal Cove patio. Fair warning, it is a restaurant, not a distillery, and locals will happily tell you about the resident ghost. Book for sunset. @mossbeachdistillery

New England Lobster Market and Eatery — 824 Cowan Rd, Burlingame. Hiding in a Burlingame industrial pocket near SFO sits the largest lobster tank on the West Coast, 75,000 gallons of Maine lobster up to ten pounds. Get the lobster roll, then hit the market counter for dinner. Weekday happy hour runs oysters and shrimp tacos cheap, 3 to 6. @newenglandlobster

Pacific Catch — 243 South B Street, San Mateo. Downtown San Mateo's West Coast fish house is California born, and the sustainable poke, sushi, and grilled fish still hold up. Grab the B Street parklet for Aloha Hour, weekdays 3 to 6, when the fresh bites and tropical drinks go easy on the wallet. Good call before a movie downtown. @pacificcatch

Cook's Seafood — 751 El Camino Real, Menlo Park. A fish market and counter restaurant since 1928, back when Menlo Park had orchards instead of venture funds. Order the fish and chips, then buy Dungeness at the counter, they will crack and clean it free. No ocean view, some of the freshest fish on the Peninsula and zero pretense. Eat it fried there or take it home to cook.

Seven for the coastside seafood run: Sam's Chowder House, Barbara's Fishtrap and La Costanera at Pillar Point, Moss Beach Distillery on the cliff, New England Lobster in Burlingame, Pacific Catch in San Mateo, Cook's in Menlo Park. Beach shack to white tablecloth, the Peninsula eats better than the Wharf. Which one is first?

item.title: San Francisco Marin Thai
item.description: Six Marin Thai kitchens worth crossing town for, from a San Rafael counter cooking since 1989 to a Sausalito spot two blocks off the waterfront. Skip the f
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Marin Thai

Six Marin Thai kitchens worth crossing town for, from a San Rafael counter cooking since 1989 to a Sausalito spot two blocks off the waterfront. Skip the freeway chains, this is where the North Bay eats its Thai.

Royal Thai Restaurant — 610 3rd St, San Rafael. The downtown anchor for Northern Thai you rarely find this side of the bridge, from sai ua sausage to the crispy nam khao rice salad. Regulars order Auntie's Thai Twist Mongolian beef and let the kitchen set the heat. Closed Tuesdays, so aim your craving at any other night. @royalthaisanrafael

Tub Tim Thai Restaurant — 510 Tamalpais Dr, Corte Madera. Tucked in the Park Madera Center since 1998, the steady neighborhood room that has outlasted every trendier place that opened around it. Lunch runs 11:30 to 2:30 for the quiet booth, dinner till 9:30, and they close Sundays. Learn that once and you'll never get caught out.

R'Noh Thai — 1000 Magnolia Ave, Larkspur. The splurge end of Marin Thai, right on walkable Magnolia, where basil Wagyu and bamee noodles under grilled pork run the menu. Order the chicken with coconut rice, almonds and raisins folded in, then stroll the block for dessert somewhere else.

Arawan Thai Cuisine — 47 Caledonia St, Sausalito. Two blocks up from the tourist crush on Bridgeway sits the local move, a small Caledonia Street kitchen doing honest Thai for pickup and dine in. Weekday lunch runs 11:30 to 2:30, so slot it between the ferry and the hills. A pocket favorite the crowds walk right past.

Calgang Thai Eatery — 194 Northgate One, San Rafael. Born in 1989 as Jhan Thong inside the old Northgate Mall food court, this family kitchen moved a block over and kept the woks going when the mall came down. Established and unfussy, tucked in the Northgate One center. Ask what the family is cooking that day.

My Thai — 1230 4th St, San Rafael. The award winning, no MSG downtown standby, strong on papaya salad, tom yum, and a mango sticky rice worth saving room for. Bonus for the west side, there's a second My Thai on Broadway in Fairfax.

Six for your Marin Thai rotation: Royal Thai, Tub Tim, R'Noh, Arawan, Calgang and My Thai. Which town plates your go to curry, San Rafael, Larkspur, Corte Madera or Sausalito?

item.title: San Francisco Marin Sushi and Japanese
item.description: Five Marin sushi counters worth crossing a bridge for, and the most decorated of them sits in Sausalito, not San Francisco. Sushi Ran keeps landing on nati
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Marin Sushi and Japanese

Five Marin sushi counters worth crossing a bridge for, and the most decorated of them sits in Sausalito, not San Francisco. Sushi Ran keeps landing on national best of lists while plenty of city spots get passed over. From the water in Sausalito up to Larkspur, this is the North Bay sushi run locals rotate through.

Sushi Ran — 107 Caledonia Street, Sausalito. Forty years in and still the name people cite when they argue the best sushi near the city isn't in the city. Book the omakase if you want the full show, or sit at the bar and let the chef read the room. That 200 bottle wine and sake list is not a bluff. @sushiran

Robata Grill and Sushi — 591 Redwood Highway, Mill Valley. Easy to blow past on the frontage road. That's half the reason regulars love it. The name is the tell: robata means the charcoal grill, so order past the rolls and get skewers and grilled fish too. Lunch on weekdays, dinner most nights. @robatagrillandsushi

Samurai Sushi — 425 Miller Avenue, Mill Valley. The Miller Avenue neighborhood spot where the specialty rolls do the talking, the soft shell crab and the baked ones especially. Fair warning, they trimmed hours to Tuesday through Saturday evenings while short staffed, so a Monday craving stays a Monday problem.

Oyama Sushi — 282 Bon Air Center, Greenbrae. Tucked into the Bon Air shopping center, the kind of place you would cruise past on a grocery run and never guess the nigiri is this clean. Lunch and dinner daily, with online pickup if you would rather eat it on your own deck. Steady and fresh, no theatrics.

King of the Roll — 552 Magnolia Avenue, Larkspur. Right on Magnolia downtown, and the move is whatever is on the specials board that week, bluefin toro, uni, oysters on the half shell. Evenings only, and they take reservations for six or more, so a big group works here. Call ahead for takeout.

Five for a Marin sushi day: Sushi Ran in Sausalito, Robata and Samurai in Mill Valley, Oyama in Greenbrae, King of the Roll in Larkspur. Omakase splurge or specials board gamble, which counter earns your first reservation?

item.title: San Francisco Marin Indian and Himalayan
item.description: Five Marin Indian kitchens worth crossing a bridge for, and most Bay Area folks can only name the one on San Rafael's Fourth Street. The good stuff hides i
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Marin Indian and Himalayan

Five Marin Indian kitchens worth crossing a bridge for, and most Bay Area folks can only name the one on San Rafael's Fourth Street. The good stuff hides in Fairfax, up in Novato, even down a back road in Lagunitas. Think organic curries, Goan shrimp, momos steamed to order. Here's the Marin run.

Lotus Cuisine of India — 812 Fourth Street, San Rafael. The Sroa family has been doing organic Indian downtown for years, naan baked in a clay pit over charcoal and samosas folded from organic dough in house. Order the vegetable momos too, a quiet nod to Nepal on an Indian menu. Then ask for it as spicy as you mean it.

Cafe Lotus — 1912 Sir Francis Drake Blvd, Fairfax. Same family as the San Rafael spot, gone casual and all organic in the middle of downtown Fairfax. Northern Indian home cooking, many of the spices carried in from India, and a patio for when Fairfax does its sunny thing. The kind of main street anchor a town gets lucky to keep.

Prabh Indian Kitchen — 24 Sunnyside Ave, Mill Valley. Tucked off the main drag with a patio and an easy, warm room. The butter chicken and tandoori do the heavy lifting, but regulars quietly order the achari soya chap and won't tell you why. Open late for Mill Valley, kitchen going till 10 most nights. @prabhindiankitchen

Little Goan Cafe — 2007 Novato Blvd, Novato. Not only Indian, Goan, the coastal state where the curries lean on clove, cinnamon and the sea. Get the shrimp xacuti and you taste the difference a coastline makes. Family run, closed Mondays, and yes there's cold Indian beer for the heat. Worth the drive up to Novato on its own.

Arti Cafe — 7282 Sir Francis Drake Blvd, Lagunitas. Yes, real tandoori this far out the San Geronimo Valley, past where the cell signal gives up. This is the West Marin village Indian spot, curries and plenty of gluten free options, even an Indian pizza the food writers keep chasing. Make it a Saturday and stay for the whole valley.

Five for a Marin curry crawl: Lotus Cuisine in San Rafael, Cafe Lotus in Fairfax, Prabh in Mill Valley, Little Goan in Novato, Arti out in Lagunitas. Organic curries, Goan seafood, momos for the Himalayan side. Which is your regular order, and who's missing from this Marin map?

item.title: San Francisco Peninsula Ramen
item.description: Five Peninsula ramen shops that settle the where to slurp argument for good. Most folks still drive up to San Francisco for a bowl. Locals know San Mateo q
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Peninsula Ramen

Five Peninsula ramen shops that settle the where to slurp argument for good. Most folks still drive up to San Francisco for a bowl. Locals know San Mateo quietly anchors the Peninsula's ramen scene, and the tourists have no idea. Cash, elbows, steam on the windows. Bring an appetite.

Ramen Dojo — 805 S B St, San Mateo. The garlic pork bowl that built this block's whole reputation, and the reason a line forms on the sidewalk before the door even unlocks. Go early or go patient, the regulars have the timing down to a science. Your coworkers will smell it on you by two. Worth every minute.

Santa Ramen — 1944 S El Camino Real, San Mateo. Before ramen became a whole personality, this was the Peninsula's original, the counter that taught the neighborhood what real tonkotsu tastes like. Order it loaded, sit near the kitchen, and maybe skip the nice shirt. Some corners age well.

Kajiken — 112 South B Street, San Mateo. The brothless one. Abura soba, naked noodles you toss yourself with sauce, chashu and a soft egg until every strand goes glossy, so it's on you if it comes out bland. Add the vinegar, thank yourself later, and finding street parking on B counts as a win. @kajikenusa

Totoro Ramen — 856 N Delaware St, San Mateo. Tucked off the main drag where the rent makes more sense, this little counter simmers pork bones 18 hours and lets you order by iPad, no small talk required. Get the black garlic, watch the broth disappear, and yes, it's named after the big fuzzy forest guy.

Marufuku Ramen — 865 Middlefield Rd, Redwood City. Creamy Hakata tonkotsu with the thin, firm noodles, and open daily while the others keep banker's hours, so it saves your Tuesday when nowhere else will. Put your name down, walk the block, come back hungry. The wait list moves like a good open house. @marufukuramenofficial

Five for the Peninsula ramen crawl: Dojo for the line, Santa Ramen for the roots, Kajiken for the brothless rebels, Totoro for the quiet neighborhood bowl, Marufuku for when everyone else is dark. Which one earns your next weeknight, and who's missing from San Mateo's B Street?

item.title: San Francisco Peninsula Pizza
item.description: Six Peninsula pizzerias worth skipping the bridge for. The best kept secret sits in a Redwood City strip mall and took a 2017 world pizza title, and almost
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Peninsula Pizza

Six Peninsula pizzerias worth skipping the bridge for. The best kept secret sits in a Redwood City strip mall and took a 2017 world pizza title, and almost nobody outside the neighborhood mentions it. Wood fired pies to grandma slices, Burlingame down to Palo Alto and over the hill to the coast.

Rise Pizzeria — 1451 Burlingame Ave, Burlingame. Family owned, wood fired, and parked right on the Avenue, so you get pizza and prime people watching in one sitting. The patio is the move on a warm night, and yes, a pizzeria that takes reservations is peak Burlingame. Grab a pie and a craft beer and let downtown do the rest. @risepizzeria

Vesta — 2022 Broadway, Redwood City. Wood fired pizza and small plates that were the downtown Broadway reservation to get long before the block filled in around them. Local, organic, quietly serious about the crust. Bring a date, split the carbonara pie, and feel smug about skipping the chain by the freeway. @vestarwc

State of Mind — 3710 Florence St, Redwood City. The 2017 World Pizza champs work out of a counter in the Marsh Manor shopping center. That's the most Peninsula thing imaginable, a world title hiding behind a strip mall parking lot. Slow proofed dough, an arcade in back, the kids occupied while the pizza does the talking. Go hungry, stay for a game. @stateofmindpub

Pronto Wood-Fired Pizzeria — 2560 El Camino Real, Redwood City. Firing wood oven pies on El Camino since 1980, outlasting every trend that showed up after. This is the old guard order, pizza plus the red sauce pastas and baby back ribs that never needed a rebrand. No line for a table most nights, no attitude. Go while it's quiet.

State of Mind Slice House — 3850 El Camino Real, Palo Alto. The Redwood City champs spun off a Palo Alto slice window. That's exactly what that busy El Camino corner was missing. Grandma and California slices, hand stretched, out fast, no reservation in sight. Call it your errands day lunch, a quick slice between open houses and the hardware store. @stateofmindslicehouse

Mezza Luna — 459 Prospect Way, Half Moon Bay. Over Highway 92, tucked in the 1906 Princeton Inn by the harbor, this coastal room has plated southern Italian comfort since 1993, and the margherita more than holds its own against the seafood. Come for the drive, the fireplace, and a pie with ocean air. The coast counts as the Peninsula too. @mezzalunarestauranthmb

Six for the Peninsula pizza map: Rise in Burlingame, then Vesta, State of Mind, and Pronto stacking Redwood City into the real pizza capital, the Slice House in Palo Alto, and Mezza Luna out on the coast. Wood fired, grandma slice, or a pie with sea air, so which one is your Friday?

item.title: San Francisco Peninsula Fine Dining and Special Occasion
item.description: Eight Peninsula restaurants worth the good reservation, the kind you book when the occasion matters. Anniversary, closing dinner, the promotion you haven't
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Peninsula Fine Dining and Special Occasion

Eight Peninsula restaurants worth the good reservation, the kind you book when the occasion matters. Anniversary, closing dinner, the promotion you haven't announced yet. Woodside down to the Half Moon Bay coast, Michelin stars to a lobster roll with an ocean view. This is the list for when someone asks where to celebrate.

The Village Pub — 2967 Woodside Road, Woodside. Don't let the humble name fool you, there's a Michelin star behind that cozy sign and a wine list running past 3,500 bottles. It's where Woodside quietly celebrates the deals it'll never post about. Book the Friday lunch if you want the room without the evening wait. @thevillagepubwoodside

Protege — 250 California Avenue, Palo Alto. It's two restaurants in one, a 10 seat bar with an a la carte lounge up front, a seven course tasting in the dining room out back. A Master Sommelier runs the wine, so trust the pairing over your own guessing. They take no phone calls, email only. That's peak Palo Alto. @protegepaloalto

Flea Street — 3607 Alameda de las Pulgas, Menlo Park. Jesse Cool has run this farm to table room since 1980, back when organic was a philosophy and not a price tag. It's candlelit, a little hard to find, and quietly one of the most romantic tables on the Peninsula. Ask about the garden the kitchen cooks from. @flea_street

Evvia Estiatorio — 420 Emerson Street, Palo Alto. The Greek sister to San Francisco's Kokkari, and the table downtown regulars book when they want warmth instead of white linen. Wood grilled fish, a fireplace, a room that's clearly full of repeat customers. Sit at the chef's table by the open kitchen if you like some theater with dinner.

Madera — 2825 Sand Hill Road, Menlo Park. It's inside Rosewood on Sand Hill Road. That means the term sheets at the next table are probably real. The kitchen works over a wood burning grill and the terrace catches the sunset over the hills. Dress smart casual, hand the keys to the valet, and let someone else pour the award winning wine. @rosewoodsandhill

Vina Enoteca — 700 Welch Road, Palo Alto. Handmade pasta and a deep Italian wine list, tucked near Stanford where you'd never think to look. There's a little market attached, so you can carry home the sauce you fell for at dinner. Come for the happy hour at the bar, stay because you didn't want to leave. @vina_enoteca

Wakuriya — 115 De Anza Boulevard, San Mateo. A one chef Japanese kaiseki counter in a strip mall. That's exactly the sort of address that tends to hide the best meal in town. Reservations open a month ahead, by phone, message only, and they fill fast. Set the reminder, call on the right date, and eat whatever the season decides.

Sam's Chowder House — 4210 North Cabrillo Highway, Half Moon Bay. The one that swaps white tablecloths for a deck over the Pacific, and earns the trade. The lobster roll made a national best sandwich list, the sunset handles the rest. Not fine dining, the place you book when the occasion is the view. @samschowderhouse

Eight Peninsula tables for the nights that matter: Village Pub and Madera for the milestone, Protege and Wakuriya for the splurge, Flea Street and Evvia for the romance, Vina Enoteca for the easy yes, Sam's for the view. Which one's getting your next anniversary?

item.title: San Francisco Peninsula Chinese Restaurants
item.description: Five Peninsula Chinese restaurants that reward a real drive, none of them the tired strip mall chow mein you keep settling for. Cantonese seafood palaces,
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Peninsula Chinese Restaurants

Five Peninsula Chinese restaurants that reward a real drive, none of them the tired strip mall chow mein you keep settling for. Cantonese seafood palaces, proper Sichuan heat, homestyle wok cooking from Daly City down to Menlo Park.

Koi Palace — 365 Gellert Blvd, Daly City. The Bay Area benchmark for Cantonese seafood since 1996, and yes, the weekend dim sum wait is real, so put your name down and wander Serramonte while the pager stays quiet. Go for the live tank crab, the har gow, the roast meats. Bring the whole family and over order on purpose. @koipalace

Hong Kong Palace — 300 El Camino Real, Millbrae. Millbrae is the Peninsula's unofficial Chinatown for banquet halls, and this is the one locals book for the private room family blowout. The salt and pepper fish is the move, the Peking duck close behind, and the lazy Susan never stops spinning. Round up nine people, reserve the back room, order the sea cucumber.

HL Peninsula Pearl — 1590 Old Bayshore Hwy, Burlingame. Book a window table and watch jets lift off SFO across the water while lobster and tender beef land in front of you. It reads wedding banquet fancy, yet the service reads your mind before you raise a hand. Come at sunset, bring out of town guests, and let them think you planned the whole show. @hlpeninsula

Crouching Tiger — 2644 Broadway St, Redwood City. Proof a Michelin Bib Gourmand can hide behind a modest downtown Broadway storefront, this is where the Peninsula goes for tongue numbing Sichuan done right. Dry fried chili shrimp, cumin heavy Xinjiang lamb, a salt pickle fish soup you will think about for days. Bring friends who can take the heat and order that soup for the table.

Fey Restaurant — 1368 El Camino Real, Menlo Park. When you want no banquet theater, only a made to order homestyle stir fry that tastes like someone's grandmother is back there, this El Camino storefront answers. Walk in for parties under five, reserve for more, take home trays when you host. The kind of weeknight spot that makes a neighborhood feel like home.

Five for the Peninsula Chinese short list: Koi Palace, Hong Kong Palace, HL Peninsula Pearl, Crouching Tiger, Fey. Seafood palaces up north, Sichuan fire mid county, homestyle wok down south. Which one earns your next family dinner?

item.title: San Francisco Peninsula Thai Restaurants
item.description: Six Peninsula Thai kitchens worth crossing town for, Palo Alto up to San Mateo. Not the food court version, the family run, pound the papaya salad, order i
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Peninsula Thai Restaurants

Six Peninsula Thai kitchens worth crossing town for, Palo Alto up to San Mateo. Not the food court version, the family run, pound the papaya salad, order it spicy real thing. Locals guard these, and you should too.

Lotus Thai Bistro — 425 S California Ave, Palo Alto. Palo Alto Weekly has named it the city's best Thai four times since 2022, this year included, so noon lunch specials vanish fast. Family run, a real patio, order on Toast when the counter line wraps. Grab the pad see ew before the tech badges claim the last outdoor table. @lotusthaibistro

Farmhouse Kitchen Thai — 1165 Merrill St, Menlo Park. Loud, lively, and built for a group photo, though the Hat Yai fried chicken and pad kee mow are the real reason to stay. A Chopped champion runs the kitchen. That explains a herbal rice salad you will replay for days. Bring people, split the curries, make peace with the wait out front. @thaifarmhouse

Bangkok Bay — 825 El Camino Real, Redwood City. A downtown adjacent standby where entrees still land in the teens and the drunken noodles come as fiery as you dare them. Order straight off their site and the kitchen keeps the delivery app cut, a point the owners will happily make. Park along El Camino, the tom yum earns the meter.

Isarn Garden — 1050 El Camino Real, San Carlos. Most Peninsula Thai leans central, this corner flies the Isan flag: laab, sticky rice, a green papaya salad pounded to order with real heat. San Carlos bills itself the City of Good Living, and a plate of grilled Isan sausage argues the point. Go hungry, lean spicy.

Chai Yo Thai Cuisine — 2116 S El Camino Real, San Mateo. The rare Thai room where vegetarians order first and everyone else catches up, though the tom kha soup converts skeptics by the second spoonful. Family run, right off Highway 92, the weeknight takeout kind where regulars get greeted by name. Get the ginger noodles.

New Thai Elephant — 200 S B St, San Mateo. Downtown San Mateo's B Street runs wall to wall restaurants, and this family run room holds the block with a kao gra prow regulars swear tastes like home. Comfort portions, a fried rice worth the walk, zero pretense or fuss. Snag a table before the B Street dinner rush lands.

Six for the Peninsula Thai shortlist: Lotus and Farmhouse for the see and be seen nights, Bangkok Bay for weeknight value, Isarn Garden for northeast heat, Chai Yo for the vegetarians, New Thai Elephant for downtown San Mateo. Which corner is your standby, and what got left off the block?

item.title: San Francisco Peninsula Breakfast and Brunch
item.description: Eight Peninsula breakfast and brunch spots worth the drive, from a 1923 Palo Alto soda fountain to a crepe griddle on the Half Moon Bay coast. Tourists hit
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Peninsula Breakfast and Brunch

Eight Peninsula breakfast and brunch spots worth the drive, from a 1923 Palo Alto soda fountain to a crepe griddle on the Half Moon Bay coast. Tourists hit the chains along El Camino. Locals line up where the eggs are cracked to order and the coffee is roasted down the street.

Peninsula Creamery Dairy Store and Grill — 900 High Street, Palo Alto. A downtown fixture since 1923, back when this was farm country and the milk came from local cows. Order the pancakes and a hand spun malt at the counter, then grab an outdoor table and watch a Stanford crowd argue the soccer score. The kind of corner a neighborhood fights to keep. Open weekday mornings, Saturdays till mid afternoon.

Hobee's — 4224 El Camino Real, Palo Alto. Feeding this stretch of El Camino since 1974, and yes, you came for the blueberry coffee cake, warm, streusel topped, worth breaking whatever diet you swore you'd start. The rest of the menu leans bright and healthy, so your table can have it both ways. Closed Mondays, open from 8 the rest of the week. They will ship that coffee cake nationwide if you ever move away and miss it. @hobeesrestaurants

Cafe Borrone — 1010 El Camino Real, Menlo Park. Family owned since '79 and still the closest thing this town has to a shared living room, everything from the pastries to the pastas made by hand. Grab a cappuccino and an egg dish on the big patio, linger past your second cup, and eavesdrop on a venture deal at the next table. Weekend breakfast and brunch runs 7 to 4. Closed Tuesdays, so plan around it. @cafeborrone

Stacks — 361 California Drive, Burlingame. The all American breakfast the whole Peninsula wishes it had on its own block, farm fresh eggs, real butter, portions built for a lumberjack. Order the crepe and French toast combo and know the line moves fast, since the regulars have their orders down to a science. Open seven days, 8 to 1:30, breakfast and lunch only. Weekends fill early, so beat the rush.

Copenhagen Bakery and Cafe — 1216 Burlingame Avenue, Burlingame. A Danish institution on Burlingame Avenue since 1977, where you order a full sit down breakfast, then lose all willpower at the pastry case on the way out. The Princess Cake alone explains the wedding cake business in back. Cafe runs 7 to 4 for breakfast and lunch, bakery open 6 to 9. Bring a box home and become the neighborhood hero. @copenhagen_bakery_and_cafe

Milagros — 1099 Middlefield Road, Redwood City. When the weekend wants a margarita with brunch instead of a mimosa, downtown Redwood City has your table. This tacos, tequila and cerveza kitchen runs brunch Saturday and Sunday, 11:30 to 2:30, with no reservations, so drop your name and wander Courthouse Square while you wait. Weekday regulars time their visit to the happy hour. Bring the friends who over order. @milagrosredwoodcity

Foreigner Cafe — 60 East 3rd Avenue, San Mateo. Voted San Mateo's best brunch in 2025, and downtown regulars will fight you on that ranking only because they want the croffle to themselves. Chef Nicolas Castillo runs a scratch kitchen, croque madame, French omelettes, coffee that runs from Philippine Barako to Oakland's Peerless. Open 8 to 4 daily, a few blocks off the downtown San Mateo Caltrain. Dog friendly patio, so the pup eats too. @foreignercafe

Mavericks Creperie — 146 San Mateo Road, Half Moon Bay. Worth the drive over Highway 92 for a coastal brunch, the kind of spot regulars confess to a long detour for the oatmeal pancakes. Sweet and savory crepes, a smoked salmon Benedict, orange juice squeezed that morning, all a short roll from the harbor. Open Friday through Monday from 8, Wednesday and Thursday from 9, dark on Tuesdays. Fuel up before you go gawk at the big waves. @maverickscreperiehmb

Eight for your Peninsula breakfast crawl: Peninsula Creamery, Hobee's, Cafe Borrone, Stacks, Copenhagen, Milagros, Foreigner, Mavericks. Soda fountains to coastal crepes, weekday counters to boozy weekend brunch, Palo Alto to Half Moon Bay. Which town earns your fork first?

item.title: San Francisco Dumplings and Xiao Long Bao
item.description: Eight San Francisco spots where the xiao long bao arrive heavy with soup, and the best of them aren't the Chinatown windows tourists queue at. A 1958 pushc
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Dumplings and Xiao Long Bao

Eight San Francisco spots where the xiao long bao arrive heavy with soup, and the best of them aren't the Chinatown windows tourists queue at. A 1958 pushcart hall, a Sunset counter with 20 kinds, a Richmond room doing rainbow soup dumplings, and the crawl runs Hayes Valley to Bernal.

Dumpling Home — 298 Gough Street, San Francisco. The Hayes Valley sit down where the pork xiao long bao come six ways, from plain to crab and pork to a numb and spicy batch that earns every napkin. Add the pan fried juicy pork bao, and time it before the symphony crowd claims the tables.

Dumpling Time — 11 Division Street, San Francisco. Watch the crew pleat soup dumplings behind glass in the Design District, from the team behind the city's Michelin starred Omakase and Niku. Xiao long bao, sharable plates, and a full bar, so put your name in before the showroom crowd beats you to it at lunch. @itsdumplingtime

Kingdom of Dumpling — 1713 Taraval Street, San Francisco. A no frills Sunset room turning out 20 kinds of dumpling, including Shanghai soup dumplings and a pan fried batch worth the grease spotted bag. Grab a sack of the frozen ones on the way out, since your freezer deserves a backup plan.

Dragon Beaux — 5700 Geary Boulevard, San Francisco. The Outer Richmond dim sum room from the Koi Palace family, known for rainbow skinned soup dumplings that taste as good as they photograph. Come hungry at lunch for the carts, or after dark when the tables flip to hot pot. @dragonbeaux

United Dumplings — 525 Cortland Avenue, San Francisco. The mom owned original on Bernal's Cortland strip, where traditional xiao long bao share the menu with Korean BBQ beef dumplings and Mission chicken potstickers. Corner spot, family recipes, and a stroller parked at half the sidewalk tables. @uniteddumplings

Dumpling Zone — 408 Dewey Boulevard, San Francisco. Tucked on a quiet Forest Hill block most people only pass on the way to West Portal, this counter hand folds crab roe xiao long bao, three fresh potstickers, and wontons in chili red oil. Park once, order the trio, and thank the TikTok that outed it.

Dumpling Kitchen — 3913 24th Street, San Francisco. The Noe Valley branch of a homegrown dumpling group, steaming soup dumplings and pan fried pork buns on a 24th Street stretch better known for strollers and slow brunch lines. Slide in for an early lunch and let the bamboo baskets stack up. @dumplingkitchenca

Yank Sing — 101 Spear Street, San Francisco. The 1958 Rincon Center institution where the Shanghai Kurobuta pork soup dumplings ride the pushcarts past your table, one of 100 plus rotating dishes. Third generation and family run, it is the special occasion splurge locals book when the whole table shows up hungry. @yanksing

Eight for your San Francisco soup dumpling map: Dumpling Home, Dumpling Time, Kingdom of Dumpling, Dragon Beaux, United Dumplings, Dumpling Zone, Dumpling Kitchen, Yank Sing. Which one gets your first order of xiao long bao?

item.title: San Francisco Thai Restaurants
item.description: Eight San Francisco Thai restaurants that reward you for skipping the pad thai autopilot. Two carry Michelin stars, one's fed the Inner Sunset since 1986,
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Thai Restaurants

Eight San Francisco Thai restaurants that reward you for skipping the pad thai autopilot. Two carry Michelin stars, one's fed the Inner Sunset since 1986, and none of them are the chain you're picturing. From Union Square to Glen Park, here's the short list worth crossing town for.

Kin Khao — 55 Cyril Magnin St, San Francisco. Chef Pim Techamuanvivit tucks a Michelin star into the Parc 55 hotel lobby, which might be the most San Francisco move on this whole list. Come for the pink crab rice and the kua kling, and make peace with Union Square parking on the way in. Book on Resy early, since walk ups rarely land a table.

Nari — 1625 Post St, San Francisco. Pim's second act lives inside Hotel Kabuki in Japantown, and it earned its own Michelin star in 2023, so the family holds two. This is the splurge end of Thai, all coconut and live fire and cocktails that photograph better than you do. Save it for the anniversary, then valet and glide in. @nari_sf

Lers Ros — 307 Hayes St, San Francisco. This Hayes Valley room has fed the symphony crowd since chef Tom Silargorn carried his Cholburi recipes west in 2008. Push past the safe stuff into the wild boar, the fermented sausage, the whole fried fish, and name your spice level with respect. Grab a table before the curtain and you'll still make the show. @lersros

Farmhouse Kitchen Thai — 710 Florida St, San Francisco. Chef Kasem won Chopped, then turned this Mission warehouse into a neon jungle where the drinks arrive smoking and the fried chicken comes with roti. It's loud, it's a scene, and the hat yai chicken earns every decibel. Bring a group, book ahead on weekends, sit outside if the fog naps. @thaifarmhouse

Marnee Thai — 1243 9th Ave, San Francisco. Chef Chai has run this Inner Sunset staple since 1986, back when the block was cheaper and the fog was exactly the same. The angel wings and the coconut heavy curries are why regulars guard their usual tables. Walk over from Golden Gate Park with an appetite and cash for the tip.

Osha Thai — 4 Embarcadero Center, San Francisco. Chef Lalita Souksamlane opened her first Osha on Geary back in 1996 and grew it into the name every downtown office already knows. The Embarcadero flagship pairs swanky plating and steady curries with a Bay view for the after work crowd. Grab a window table at sunset and let someone else expense it. @oshathai

Nakorn Thai — 639 Clement St, San Francisco. This Inner Richmond hole in the wall took over the old King of Thai space, and the open kitchen still sends out fried rice under a crisp chicken cutlet that regulars order on repeat. Thirty years of wok time hide behind a plain storefront, so trust the char. Closed Thursdays, so time the craving around it.

One Waan Thai — 2922 Diamond St, San Francisco. Step off the Glen Park BART and the kitchen plates Thai fusion with sweeping city views, the rare neighborhood spot that feels like fine dining without the downtown markup. Think spicy basil with Angus and tom kha that arrives in a little flaming pot. Reserve for dinner, since they open at 4:30 and skip Sundays. @onewaanthai

Eight for the San Francisco Thai short list: Kin Khao and Nari for the Michelin splurge, Lers Ros for Hayes Valley, Farmhouse for the scene, Marnee for the 1986 classic, Osha on the Embarcadero, Nakorn on Clement, One Waan in Glen Park. Which neighborhood did I miss?

item.title: San Francisco San Jose Taquerias and Mexican
item.description: Eight San Jose taquerias worth the drive across town, ranked by nobody, argued over by everybody. Orange sauce, Oaxacan mole, Alum Rock carnitas, a Willow
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco San Jose Taquerias and Mexican

Eight San Jose taquerias worth the drive across town, ranked by nobody, argued over by everybody. Orange sauce, Oaxacan mole, Alum Rock carnitas, a Willow Glen salsa bar.

La Victoria Taqueria — 140 E San Carlos St, San Jose. The downtown one by SJSU, open to 3AM, home of the orange sauce people smuggle out in bottles. Get a super taco and drown it, that is the entire point. A staple since 1998 and the line still moves. @la_victoria_taqueria

Mezcal — 25 W San Fernando St, San Jose. Sit down Oaxacan behind the cathedral, where mole negro and coloradito come from Dona Libo's family recipes. Order the mole and let someone else fight the parking. A downtown room that feels like an occasion on a Tuesday. @mezcalrestaurant

Angelou's Mexican Grill — 78 South 1st St, San Jose. Scratch kitchen in the SoFA stretch of downtown, known for the Cali Moco burrito packed with fries. Closed Sundays, so time your craving accordingly. Come hungry and skip lunch first. @angelousmexicangrill

Taqueria El Abuelo — 1005 Lincoln Ave, San Jose. A Willow Glen fixture on the strip since 1997, with a self serve salsa bar you will work like a buffet. Barbacoa, lengua, tripita for the bold, plus a michelada. The kind of corner spot that anchors a neighborhood.

Taqueria Milagro — 2222 Lincoln Ave, San Jose. Down the same Willow Glen strip, a Jalisco family cooking street tacos and tortas since 2018. Grilled fish taco with that chipotle sauce, an agua fresca lemonade you did not know you needed. Patio for the after work crowd. @taqueriamilagro_ca

Mexico Lindo — 1415 Foxworthy Ave, San Jose. A Cambrian sit down run by the Valencia family since 1987, comfy booths, mariachi on party nights, enchiladas the way your abuela threatens to make them. Bring everyone, book the back room for the birthday. @mexicolindosanjose

Carnitas El Rincon — 3141 Alum Rock Ave, San Jose. Alum Rock carnitas specialists since 2004, Michoacan style, sold by the pound with buche and cueritos for the purists. Weekends add barbacoa de borrego and lamb consome, so get there early. Grab a mixta and host Sunday yourself. @carnitaselrincon_alumrock

Super Taqueria — 1095 S White Rd, San Jose. An East Side standby for carne asada done loud and cheap, the super taco dorado a local rite of passage. Lengua and buche if you know, horchata to cool it down. Portions built for two, priced for one. @supertaqueria

Eight for the South Bay taco crawl: a neighborhood is only as strong as its taqueria, and San Jose stacks deep. Orange sauce downtown, mole by the cathedral, Alum Rock carnitas, Willow Glen salsa bars. Which corner gets your weekend, and who got left off?

item.title: San Francisco South Bay Indian Restaurants
item.description: Eight South Bay Indian tables locals keep in rotation, from Mountain View down to Milpitas. The tell is always the crowd. Tables of engineers on lunch brea
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco South Bay Indian Restaurants

Eight South Bay Indian tables locals keep in rotation, from Mountain View down to Milpitas. The tell is always the crowd. Tables of engineers on lunch break, a family splitting a dosa the size of a forearm, nobody photographing the menu. Skip the food court. This is the map.

Zareen's — 1477 Plymouth St, Mountain View. The Michelin inspectors and half of Google agree on this little strip mall counter. That tells you plenty. Order the chicken Memoni samosas, a recipe only a few grandmothers supposedly know, plus a gola kabab roll. Closed Mondays, so plan around it. @zareensrestaurant

Sri Ananda Bhavan — 920 E Arques Ave, Sunnyvale. Pure vegetarian South Indian, and you will not miss the meat once the podi dosa hits the table. Get the Kalyana Sappadu, a banana leaf feast built for a wedding you were not invited to, and a steel tumbler of filter coffee. Go hungry. @anandabhavanusa

Urban Grill — 1214 Apollo Way Ste 404B, Sunnyvale. The move is the grand buffet, a daily tour from North West Frontier kebabs to coconut Kerala curries, reset every morning. Weekday lunch runs 16.99 and the tandoor earns it. Come starving, pace yourself, ignore the salad. @urbangrill_sunnyvale

Anjappar Chettinad — 777 Lawrence Expy Ste 8, Santa Clara. This is the deep end of the spice pool, Chettinad cooking from a chain born in 1964 Chennai that now spans 25 countries. Order the pepper chicken and a Chettinad chicken biryani, keep the water glass close. The heat is the point, not a warning.

Sakoon — 3701 El Camino Real, Santa Clara. Sakoon means peace, and the room commits to it with hand carved Buddha panels and a small indoor waterfall, a rare South Bay Indian spot built for a date and not a to go bag. Book the weekend buffet or splurge on the lamb dum biryani. Dress up one notch. @sakoon_restaurant

Fitoor — 377 Santana Row, San Jose. Santana Row finally has an Indian grill and lounge worth the valet, coastal chic wood with cocktails and tikka sharing one table. Come for weekend brunch or a happy hour that skips the sad chips. This one landed from a reader tip, and a good one.

Naan and Curry — 375 Saratoga Ave E, San Jose. A counter spot in a West San Jose strip mall where the owner treats a first timer like a regular. Nothing fancy, only fresh butter chicken, lamb curry, and a chicken tikka wrap that travels well. Weeknight dinner, sorted.

Tirupathi Bhimas — 1208 S Abel St, Milpitas. A Bay Area vegetarian institution since 2004, parked by the Great Mall where finding a spot is a bigger fight than the menu. Go for the South Indian thali, the ghee pongal, and dosas that keep the regulars loyal. Closed Mondays. @tirupathibhimas

Eight for the South Bay Indian run: Zareen's, Sri Ananda Bhavan, Urban Grill, Anjappar, Sakoon, Fitoor, Naan and Curry, Tirupathi Bhimas. Veg thalis, Chettinad heat, Santana Row cocktails, one 20 minute drive between them. Which gets your first table?

item.title: San Francisco Filipino Restaurants
item.description: Five San Francisco Filipino spots a local keeps in rotation, from a Tenderloin tasting counter to a Mission sisig burrito with a line out the door to turo
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Filipino Restaurants

Five San Francisco Filipino spots a local keeps in rotation, from a Tenderloin tasting counter to a Mission sisig burrito with a line out the door to turo turo pancit near Balboa Park. They stretch across SoMa, the Mission, the Tenderloin, and downtown, and every stop earns the trip.

The Sarap Shop — 171 Stillman St, San Francisco. Tucked into the SoMa Pilipinas cultural district, this family run spot keeps limited lunchtime cafe hours out of its test kitchen HQ, so timing is half the fun. The Impossible lumpia and halo halo built its name, and the crew runs a food stand at Chase Center too. Roll in early or roll in hungry. @thesarapshop

Senor Sisig — 990 Valencia St, San Francisco. What began as a 2010 food truck is now a Mission anchor for Filipino fusion, and the sisig burrito is the reason the line barely moves. Get it with garlic fries and do not overthink the rest. If Valencia is slammed, they also hold down the Ferry Building and Thrive City. @senorsisig

Ox and Tiger — 552 Jones St, San Francisco. An eight seat counter in a Tenderloin pocket where two chefs braid Filipino and Japanese cooking into a four course tasting menu, think kurobuta cheek with bagoong. Reservations only, Thursday through Sunday, three seatings a night, so it is a plan ahead kind of night out. Book the counter and let them drive. @oxandtiger

Turo Cafe and Grill — 2275 San Jose Ave, San Francisco. A no frills turo turo counter near Balboa Park where you point at what looks good and walk out full. Thrillist named their pancit the best in the Bay, and the regulars will not argue the call. Open mornings through early evening, closed Sundays, so keep it a weekday breakfast move. @turocafeandgrill

Foundation Cafe — 335 Kearny St, San Francisco. A family owned coffee shop in the Financial District plating California breakfast and lunch with a Filipino streak, from savory empanadas to the Filipino mango bars by the register. Call it the desk lunch hero hiding in plain sight downtown. Grab a mango bar with your coffee. @foundationcafe

Five for a San Francisco Filipino food crawl: The Sarap Shop, Senor Sisig, Ox and Tiger, Turo Cafe and Grill, and Foundation Cafe. Which neighborhood earns your first stop, SoMa or the Mission?

item.title: San Francisco Pizza
item.description: Five San Francisco pizzas worth planning a day around, mapped so you skip the wrong line. Three cluster in North Beach, where a 13-time world champion sits
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Pizza

Five San Francisco pizzas worth planning a day around, mapped so you skip the wrong line. Three cluster in North Beach, where a 13-time world champion sits a short stroll from a focaccia window selling squares since 1978. Tourists wait blind. You can phone ahead and walk the rest. Here is where the crust earns it.

Tony's Pizza Napoletana — 1570 Stockton Street, San Francisco. The anchor of North Beach pizza, run by a 13-time world champion with twelve styles baked across seven ovens. The Neapolitan margherita is the reason to arrive early. Weeknights the line builds fast, so put your name on the list before you are hungry. @tonyspizza415

Golden Boy Pizza — 542 Green Street, San Francisco. A focaccia-square window that has held the same Green Street corner since 1978, which in this town counts as ancient. They sell it by the slice or by the sheet, hot from the case, and the line tends to move. Take-out only, so grab a square and keep walking toward Washington Square. @goldenboypizza

Il Casaro Pizzeria — 348 Columbus Avenue, San Francisco. Tucked on Columbus since 2014 with a wood oven shipped over from Naples and a mozzarella bar built around burrata and bufala. The name means cheese maker, so lean into that and start with the mozzarella before the pies. Walk-ins go on a waitlist, so add your name and wander. @il_casaro_pizzeria

Pizzetta 211 — 211 23rd Avenue, San Francisco. A tiny Outer Richmond corner where the menu changes every couple weeks and the housemade desserts are the neighborhood open secret. Portions are modest and the room is small, so the wait is part of the deal. Come at the edge of the fog for a galette and a rotating pie, walk-ins welcome. @pizzetta211

Little Star — 400 Valencia Street, San Francisco. The Mission home of Chicago-style deep dish, the kind that needs a fork and a plan for the rest of your night. Happy hour runs weekday afternoons from three, and first Mondays send a slice of dinner sales to local schools. Book ahead, since deep dish rewards the patient. @littlestar.pizza

Five for a San Francisco pizza crawl: Tony's Pizza Napoletana, Golden Boy, Il Casaro, Pizzetta 211 and Little Star. Three North Beach heavyweights, one foggy Richmond gem, one Mission deep dish. Which crust is your hill to die on, thin Neapolitan or fork and knife deep dish?

item.title: San Francisco Burgers
item.description: Seven San Francisco burgers worth crossing town for, the ones locals defend and tourists never find. A Marina smash patty, a lunch-only classic on rosemary
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Burgers

Seven San Francisco burgers worth crossing town for, the ones locals defend and tourists never find. A Marina smash patty, a lunch-only classic on rosemary focaccia, a West Portal bison burger most people drive past. Here's the SF crawl your group chat keeps relitigating. Bring napkins.

Causwells — 2346 Chestnut St, San Francisco. The Marina's grown-up burger, an Americana smash patty quietly collecting awards on Chestnut since 2014. Come for the burger, stay because the patio heaters make October feel like a personal favor. It's the kind of corner that sells the whole block in one bite. @causwells

Wesburger 'n' More — 2240 Mission St, San Francisco. Wes Rowe brought his Texas smash technique to the Mission, and the neon sign out front does not oversell it. Thin crispy-edged patties, chili con carne if you're committing, fries you'll fight over. Tiny room, big payoff, the kind of block that rewards anyone who wanders off Valencia. @wesburger_n_more

Zuni Cafe — 1658 Market St, San Francisco. Everyone name-drops the roast chicken, but the grass-fed burger on rosemary focaccia is the sleeper order, aioli, Zuni pickles, gone by mid-afternoon. It runs lunch only Friday through Sunday, so this one takes planning. A 1979 institution near the Symphony that has outlasted half the addresses around it. @zunicafe

Balboa Cafe — 3199 Fillmore St, San Francisco. Open since 1913, back when this corner was a working saloon, and still slinging the Balboa Burger on a baguette like it's the only sensible shape for one. Order it at the bar with an Espressotini and watch Cow Hollow do its thing. Proof a good address only improves with a century on it. @balboacafesf

The BullsHead — 840 Ulloa St, San Francisco. West Portal's throwback since 1979, where the western bison burger arrives with a salad bar nobody under forty remembers the rules to. The back room feels like a tavern out of a fantasy novel, dim and wood-paneled and gloriously stuck in time. Worth the ride to the far side of Twin Peaks. @bullsheadrestaurantsf

Gott's Roadside — 1 Ferry Building, San Francisco. The waterfront patio has been the reward at the end of a Ferry Plaza Farmers Market lap since 2004. Get the California Burger (fried egg, bacon, balsamic onions) and a shake, claim a communal bench, and let the Bay do the entertaining. Touristy, sure, but the locals never stopped coming. @gottsroadside

Nopa — 560 Divisadero St, San Francisco. The restaurant that named the neighborhood, still wood-firing at an hour when most kitchens have mopped up. The cheeseburger is the move, grass-fed Stemple Creek beef ground daily, house-baked brioche bun, pickled onions, basil parmesan aioli. Snag a late seat at the bar after a Divisadero night out. @nopasf

Seven for the great SF burger argument: Causwells for the Marina smash, Wesburger for the Mission char, Zuni for the focaccia lunch, Balboa for the baguette, BullsHead for the bison, Gott's for the waterfront, Nopa for the midnight patty. Which block gets your vote, and which one got left off?

item.title: San Francisco Indian Restaurants
item.description: Eight San Francisco Indian restaurants that turn dinner into a citywide itinerary, neighborhood by neighborhood. From Gujarati fine dining in Dogpatch to a
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Indian Restaurants

Eight San Francisco Indian restaurants that turn dinner into a citywide itinerary, neighborhood by neighborhood. From Gujarati fine dining in Dogpatch to a Tenderloin counter older than half the block, here's where locals eat on repeat, white tablecloth to counter stool.

Besharam — 1275 Minnesota St, San Francisco. Chef Heena Patel turned a Gujarati word meaning shameless into a Dogpatch tasting room the Chronicle keeps naming to its Top 100. Vegetarian plates and a spice program that earn the noise, tucked inside the Minnesota Street Project galleries. Closed Monday and Tuesday, so plan the week around it.

Rooh — 333 Brannan St, San Francisco. Progressive Indian in South Beach where the cocktails get as much choreography as the plates, a short walk from the ballpark. Come for a pre-Giants dinner or a slow weekend table and let the tasting menu argue that Indian food belongs in a design magazine. Book ahead on event nights.

Copra — 1700 Fillmore St, San Francisco. Michelin-recognized chef Srijith Gopinathan brings coastal Kerala, Tamil Nadu and Sri Lanka to a greenhouse-bright Fillmore room. Seafood curries and small plates that reward a lingering table, one of the better date-night rooms on this stretch. Large parties run a family-style prix fixe.

Tiya — 3213 Scott St, San Francisco. The Sarkar brothers cook the Indian food they grew up on, refined with everything learned since, in a bright Marina corner near Chestnut. Sunday brunch is the neighborhood's quiet flex, the cocktails hold up, and a table for six or more wants an email. Worth the walk from Fort Mason. @tiya.social

Apna Chulha — 550 Valencia St, San Francisco. Newer Mission arrival whose name means our stove, a full bar and a lunch buffet pulling Valencia foot traffic. Northern Indian tandoor, watch them slap naan onto the oven wall, and the staff hands out chai samples like it's a neighborhood open house. @apnachulha.sf

Masala Dosa — 1375 9th Ave, San Francisco. Inner Sunset counter a five-minute walk from Golden Gate Park, crisp gluten-free dosas the size of your forearm plus a North Indian tandoor. Halal-friendly, fast, and cheaper when you order direct instead of the apps. Fuel up before the park or after a foggy Ocean Beach walk. @masaladosa.sf

Kasa — 1356 Polk St, San Francisco. Homestyle Punjabi since 2008, kati rolls wrapped for the walk and thali plates for when you sit down. The Polk counter moves quick at lunch, with a second Kasa in the Castro at 4001 18th St for when you're across town. Best chai in the neighborhood, and they mean it. @kasaindian

Shalimar — 532 Jones St, San Francisco. Tenderloin halal institution where regulars have counted 25 years of chicken tikka and bottomless chai. Nobody comes for the decor and everybody knows it, they come for biryani that ruins you for anywhere else. Open till 11 every night, so dinner runs late. @shalimarrestaurant2

Eight for a city that argues about Indian food by neighborhood: Dogpatch fine dining, Fillmore coastal, Mission tandoor, Sunset dosa, Tenderloin biryani. Which one are you booking first?

item.title: San Francisco Vietnamese and Pho
item.description: Six San Francisco Vietnamese kitchens worth crossing town for, where the broth does the talking and the tourist bowls near the wharf stay forgettable. Nort
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Vietnamese and Pho

Six San Francisco Vietnamese kitchens worth crossing town for, where the broth does the talking and the tourist bowls near the wharf stay forgettable. Northern-style chicken pho downtown, weekday pho counters in SoMa, a North Beach wine bar plating it upscale. Your foggy-season rotation, sorted.

Turtle Tower — 220 California St, San Francisco. The Tenderloin classic that closed and came back downtown, still the northern-style bowl the purists guard. Clear chicken broth, no hoisin, no basil bush, so the stock itself carries the bowl. Come at open before the FiDi lunch rush claims every stool. @turtletower.sf

Bodega SF — 700 Columbus Ave, San Francisco. Vietnamese that swaps the fluorescent lights for a proper wine and beer list, right where North Beach spills toward the water. The plates arrive composed, the room hums, and the bill reflects both. This is the one you book when the in-laws visit and the table needs to impress. Date-night Vietnamese, not a desk-lunch bowl. @bodegasf

Sai's Vietnamese — 42 Columbus Ave, San Francisco. Family-run since 1982, holding its corner near Jackson Square while the storefronts around it turned over a dozen times. This is the weekday Vietnamese lunch the office crowd keeps quiet about so the line stays short. Family pride on the plate, open till 9 most nights when your day runs long.

Tin Vietnamese — 937 Howard St, San Francisco. The SoMa lunch spot the Chronicle called Vietnamese at its best, and the badge-wearing convention crowd clearly listened. The Howard kitchen is the one pouring pho bo, pho ga and a real bun bo hue, so aim here over the smaller Kearny and Spear take-out windows. Weekday lunch only, so plan the meeting around it. @tinvietnamesecuisine

Kevin's Noodle House — 1833 Irving St, San Francisco. Also signed Pho Huynh Hiep, the Bay-wide pho spot regulars still rank by the beef ball and the broth. The Irving branch anchors the Sunset's unofficial pho row, steamy windows and all. Open 11 to 9 daily. That's the whole point on a foggy Tuesday when nothing else out here feels open.

Gao Viet Kitchen — 1900 Irving St, San Francisco. A block from Kevin's on the same Sunset strip, this is the dressed-up cousin: a full bar, cocktails, Vietnamese plated for a night out, not a quick slurp. Handy when half your table wants pho and half wants a drink menu. Closed Tuesdays, dinner runs late into the fog, and weekends fill up, so reserve. @gaovietkitchen

Six for your San Francisco pho rotation: Turtle Tower and Kevin's for the purist broth, Tin for a weekday lunch, Sai's for old-school, Bodega and Gao when the night calls for a wine list. Which bowl gets you through the next fog season?

item.title: San Francisco Korean Restaurants
item.description: Eight San Francisco Korean spots worth crossing town for, from Michelin charcoal to 1am soju. Kimchi, bulgogi, pork belly, corn cheese hot off the grill, m
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Korean Restaurants

Eight San Francisco Korean spots worth crossing town for, from Michelin charcoal to 1am soju. Kimchi, bulgogi, pork belly, corn cheese hot off the grill, mapped from the Mission out to the beach. Your next craving now has a plan.

San Ho Won — 2170 Bryant St, San Francisco. Corey Lee's Mission charcoal BBQ is the rare Korean room wearing a Michelin star, and it stays low-key about it. Wood smoke, sharp banchan, a small dining room that books out early, so plan the reservation the way you'd plan an open house. @sanhowon

SSAL — 2226 Polk St, San Francisco. Chef Junsoo Bae serves one Michelin-starred tasting menu a night on Polk, Korean flavors through a French lens, all facing the open kitchen. It is a splurge at around $270 a head before wine, so treat it like the anniversary, not the Tuesday. @ssalsf

Um.Ma — 1220 9th Ave, San Francisco. Homestyle Korean a block off Golden Gate Park, named for the Korean word for mom and cooking the part. Come for bubbling soondubu and gochujang pork belly with sliced apple, stay for the back patio under 80-year-old trees, 90s hip hop, and cold soju.

Zzan — 643 Post St, San Francisco. Zzan means cheers, and this narrow Lower Nob Hill room near Union Square runs on soju, chicken wings, and K-pop videos on the projector until 1am. Reasonable prices, trendy crowd, the after-shopping spot you wish your own block had. @zzan_sf

707 Sutter — 707 Sutter St, San Francisco. A modern industrial Korean room hiding in plain sight downtown, built for the long group dinner that slides into drinks. The kitchen runs to 2am most nights. That's either a feature or a warning depending on your morning. @707sutter

Jijime — 5524 Geary Blvd, San Francisco. Outer Richmond Korean fusion where the boneless fried chicken lands in honey butter, soy garlic, or spicy, and the okonomiyaki fries have no business being that good. A low-key Geary storefront and a neighborhood workhorse you can bank on. @jijime_official

Toyose — 3814 Noriega St, San Francisco. Buried in the Outer Sunset between 45th and 46th, this is the phone-in Korean takeout the avenue locals would rather keep quiet. No frills, no scene, order over the phone and eat where the fog rolls in. The far edge of the city earns the drive.

Jin Mi — 366 Golden Gate Ave, San Francisco. Civic Center's honest Korean lunch counter on the Golden Gate and Larkin corner, big on portions and easy on the wallet. Order the soy sauce wings and a tofu soup, skip Saturday when they close, and walk out with leftovers you'll fight over.

Eight for every SF Korean mood, from Michelin counters to fog-line takeout and 1am soju: which neighborhood are you eating your way through first?

item.title: San Francisco South Bay Korean Restaurants
item.description: Seven South Bay Korean spots worth planning a night around, and the densest stretch hides in plain sight on Santa Clara's El Camino Real. Locals treat that
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco South Bay Korean Restaurants

Seven South Bay Korean spots worth planning a night around, and the densest stretch hides in plain sight on Santa Clara's El Camino Real. Locals treat that strip like a Koreatown while everyone else speeds past toward the freeway. Tofu stews, tabletop BBQ, late galbi runs.

Jang Su Jang — 3561 El Camino Real, Santa Clara. The South Bay's grande dame of Korean dining, tucked into Lawrence Square beside Galleria Korean Market, with a Michelin Guide nod backing up the tabletop galbi and bubbling tofu jjigae. Book ahead on weekends, because the regulars already did.

Shu's Korean Restaurant — 3258 El Camino Real, Santa Clara. A homey, unfussy room made for 10pm cravings: bulgogi ttukbaegi in a sizzling stone bowl, spicy ramen, tteok bokki. There's a private room that seats 30 when the whole crew shows up hungry. Closed Mondays, so aim for any other night.

Ondam — 2450 El Camino Real, Santa Clara. The newer, softly lit spot on the strip, where the kitchen runs from tidy little gimbap rolls to a bubbling jeongol hot pot built for the whole table. Doors stay open to midnight, which your post-work self will thank you for.

Mapo BBQ — 3395 El Camino Real, Santa Clara. Come for the tabletop grill, stay for the deep cuts most menus skip: bossam, agujjim, a proper seafood jeon. Open to 10 every night, the kind of room where the banchan keeps arriving and nobody rushes you toward the door.

SJ Omogari — 154 Jackson Street, San Jose. The standout Korean table sits right in the heart of San Jose's Japantown, and the bibimbap lands in a stone bowl filled to the rim. Get the galbi and the seafood pancake, and steer clear of Sunday, when they're closed.

Saratoga SGD Tofu House — 491 Saratoga Avenue, San Jose. A cozy mom-and-pop ladling soft soondubu since 2012, the bowl still boiling when it reaches your table. They hold late nights and Sunday hours when half the block goes dark, a quiet gift for anyone off the clock. @saratogatofuhouse

Bibimbowl — 415 N Mary Ave Ste 107, Sunnyvale. The build-your-own answer to a fast, clean Korean lunch: pick a base, a protein, a sauce, and watch it layered into a fresh or hot-stone bowl. Chipotle energy, gochujang soul. There's a San Jose location too if Mary Ave sits out of your way.

Seven for your South Bay Korean rotation: Jang Su Jang, Shu's, Ondam, Mapo, SJ Omogari, Saratoga SGD, and Bibimbowl. Cooler nights are soondubu nights. Which stone bowl earns your first table?

item.title: San Francisco South Bay Japanese and Sushi
item.description: Eight South Bay Japanese spots worth crossing town for, from Campbell rolls to a Cupertino izakaya to a Mountain View omakase seat. The kind of counters wh
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco South Bay Japanese and Sushi

Eight South Bay Japanese spots worth crossing town for, from Campbell rolls to a Cupertino izakaya to a Mountain View omakase seat. The kind of counters where regulars know the chef's name and the parking lot is its own adventure.

Sushi Confidential — 247 E Campbell Ave, Campbell. Downtown Campbell's rowdy favorite for showy rolls and cocktails, the spot that turned one location into a South Bay handful. Come for happy hour on a weeknight, when the patio's lively but you can still hear your table. Weekends the wait tells you what the neighborhood already decided. @sushiconfidential

Kaita — 215 Jackson St, San Jose. A family-run counter in Japantown between 5th and 6th, known for handwritten daily specials and Japanese comfort food that doesn't chase trends. They cap the credit cards per table and wave off tap-to-pay, so bring a little cash and some patience. Closed Sundays and Mondays, and worth planning your week around.

Ozumo — 355 Santana Row, San Jose. The dressed-up end of the list, a contemporary izakaya doing sushi, share plates, and a serious sake list on Santana Row. Yes, you'll circle for parking behind the shoppers, and yes, the bill climbs. Grab a seat at the sushi bar, order a spread of small plates and something poured cold, and let the people-watching earn its keep. @ozumosantanarow

Gochi Japanese Fusion Tapas — 19980 E Homestead Rd, Cupertino. Hidden in a Homestead Road strip mall. That's the South Bay's favorite disguise for a great meal. It's small-plate izakaya fusion, packed most nights, and the regulars order like they've memorized the menu. Closed Mondays, no shortcuts on the wait, so put your name down early and settle in. @gochicupertino

Tanto — 1063 E El Camino Real, Sunnyvale. An izakaya running since 2000, which in Silicon Valley years makes it practically a landmark. This is where engineers unwind over sashimi, grilled specialties, and cold beer in a room that never pretended to be fancy. Dinner runs a tight window each night, so aim for the early seating or expect to loiter. @tanto_japanese_restaurant

Adachi — 409 San Antonio Rd, Mountain View. A calm sushi room by San Antonio Center where the omakase is the reason to come, the fish flies in from Tokyo's Toyosu market, and the seat at the counter is the one to book. Dinner runs in two seatings, so pick your hour, let the chef steer, and pace yourself before the nigiri hits its stride. The good spots go to people who planned. @sushiadachi_bayarea

HiroNori Craft Ramen — 4300 Great America Pkwy, Santa Clara. Craft bowls with noodles made in-house, tucked by Levi's Stadium where game days turn the whole area into a parking lot. Seating's tight enough that Santa Clara runs on reservations, so book your slot, order the tonkotsu, and add the seasoned egg. Aim for a non-game day unless sitting in traffic is your warm-up. @hironoriramen

Amazing Katsu — 2670 El Camino Real, Santa Clara. A specialist that made katsu its entire personality, and the shattering crunch backs up the swagger. Panko-fried pork, chicken, shrimp, plus a Korean cheese katsu that pulls into strings, packed in vented boxes so it stays crisp on the drive. It's takeout only, so grab a combo and thank yourself later at the kitchen table. @amazingkatsu_official

Eight for a South Bay Japanese crawl: Campbell rolls, Japantown comfort, Santana Row splurge, Cupertino tapas, Sunnyvale izakaya, Mountain View omakase, and a pair of Santa Clara ends for ramen and katsu. Half the fun of knowing an area is knowing which counter to drive to on a Tuesday. Which one's your table?

item.title: San Francisco Peninsula and South Bay Barbecue
item.description: Eight barbecue joints across the South Bay and Peninsula that smoke it low and slow, San Mateo down to San Jose. Brisket that takes longer than an escrow t
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Peninsula and South Bay Barbecue

Eight barbecue joints across the South Bay and Peninsula that smoke it low and slow, San Mateo down to San Jose. Brisket that takes longer than an escrow to close, ribs off the bone, burnt ends that wreck your diet in the best way. Proof the Bay Area does real smoke, not the sad grocery-store version. Here's the crawl, stop by stop.

Armadillo Willy's — 2260 Bridgepointe Pkwy, San Mateo. Forty years of Texas wood-fired brisket, and after the Sunnyvale, Santa Clara, and Blossom Hill locations closed in 2025, this Bridgepointe spot is the last one standing. The brisket and baby back ribs are the move, corn bread muffins on the side. Go at an odd hour so the Bridgepointe lunch crowd doesn't beat you to the ribs. @armadillowillysbbq

Empire Armadillo BBQ and Deli — 161 E El Camino Real, Sunnyvale. When Armadillo Willy's Sunnyvale closed, that team regrouped here with a twist: Texas smoke meets New York deli. Order the smoked brisket by the pound, or stack it into a pastrami Reuben and let two food traditions fight it out on one plate. Open daily 11 to 8, an easy stop for a late lunch between showings. @empirearmadillo

Wagon Wheel BBQ — 861 Leong Dr, Mountain View. Tucked in a Mountain View industrial pocket where the tech-lunch crowd queues for brisket, pulled pork, and ribs smoked till they sell out. They run beer tap takeovers, so a local pour rounds out the tray. Roll in early on a weekend, because when the meat's gone, the doors close. @wagonwheelbarbeque

Smoking Pig BBQ — 1144 N 4th Street, San Jose. Fifteen years of low and slow off North 4th, real wood, real patience, no shortcuts on the menu or the clock. The brisket and the pulled pork sandwich carry the name, and the noon line backs it up. Weekday lunch beats the weekend wait, and street parking is kinder here than you'd expect. @smokingpigbbq

Sam's Bar-B-Que — 1110 South Bascom Avenue, San Jose. The Carlino family has smoked oak-fired ribs and brisket in Willow Glen since 1992, and the patio still smells like the reason you drove over. Kansas City baby backs, Carolina pulled pork, prime rib on Friday and Saturday nights. Cash earns a small discount, so hit the ATM first and thank yourself later. @samsbbqsj

Henry's Hi-Life — 301 Sharks Way, San Jose. Oak-wood ribs since 1960, two blocks from the arena, in a building they relocated when I-280 came through. Baby back ribs, garlic bread, and a booth that's watched sixty years of Sharks fans file past, zero pretense. Reserve ahead on a game night or kiss the wait goodbye. @henrys_world_famous_hilife

South Winchester BBQ — 1362 S Winchester Blvd, San Jose. A block off the Winchester Mystery House, this one keeps winning Best BBQ in Silicon Valley and smokes every day until it runs out. Brisket, tri-tip, and a breakfast-taco window that opens at 7am for the early birds. Come hungry and come early, since sold out here means sold out. @southwinchesterbbq

Jackie's Place — 840 N 1st Street, San Jose. Silicon Valley's soul food corner, Black-woman-owned and family-run, where the BBQ shares a plate with fried chicken, gumbo, and candied yams. Smoky ribs, collard greens, a full bar, and a second spot down in SoFA if North First is slammed. Save room for the peach anything. @jackiesplacesj

Eight for the South Bay smoke trail: San Mateo's last Texas holdout, a BBQ and deli mashup in Sunnyvale, Mountain View trays gone by two, four San Jose pitmasters, and a soul food corner to close it out. Which one's earning your Saturday?

I'm an East Bay agent who eats all over the Bay Area. When you want the East Bay version of any of this, Alameda, Contra Costa, and San Joaquin counties are my home turf.

item.title: San Francisco Sushi and Japanese
item.description: Eight sushi counters that make San Francisco worth the wait, ranked by how fast the line forms and how quiet you get once the fish lands. From omakase temp
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Sushi and Japanese

Eight sushi counters that make San Francisco worth the wait, ranked by how fast the line forms and how quiet you get once the fish lands. From omakase temples to family-run neighborhood staples, here is where the rice runs warm and the catch came in that morning.

Ju-Ni — 1335 Fulton Street, San Francisco. One chef, four seats, an omakase built piece by piece while the knife works up close. It sits tucked near Divisadero, the kind of counter you book weeks out and clear your whole evening for. Reserve on Tock before the date you want disappears.

Akiko's — 430 Folsom Street, San Francisco. A sleek SoMa room where the nigiri leans modern and the sake list rewards a slow night. It lands walkable from the Embarcadero, an easy anchor for dinner before a waterfront stroll. Sit at the bar and let the chef read the table. @akikosrestaurant

Kusakabe — 584 Washington Street, San Francisco. Sushi in the Kaiseki style, a multi-course omakase that moves like a quiet performance near Jackson Square. The chef holds a world sushi title, so trust the pacing and drop the a la carte instinct. Two seatings a night, take the early one if you talk with your hands. @kusakabe_sf

Ebisu — 1283 9th Avenue, San Francisco. A family-run Inner Sunset staple that has fed the neighborhood for forty years, steps from Golden Gate Park and the N-Judah. No reservations, so add your name to the paper list and wander the block while you wait. That line out front is the review. @ebisu_sushi_sf

Live Sushi Bar — 2001 17th Street, San Francisco. Fast, fresh, and plated with care on the edge of the Mission and Potrero, a solid weeknight move when you want the good stuff without the omakase commitment. The uni here has a following. Grab a counter seat and start with whatever the chef points at. @livesushisf

Domo — 511 Laguna Street, San Francisco. A mighty little Hayes Valley counter where the chef has held the line on quality since 2008, market fresh and refreshingly unfussy. It stays small, so no reservations, which keeps it honest. Come early or come off-peak and settle in before the pre-theater rush finds it.

Saru — 3856 24th Street, San Francisco. A Noe Valley favorite tucked on a walkable stretch of 24th, walk-in only and proud of it. Put your name down, browse the shops, and come back for nigiri that punches above the cozy room. The specialty rolls are where the kitchen shows off.

Chisai Sushi Club — 3369 Mission Street, San Francisco. A small, warm counter down in the La Lengua pocket of Mission Street, omakase and inventive rolls without the downtown price of admission. Dinner only, running late on weekends. Book through Resy and bring someone who trusts your ordering. @chisaisushiclub

Eight for San Francisco sushi worth the detour: Ju-Ni, Akiko's, Kusakabe, Ebisu, Live Sushi Bar, Domo, Saru, and Chisai Sushi Club. Omakase splurge or neighborhood counter, which one gets your first reservation?
