item.title: San Francisco Chinese Restaurants
item.description: Six San Francisco Chinese restaurants where the sit-down dinner still outclasses the takeout box, ranked by the dish locals cross town for. Chinatown to th
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Chinese Restaurants

Six San Francisco Chinese restaurants where the sit-down dinner still outclasses the takeout box, ranked by the dish locals cross town for. Chinatown to the Inner Sunset, no dim-sum carts here, that is a whole other list. Come hungry and maybe loosen a belt notch.

Mister Jiu's — 28 Waverly Place, San Francisco. Brandon Jew took a former Chinatown banquet hall and earned it a Michelin star cooking Chinese with a California accent, roast duck, salt and pepper crab, the works. Slip upstairs to Moongate Lounge for a cocktail if the dining room is booked, which, fair warning, it often is. @misterjius

China Live — 644 Broadway, San Francisco. George Chen's two-story marketplace is Chinatown's splashiest table, open kitchens, dumplings, roast meats, and a Cold Drinks Bar upstairs that lands on world's-best lists. Bring a group and graze wide, or perch at the bar solo and let the wok fire do the talking. @chinalivesf

Z & Y Restaurant — 655 Jackson Street, San Francisco. Chef Han cooked for two Chinese presidents, then set up a Sichuan kitchen that has held a Michelin Bib Gourmand since 2012. Order the fish in flaming chili oil and the chicken with explosive chili pepper, and keep the tea close, your mouth will thank you later. @zandyrestaurant

R&G Lounge — 631 Kearny Street, San Francisco. Cantonese since 1985, and the salt and pepper Dungeness crab is why the Financial District lunch crowd keeps a standing table here. Get the crab, get the Peking duck, split a whole steamed fish, and do not fill up on rice before the good stuff lands. @randglounge

House of Nanking — 919 Kearny Street, San Francisco. Open since 1988 and famous for a house move where you barely order, the staff sizes you up and brings what they think you need. Lean into it, the sesame chicken and the seared scallops rarely miss, and the line out the door is its own zip code.

San Tung — 1031 Irving Street, San Francisco. The Inner Sunset wing pilgrimage, dry-fried and lacquered in a sweet garlic soy glaze that people cross the bridge for. They close Tuesday and Wednesday, so plan around it, and expect a wait that moves slower than the N-Judah at rush hour.

Six for a proper Chinese dinner in San Francisco: Michelin poise at Mister Jiu's, marketplace sprawl at China Live, Sichuan fire at Z & Y, Cantonese crab at R&G, the chef's-choice gamble at Nanking, wings worth the wait at San Tung. Which one is your table this weekend?

item.title: San Francisco San Jose Pizza
item.description: Eight San Jose pizza spots locals drive across town for, downtown to Willow Glen to a Campbell corner, and not one national chain in the list. The tourist
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco San Jose Pizza

Eight San Jose pizza spots locals drive across town for, downtown to Willow Glen to a Campbell corner, and not one national chain in the list. The tourist grabs a slice at the mall. You know better.

Pizza Bocca Lupo — 87 N San Pedro Street, San Jose. Tucked inside San Pedro Square Market, this family run spot fires a wood oven with Neapolitan pies, 00 flour and fresh mozzarella. Grab the Joe's Special, snag a patio table on the historic plaza, and yes, the garage across the street gives you 90 free minutes. Dogs welcome outside. @pizzaboccalupo

Sammy G's — 330 S 10th Street, San Jose. Steps from SJSU, this is where innovative pies meet craft beer and their famous loaded tots. Order the Buffalo Mac or the El Presidente with carnitas and orange sauce, then settle in for gameday on the big screens. The kind of corner that makes a neighborhood feel lived in. @sammygspizza

Jtown Pizza — 625 North 6th Street, San Jose. Deep in Japantown, one of the last three historic Japantowns in the country, they run Godzilla sized combos and a Signature pie with okonomiyaki flavors, furikake, nori, sweet mayo. Half the fun is the monster movie menu names. No web handle to tag, so wander in and see for yourself.

Bibo's NY Pizza — 1431 Bird Ave, San Jose. Fresh dough made daily at every location, and this Bird Avenue shop near Willow Glen is the sit down flagship. Fold a wide New York slice, or go big with a Pizza and Pasta pie. Bird Ave has quietly become one of the tastier stretches to live near. @bibosnypizza

Pizza Antica — Santana Row, San Jose. The grown up option on the Row, thin crust blistered in a wood oven, house made pastas, an approachable wine list. The chef leans on local farms, so the menu shifts with the season. Pair a pie with people watching on the promenade. That's half the reason anyone comes to Santana Row anyway. @pizzaantica

A Slice of New York — 3443 Stevens Creek Blvd, San Jose. A worker owned cooperative slinging real New York slices since 2006, awards stacked from the Merc to the Metro. Foldable, wide, blistered underneath, open late near Santana Row when the craving hits at 10pm. Proof that good pizza and shared ownership can live on the same block. @asliceofny

Giovanni's Pizza — 862 North 13th Street, San Jose. Same owners, one neighborhood, more than 17 years. Hand tossed pies baked to order in an antique brick oven, dough made fresh daily, closed Mondays like the old school places should be. No handle to tag, so let the brick oven do the talking.

Blue Line Pizza — 415 E Campbell Ave, Campbell. Downtown Campbell's local favorite in a made over historic building, famous for cornmeal crust deep dish alongside NY thin. Big bar, heated dog friendly patio, walkable to the farmers market strip. The sort of anchor tenant that tells you a downtown is doing fine. @bluelinepizza

Eight for the South Bay pizza run: Bocca Lupo and Sammy G's downtown, Jtown in Japantown, Bibo's on Bird, Antica and A Slice on the Santana Row side, Giovanni's off 13th, Blue Line in Campbell. Which slice wins your Friday?

item.title: San Francisco South Bay Thai Restaurants
item.description: Eight South Bay Thai spots worth the drive, spread across San Jose, Mountain View, Sunnyvale, and Cupertino, the ones locals keep coming back to. Curries,
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco South Bay Thai Restaurants

Eight South Bay Thai spots worth the drive, spread across San Jose, Mountain View, Sunnyvale, and Cupertino, the ones locals keep coming back to. Curries, khao soi, papaya salad, crispy wings.

Original Krung Thai — 642 S Winchester Blvd, San Jose. Family run since 1988, which in South Bay restaurant years is basically ancient royalty. Generous portions, rich curries, the comfort food that outlasts every trend near Santana Row. Come as you are, they mean it. @krungthaisanjose

Lanna Thai Cuisine — 2043 Camden Ave, San Jose. Run by the Singard family from Chiang Rai, so the khao soi and northern dishes carry real hometown weight. Tucked in a Cambrian strip mall you would drive past a hundred times. That's where the good stuff hides. Green curry, red dragon, done right. @lannathaisj

Khaosan Thai — 2062 Curtner Ave, San Jose. Street food energy, bold spice, and a free Thai iced tea if you check in on Yelp, the most South Bay flex there is. Open all day on weekends, so it slots in whether you want a quick lunch or a lazy Sunday feast. Bring a spice tolerance. @khaosan_thai_restaurant

Amarin Thai Cuisine — 147 Castro St, Mountain View. Twenty-six years on Castro Street and a wall of Best of Mountain View wins since 1999, so the locals settled this debate long ago. Family recipes, BBQ pork shoulder, curries with depth. Prime downtown perch for a walkable dinner. @amarin_thai_cuisine

Shana Thai — 311A Moffett Blvd, Mountain View. Open since 2008 on a quiet stretch of Moffett, cooking every dish like it is headed to their own family table. Grilled eggplant salad, chili rib eye, the noodle soups that fix a gray day. A neighborhood keeper, patio seating and all.

Siam Taste — 172 S Murphy Ave, Sunnyvale. Right on historic Murphy Avenue, the walkable downtown strip where half of Sunnyvale ends up on a Friday night. Pompano, lamb chops, and the outdoor seating that makes the wait feel like part of the plan. Easy stroll from Caltrain. @siamtastethai

The Old Siam — 1111 W El Camino Real, Sunnyvale. An El Camino mainstay that has quietly outlasted the strip malls reshuffling around it. Classic Thai done without fuss, big enough to feed a crew, dependable enough that regulars stop reading the menu. Catering if you are feeding a whole block. @_theoldsiam

Pineapple Thai — 19369 Stevens Creek Blvd, Cupertino. Silicon Valley crowd favorite with a seven-day happy hour, patio seats, and pineapple fried rice served with a bit of theater. Duck dynasty, chive cakes, green curry. The date-night pick when you want the room to feel a little lively. @pineapplethaiofficial

Eight for the South Bay Thai shortlist: Original Krung Thai, Lanna, Khaosan, Amarin, Shana, Siam Taste, The Old Siam, Pineapple Thai. Which one is your go-to, and who did we miss between Milpitas and Campbell?

item.title: San Francisco South Bay Chinese Restaurants
item.description: Eight South Bay Chinese restaurants worth the drive, from Los Altos banquet rooms to Milpitas seafood tanks. Sit-down places locals book for the big nights
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco South Bay Chinese Restaurants

Eight South Bay Chinese restaurants worth the drive, from Los Altos banquet rooms to Milpitas seafood tanks. Sit-down places locals book for the big nights, not the food-court quick fix.

Chef Chu's — 1067 N San Antonio Rd, Los Altos. Open since 1970 and still the corner where the Peninsula celebrates, with lettuce cups and glazed walnut prawns regulars order on autopilot. The dining room hums on a Friday, so reserve if your party runs past four. Ask for the deluxe gourmet dinner when someone else is paying.

Dynasty Chinese Seafood — 1001 Story Rd, San Jose. Up on the second floor of Grand Century Mall, this is the Cantonese banquet hall your neighbors book for red-egg parties and Lunar New Year. Carts roll at lunch, tanks stock the dinner, round tables seat the whole extended family. Come hungry, come early on weekends, the dim sum favorites vanish fast.

Darda Seafood — 296 Barber Ct, Milpitas. Halal Chinese from the northwest, tucked in a Barber Lane plaza where the lamb and hand-cut noodles pull a line most weekends. Order the sesame beef and the cumin lamb, then watch the table next to you do the same. Lunch runs 11 to 2:30, dinner picks up at 5, so time it or wait.

Home Eat — 20588 Stevens Creek Blvd, Cupertino. Home-style Chinese comfort that keeps the lights on 365 days, which your schedule will appreciate the night nothing else is open. The cumin dishes and braised classics taste like someone's grandmother is back in the kitchen. The kitchen serves past 11, a rare thing this side of Stevens Creek. @homeeatus

Hunan House — 122 S Sunnyvale Ave, Sunnyvale. Downtown Sunnyvale's address for real Hunan heat, the kind that shows up in a clay pot of spicy grilled catfish and fragrant sizzling plates. Order family style and keep the rice coming, your table will thank you. Steps from the Murphy Ave strip, so park once and make a night of it.

JX Cuisine — 3581 Homestead Rd, Santa Clara. A tidy Homestead Road standby where the wok work stays sharp and the lunch crowd files in from the nearby offices. Come for the clean, punchy home-cooking plates that make the strip-mall front door a pleasant surprise. Open late on Saturdays to 10, when the after-errand hunger hits.

Seasons Noodles and Dumplings Garden — 702 Villa St, Mountain View. Watch the cook pull noodles by hand through the window, then order the braised beef bowl and a steamer of dumplings made that morning. A downtown Mountain View favorite that runs 10:30 to 9 daily, handy when the tour ran late. Bring a friend who claims they don't like Chinese food.

China Inn — 1401 The Alameda, San Jose. A family-run wok shop on The Alameda that regulars have leaned on for a decade, no MSG on the menu and none of the bloat after. The fried rice, chow fun and kung pao come out hot per order. That explains the steady takeout parade. Dinner most nights from 4:30, a solid weeknight fallback near downtown.

Eight for the South Bay Chinese table: Chef Chu's, Dynasty, Darda, Home Eat, Hunan House, JX, Seasons, China Inn. Banquet halls, Hunan heat, halal lamb, hand-pulled noodles, all sit-down, all worth a real reservation. Which one is your family's spot?

item.title: San Francisco Marin Bakeries and Pastry
item.description: Five Marin bakeries worth the drive, ranked by how hard it is to leave with only one thing. From Larkspur out to Point Reyes Station, this is the pastry cr
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Marin Bakeries and Pastry

Five Marin bakeries worth the drive, ranked by how hard it is to leave with only one thing. From Larkspur out to Point Reyes Station, this is the pastry crawl locals text each other about whenever someone new moves to the county.

Rustic Bakery — 1139 Magnolia Ave, Larkspur. The Magnolia shop is where the whole thing started in 2005, those sourdough flatbread crackers that now turn up on cheese boards statewide. Grab a morning bun and an Equator coffee, claim a patio seat, and watch Larkspur wake up. Weekend parking is its own sport. @rusticbakery

Emporio Rulli — 464 Magnolia Ave, Larkspur. Gary Rulli trained under pastry chefs in Milan and Turin, then brought it all home to downtown Larkspur in 1988, so the espresso and panettone taste like a detour to Italy. Order a sfogliatella, sit under the awning, pretend your afternoon has nowhere to be. @emporiorulli

M.H — Bread and Butter. 101 San Anselmo Avenue, San Anselmo. Organic flour, local farm eggs, and a laminated pastry case that thins out fast by mid-morning. The kouign amann is the move, though the croissants vanish for a reason. Come by 8, linger on the avenue, and you see why San Anselmo kept the kind of downtown people pay up to live near. @mhbreadbutter

Flour Craft Bakery — 129 Miller Ave, Mill Valley. Marin's gluten free bakery hides inside the Mill Valley Lumber Yard, and the tell is that people who can eat gluten still line up here. Scones, focaccia, seasonal galettes, none of the sad cardboard energy the category tends to carry. An easy post-hike stop near Old Mill Park. @flourcraft

Brickmaiden Breads — 40 4th Street, Point Reyes Station. Baking artisan sourdough and pastry in West Marin since 2000, tucked a block off the main drag where the whole town smells like a bake oven by 8am. Grab a morning bun and a loaf for later, then wander Point Reyes Station before the Saturday crowd rolls in from the coast. @brickmaidenbreads

Five for the Marin pastry crawl: Rustic and Emporio Rulli in Larkspur, M.H. Bread and Butter in San Anselmo, Flour Craft in Mill Valley, Brickmaiden out in Point Reyes Station. Which one earns your first stop, and who did I leave off?

item.title: San Francisco Seafood and Oyster Bars
item.description: Seven San Francisco seafood and oyster spots where the ice stays loud and nobody rushes your dozen. Locals send you here, the guidebooks send you to the Wh
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Seafood and Oyster Bars

Seven San Francisco seafood and oyster spots where the ice stays loud and nobody rushes your dozen. Locals send you here, the guidebooks send you to the Wharf.

Swan Oyster Depot — 1517 Polk Street, San Francisco. An 18-stool marble counter that has held the same Polk Street address since 1912, which in this city counts as a miracle of tenure. Sicilian sashimi, crab back on sourdough, a chowder thinner than you expect. Bring cash, come before 10, and make peace with the line.

Hog Island Oyster Co — 1 Ferry Building, San Francisco. The Sweetwaters and Kumamotos ride in from the Tomales Bay farm, so freshness is a supply chain and not a slogan. Grab a seat facing the Bay Bridge, order a dozen and the Manila clams, and let the ferry crowd blur past. No reservations, which keeps everyone honest. @hogislandoysterco

Waterbar — 399 The Embarcadero, San Francisco. The widest oyster selection on the West Coast under a glass caviar chandelier, with the Bay Bridge lights doing the decorating for free. Happy hour runs 2:30 to 5 daily, the civilized hour to work a raw bar with a skyline in the window. Sit outside if the fog takes the night off. @waterbarsf

Leo's Oyster Bar — 568 Sacramento Street, San Francisco. Green palm wallpaper, a checkerboard floor, and a raw bar built for the Financial District's better lunch hours. It photographs like a 1940s garden party and pours cocktails to match, so dress a notch up. Weekday lunch and happy hour are the sweet spot before the after-work suits claim every stool.

Scoma's — Pier 47, Al Scoma Way, San Francisco. The Wharf spot locals will admit to, tucked on a working pier where the boats still unload out back. Order the cioppino or the lazy man's version and let someone else wrestle the shells. It has anchored this dock since 1965, longer than most of the Wharf's souvenir shops have held their leases. @scomassf

Sotto Mare — 552 Green Street, San Francisco. A tight North Beach room that bills its cioppino as the best one in the city and then makes you believe it. Oysters and clams on the half shell, seafood risotto, elbow-to-elbow tables, a wait you will happily eat through. Come early or come patient, since the block fills the moment the Beach empties out.

Woodhouse Fish Co — 1914 Fillmore Street, San Francisco. A New England fish shack that wandered onto Fillmore, all lobster rolls, oyster happy hours, and paper on the tables. Walk-ins welcome and open daily to 9:30, so it works for a solo counter dinner or a low-key group without the reservation choreography. Come Tuesday, Friday, or Saturday when they stay open later. @woodhousefish

Seven for the shuck: which San Francisco counter gets your first dozen, the 1912 marble at Swan or the Bay Bridge glow at Waterbar?

item.title: San Francisco Brunch Spots
item.description: Five San Francisco brunch spots worth setting a Sunday alarm for, ranked by how fast the line forms and how little you care once the plate lands. Neighborh
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Brunch Spots

Five San Francisco brunch spots worth setting a Sunday alarm for, ranked by how fast the line forms and how little you care once the plate lands. Neighborhood by neighborhood, the ones locals text each other about before the fog burns off.

Plow — 1299 18th Street, San Francisco. Potrero Hill's farm-to-table breakfast that put a pig on the sign and the Plow potatoes on every table around you. Get there before 9 or the sidewalk becomes your waiting room, coffee in hand. The lemon ricotta pancakes are the move. @plowsf

Zazie — 941 Cole Street, San Francisco. Cole Valley's French bistro where the back garden patio is the whole point and brunch stays first come first serve, so no reservation saves you here. Gingerbread pancakes, a dog at the next table, sun if the fog cooperates. Worth the wander up the hill.

Brenda's French Soul Food — 652 Polk Street, San Francisco. The Tenderloin corner where New Orleans lands on your plate: crawfish beignets, cream biscuits, grits done four ways. Weekday mornings the five-dollar Kickass Breakfast Club sandwiches are the quiet local secret. Come hungry, leave plotting a return.

Sweet Maple — 2101 Sutter Street, San Francisco. Lower Pac Heights brunch famous for Millionaire's Bacon, that candied thick-cut strip people cross town for. First come first serve, no reservations, so bring patience and an appetite. The kind of block that turns renters into buyers once they eat here twice.

Just For You Cafe — 732 22nd Street, San Francisco. Dogpatch diner since 1990, beignets and Creole plates at a counter where the neighbors know each other's orders. There's a parklet out front the block built together. That tells you everything about the street. Cash-friendly, big portions, zero pretense. @justforyoucafe

Five for the best brunch in San Francisco: Potrero Hill pancakes, a Cole Valley garden, Tenderloin beignets, Millionaire's Bacon, and a Dogpatch counter. Which neighborhood gets your Sunday first?

item.title: San Francisco Peninsula Cocktail Bars
item.description: Six Peninsula cocktail bars worth the drive down 101. Everyone books a table across the bridge and forgets the good glass sits closer to home, from Redwood
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Peninsula Cocktail Bars

Six Peninsula cocktail bars worth the drive down 101. Everyone books a table across the bridge and forgets the good glass sits closer to home, from Redwood City to Palo Alto. These are the rooms where the bartenders muddle their own bitters and the neighborhood still feels like a neighborhood.

Nighthawk — 2033 Broadway St, Redwood City. A dim downtown lounge shaking seasonal drinks since 2018, with a happy hour that shifts by whatever produce and aromatics are ripe that week. Come early for a quiet seat at the bar, stay for the Friday night DJ. @nighthawkrwc

Town — 716 Laurel Street, San Carlos. Set in the old Tivoli building, this is where San Carlos goes for a hand-cut steak and a proper cocktail without a trip over the bridge. No reservations, so put your name in and open with the bourbon Back Nine. @townsancarlos

British Bankers Club — 555 Santa Cruz Ave, Menlo Park. Every cocktail wears a banking pun, and the Old Money earns its name, aged in an oak barrel behind the bar. Angle for the rooftop on a Friday or Saturday when it opens at four. @thebritishbankersclub

Nola — 535 Ramona St, Palo Alto. Two floors of New Orleans in a 1908 landmark, eight rooms of Southern folk art, a courtyard, and a bar pouring craft cocktails until 1am on weekends. Order a Hurricane and wander until you find your corner. @nolapaloalto

Timber & Salt — 881 Middlefield Rd, Redwood City. Ten years in, the bar team makes every syrup, infusion, and clarification in house, and the menu turns over with new specials each week. Sit at the bar, ask what dropped this week, let them steer. @timberandsaltrwc

Reposado — 236 Hamilton Avenue, Palo Alto. The tequila and mezcal list runs longer than most wine menus, from a picante margarita to a smoky Mula Oaxaquena. Grab a bar seat at happy hour, 4 to 6 on weekdays, and work through a mezcal flight. @reposadorestaurant

Six for a Peninsula nightcap: Nighthawk, Town, British Bankers Club, Nola, Timber & Salt, Reposado. Six good bars, no bridge toll, no city parking. Which one gets your first round?

item.title: San Francisco Peninsula Delis and Sandwich Shops
item.description: Five Peninsula delis worth the mid-week detour, Burlingame down to Menlo Park. The kind of counters where whoever builds your sandwich knows the regulars b
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Peninsula Delis and Sandwich Shops

Five Peninsula delis worth the mid-week detour, Burlingame down to Menlo Park. The kind of counters where whoever builds your sandwich knows the regulars by order, not name. Where locals eat, stop by stop.

CJ's Gourmet Deli — 290 Primrose Rd, Burlingame. Family run for a quarter century, tucked a block off Burlingame Ave where parking is a competitive sport. Order at the counter, watch it built to spec, grab a sidewalk seat before the downtown lunch crowd claims them. Open 10 to 4, so this is a daylight mission. @cjs_gourmetdeli

Avocado Toast — 226 E 3rd Ave, San Mateo. Yes the name is on the nose, but the sandwiches, wraps and breakfast burritos carry the place well past brunch cliche. Downtown San Mateo spot that draws the before-work crowd, so early birds get the quiet room. Soy chorizo option for the vegetarians you keep forgetting to feed. @myavocadotoast_

Two Cousins Deli — 1331 Old County Rd, Belmont. Boar's Head meats on Boudin sourdough delivered daily, run by family who cheerfully admit they agree on little besides the sandwiches. Get the Reuben or the buffalo chicken they call Let's Blaze. Breakfast subs until 11, then it flips to lunch, so time your Belmont errands right.

The Sandwich Spot — 2420 Broadway, Redwood City. Forty-plus specialty sandwiches with names like the Bombastic, plus beer, wine and a patio that turns into a neighborhood hang. On the Broadway strip near the theater, so pair it with a walk you keep meaning to take. Order online if the lunch line looks like a Giants game let out. @thesandwichspotrwc

Draeger's Market — 1010 University Dr, Menlo Park. The gourmet grocery locals raid before dinner parties hides a proper Deli and Cheese counter worth the stop on its own. Build a sandwich, grab a wedge of something you can't pronounce, browse the wine wall you told yourself you'd skip. A Menlo institution near downtown. @draegersmarket

Five for the Peninsula lunch run: CJ's Burlingame, Avocado Toast San Mateo, Two Cousins Belmont, The Sandwich Spot Redwood City, Draeger's Menlo Park. Which counter earns your standing order, and who got left off your block?

item.title: San Francisco San Jose Burgers
item.description: Six South Bay burgers worth the drive, spanning Campbell, San Jose, and Sunnyvale. Charcoal char, smash crust, halal Angus, and a 50s diner that still pull
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco San Jose Burgers

Six South Bay burgers worth the drive, spanning Campbell, San Jose, and Sunnyvale. Charcoal char, smash crust, halal Angus, and a 50s diner that still pulls a crowd. If you know these corners, you know the parking is half the adventure. Here is your map for the next lunch break.

Kirk's Steakburgers — 2509 S Bascom Ave, Campbell. Charcoal broiled the old fashioned way, and that smoke gets into everything in the best possible way. Get a double, add a shake, and pretend you scored the last no-line table on Bascom Ave. The kind of low-key corner the locals quietly guard once a neighborhood heats up. @kirksburgerscampbell

iniBurger — 1700 W Campbell Ave, Campbell. Gourmet Angus done halal, with fries that hold up on the drive home (a rare and underrated quality). It reads fast casual, but the patties get real respect. Good stop after touring open houses two streets over in the Village. @iniburger

Dough Burger — 1751 N First St, San Jose. Smash patties with lacy crisp edges and an Open Late sign that has rescued more than a few North First Street evenings. They letter Bay Area's number one across the window, a bold thing to promise a Silicon Valley lunch crowd. Light Rail runs past the door, so parking is somebody else's problem.

Fred's Burger — 1759 Technology Dr, San Jose. Halal Angus from Harris Ranch, fire grilled and stacked without apology. Tucked in a tech park off North First, so weekday lunch fills with badge lanyards and the occasional agent between showings. Closed weekends, so plan around it. @fredsburgerusa

The Farmers Union — 151 W Santa Clara St, San Jose. An American tavern near SAP Center where the burger quietly outshines the 50 plus beers on tap, which feels backward and works anyway. Grab a patio seat near San Pedro Square and watch downtown do its thing. Easy pregame before a Sharks night. @thefarmersunion

Peggy Sue's — 691 Tasman Dr, Sunnyvale. A 50s diner that leans all the way into the bit: chrome, milkshakes, a third pound Angus patty, and a jukebox of nostalgia. Open till 11 seven days, which the South Bay does not offer often. Bring the kids, or a date who appreciates a spiked shake. @peggysuessunnyvale

Six for South Bay burger runs: Kirk's char, iniBurger halal Angus, Dough's smash crust, Fred's Harris Ranch stack, Farmers Union's sleeper tavern patty, Peggy Sue's diner nostalgia. Which corner gets your next lunch break?

item.title: San Francisco San Jose Breakfast and Brunch
item.description: Eight San Jose breakfast and brunch spots worth setting an alarm for, from Willow Glen to Campbell. The kind of table you picture when you imagine weekend
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco San Jose Breakfast and Brunch

Eight San Jose breakfast and brunch spots worth setting an alarm for, from Willow Glen to Campbell. The kind of table you picture when you imagine weekend mornings in a neighborhood you would want to live in.

Bill's Cafe — 1115 Willow St, San Jose. A Willow Glen breakfast institution since 1977, back when these bungalows sold for pocket change. Order the eggs Benedict with home fries and grab a sidewalk table so you can watch the neighborhood wake up. Expect a wait on weekends, it earns it. @billscafe

The Table — 1110 Willow St, San Jose. Willow Glen's grown-up brunch, seasonal plates and a Bloody Mary program that takes itself seriously in the best way. Weekend brunch runs Friday through Sunday, and the patio fills fast. Book ahead if your party creeps past six, they will want a card on file. @thetablesj

Uncle John's Pancake House — 1205 The Alameda, San Jose. A decades-old name revived on The Alameda, open kitchen, fluffy blueberry-batter pancakes, and a Cuban Benedict people drive across town for. Add a bacon slice to the Bloody Mary and call it research. Open seven days, 7 to 2. @unclejohnsca

Scrambl'z Almaden — 5055 Almaden Expressway, San Jose. Everything made from scratch, oranges squeezed on site, and yes there is a converted VW bus parked in the dining room. Almaden Valley families pack it by nine, so come early or come patient. Open every day, 7 to 2.

Water Tower Kitchen — 201 Orchard City Dr, Campbell. Downtown Campbell's brunch winner, named Metro Silicon Valley's best in 2024, with a patio made for a slow mimosa and nineteen screens if the game calls. Sunday brunch starts at ten. Walk it off along the Los Gatos Creek Trail after. @watertowerkitchen

Mix Huevos — 5365 Camden Ave, San Jose. A family-run Cambrian spot that calls itself the best breakfast in San Jose and then backs it up with chilaquiles and towering plates. Small room, big flavors, so weekend mornings move quick. Open at eight, closes at two on weekdays, three on weekends. @mixhuevos

Cup and Saucer — 1375 Blossom Hill Rd, San Jose. Homemade comfort food in Princeton Plaza since 1990, the kind of unpretentious neighborhood diner that quietly anchors a whole Cambrian pocket. Big portions, bottomless coffee, zero attitude. Open at seven daily. @cupandsaucersj

John's of Willow Glen — 1238 Lincoln Ave, San Jose. Forty-five years on Lincoln Avenue serving Greek and American plates, with a brunch built around a famous Bloody Mary and easy indoor-outdoor seating. Post up outside and people-watch the Willow Glen strip. Open at eight, later on weekends.

Eight for the weekend rotation: Willow Glen for the classics, Campbell for the patio, Cambrian and Almaden for the family-run gems, The Alameda for pancakes worth the drive. Which San Jose table gets your next slow Sunday?

item.title: San Francisco Marin Wine Bars and Tasting Rooms
item.description: Six Marin wine bars and tasting rooms worth the drive, from the Sausalito waterfront to a Point Reyes bee farm. If you scout Marin the way you scout a neig
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Marin Wine Bars and Tasting Rooms

Six Marin wine bars and tasting rooms worth the drive, from the Sausalito waterfront to a Point Reyes bee farm. If you scout Marin the way you scout a neighborhood, this is your pour list.

Bacchus & Venus — 769 Bridgeway, Sausalito. A cozy shop and tasting room stacked with California boutique bottles, no reservation needed, so you can duck in off the Bridgeway crowds and let the staff steer you toward something you'd never pull off a grocery shelf. The upstairs loft overlooks the Bay, the kind of view locals quietly hoard. @bacchusandvenus

Real Napa — 611 Bridgeway, Sausalito. Fotsch Vineyards pours its family-made Napa reds and whites in this small waterfront room, a few doors from Bacchus, so one block of Bridgeway becomes an easy two-stop crawl. Boutique winery, no Highway 29 traffic, same wine in your glass. @realnapawine

Zinz Wine Bar — 207 Corte Madera Ave, Corte Madera. Tucked into Old Town Square, Zinz leans small-production and warm, with Friday tastings, live music some Saturdays, and small plates that make it easy to lose an evening. Kyle curates the list, so ask what's open and follow his lead. Walkable charm, minus the parking hunt. @zinzwinebar

Kermit Lynch Wine Merchant — 1003 Larkspur Landing Circle, Larkspur. The famed Berkeley importer opened its second shop here, steps from the Larkspur ferry, hauling decades of terroir-driven French and Italian bottles across the bridge. Staff pour with the same low-key expertise as the original, so come curious and leave with something no chain carries.

Pacheco Ranch Winery — Novato. One of Marin's oldest family wineries, dry-farming estate Cabernet on the slopes around the historic Pacheco homestead since the 1970s. Tastings run by appointment, which keeps it intimate, so call ahead and you'll likely get a pour from the family. A working piece of Novato history, quietly making serious Cab. @pachecoranchwinery

Heidrun Meadery — 11925 State Route 1, Point Reyes Station. Not grapes, honey. Heidrun ferments sparkling varietal mead by the Champagne method, dry and delicate, on a former dairy turned bee-forage oasis. The tasting room pours daily 11 to 5, and a flight out here earns the drive past Tomales Bay. Reserve, then make a whole afternoon of West Marin. @heidrunmeadery

Six for a Marin wine day: waterfront pours in Sausalito, Old Town Corte Madera, a French cellar off the Larkspur ferry, estate Cab in Novato, and sparkling honey in Point Reyes. Which stretch of the North Bay are you pouring first?

item.title: San Francisco San Jose Coffee Roasters and Cafes
item.description: Six San Jose coffee roasters and cafes worth the drive across the South Bay, from Willow Glen to Japantown. You can taste the difference between a shop tha
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco San Jose Coffee Roasters and Cafes

Six San Jose coffee roasters and cafes worth the drive across the South Bay, from Willow Glen to Japantown. You can taste the difference between a shop that buys its beans and one that roasts them out back. Here is where locals park and linger over a cup.

Chromatic Coffee Co — 460 Lincoln Ave, San Jose. The Willow Glen roastery voted best in Silicon Valley more than once, with beans roasted to order behind the counter you order at. Come for a single origin pourover, stay because the staff will talk cultivars until you miss your next meeting. @chromaticcoffee

B2 Coffee — 170 W St John St, San Jose. Tucked inside San Pedro Square Market, this is Bellano's downtown outpost pouring their own Kickback roast. Order the nitro cold brew or the iced almond milk vanilla latte made from house vanilla syrup, then wander the market stalls like you meant to.

Voyager Craft Coffee — 111 W St John St, San Jose. The downtown location of the hyperlocal Santa Clara favorite, an easy walkable stop for a Manila ube latte and a Dubai chocolate croissant. Bring the laptop, bring the dog, nobody will rush you out. @voyagercraftcoffee

Academic Coffee — 499 S 2nd St, San Jose. A design forward downtown roaster where the house blends carry neighborhood names, Alum Rock and Rose Garden. Grab a matcha and a seat, and try not to adopt it as your remote office by week two. @academiccoffeeco

Roy's Station — 197 Jackson St, San Jose. A family run shop in historic Japantown, built where Grandpa Roy's Mobil gas station once stood, now pouring Verve coffee and Firebrand croissants that tend to vanish before noon. Corner of 5th and Jackson, an established neighborhood anchor worth a slow Saturday. @roysstation

Nirvana Soul — 315 S 1st St, San Jose. Sisters Jeronica and Be'Anka roast on a Loring in North San Jose and run this bright downtown cafe on First Street, with waffles, specialty lattes, and open mic every Friday night. A local hub that earns the line out the door. @nirvanasoulcoffee

Six for a South Bay coffee crawl: Chromatic and Academic if you want it roasted in front of you, Voyager and Roy's Station for a lingering morning, Nirvana Soul and B2 for downtown character. Which First Street stool is yours?

item.title: San Francisco Peruvian Restaurants
item.description: Five San Francisco Peruvian kitchens worth crossing town for, from a Potrero Hill anchor to a Noe Valley room back in business after a long dark stretch. C
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Peruvian Restaurants

Five San Francisco Peruvian kitchens worth crossing town for, from a Potrero Hill anchor to a Noe Valley room back in business after a long dark stretch. Ceviche, lomo saltado, pollo a la brasa, and pisco sours poured with a heavy hand. Here is where the neighborhood eats.

Mochica — 1469 18th Street, San Francisco. Chef Carlos Altamirano's first spot and still the Potrero Hill anchor of the family, an established corner room with a full bar and a happy hour built for lingering. Order the yucca balls with Peruvian curry and a pisco sour, and let the DJ nights surprise you. @mochicasf

Fresca — 3945 24th Street, San Francisco. The Noe Valley favorite is back on 24th Street after a long dark stretch, ceviche and pisco cocktails returned. Grab a bar seat during the everyday happy hour and start with the leche de tigre. Reserve, the reopening crowd is real. @fresca_sf

Roosters Peruvian Rotisserie — 2859 Mission Street, San Francisco. Pollo a la brasa is the whole point here, tender chicken with crackly skin off the rotisserie, plus lomo saltado and arroz con mariscos. A Mission Street room with Peruvian street art on the walls and chicha morada by the glass. Takeout travels well. @roosters.sf

El Aji — 3015 Mission Street, San Francisco. A neighborhood ceviche counter that locals rank among the city's best, walkable from the 24th Street BART and built for a bright, quick lunch. Order the mixed ceviche and a chicha morada, grab a stool, and do not overthink it. @elajisf

My Bocado — 701 Folsom Street, San Francisco. A SoMa hub for Peruvian comfort cooking, from ceviche samplers and empanadas to the jalea piled with whole fish, shrimp, calamari and mussels. Fresh ingredients, pisco sours, and a room that wants you to stay a while. Bring friends, the jalea is a group sport. @mybocadosf

Five for a proper Peruvian crawl across San Francisco: Mochica, Fresca, Roosters, El Aji and My Bocado. Ceviche, lomo saltado, and pollo a la brasa across the city. Which pisco sour wins your night?

item.title: San Francisco San Jose Wine Bars and Tasting Rooms
item.description: Five San Jose wine bars and tasting rooms worth the drive, from downtown pours to a Los Gatos patio under the vines. Locals skip the chain-restaurant list
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco San Jose Wine Bars and Tasting Rooms

Five San Jose wine bars and tasting rooms worth the drive, from downtown pours to a Los Gatos patio under the vines. Locals skip the chain-restaurant list and go where a somm picks the bottle. Worth a detour on date night or a house-hunting break in the South Bay.

Enoteca La Storia — 416 North Santa Cruz Ave, Los Gatos. Open since 2010, this is the Italian wine bar people mean when they say Los Gatos date spot: a vine-draped patio, sfizi small plates, and a wine list voted the best in Silicon Valley. Grab the patio if the fog stays north, and let the somm steer you off the usual Cabernet. @enoteca_la_storia

Ancora Vino San Jose — 320 West St John St, San Jose. The Enoteca family's downtown tasting bar and bottle shop, tucked into the old Little Italy blocks most commuters blow past. Sommeliers stock it, so you can taste something obscure, then carry the bottle home. The name means more wine. That tells you how the afternoon tends to go. @_ancoravino_

Nomikai — 48 South First Street, San Jose. A downtown drinkery where the wine list shares the room with sake, and the happy hour runs nine dollars before nine, Thursday through Saturday. It is a 21-plus, later-night kind of spot, so save it for after the open house, not before. @nomikaisj

Testarossa Winery — 300 College Avenue, Los Gatos. Tastings pour daily inside the stone Novitiate cellars, a working winery making Pinot Noir and Chardonnay since 1993, with the 107 Bistro and Wine Bar next door for when a flight turns into dinner. Book the patio, wear layers, and pretend you are not eyeing the hillside homes above town. @testarossawinery

Tessora's Barra di Vino — 234 East Campbell Avenue, Campbell. Downtown Campbell's only dedicated wine bar leans women-owned, organic, and a few Mexican labels you will not find on the grocery shelf, plus alcohol-removed pours for the designated driver. Seasonal small plates, a walkable main street, and none of the Santana Row parking drama. @tessorasbarradivino

Five for a South Bay wine crawl: downtown pours at Ancora Vino and Nomikai, a Los Gatos patio at Enoteca and Testarossa, and Campbell's own at Tessora's. Which corner of San Jose gets your next pour?

item.title: San Francisco San Jose Cocktail Bars
item.description: Seven San Jose cocktail bars worth leaving the couch for, from a downtown speakeasy basement to a tequila patio on Santana Row. Most people default to the
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco San Jose Cocktail Bars

Seven San Jose cocktail bars worth leaving the couch for, from a downtown speakeasy basement to a tequila patio on Santana Row. Most people default to the same two spots downtown. Locals work the whole map. Here's the route, neighborhood by neighborhood.

Paper Plane — 72 S 1st St, San Jose. Downtown's craft cocktail anchor since 2013, with one of the biggest bottle collections in the Bay Area, so the move is to tell the bartender what you like and let them go off-menu. Order one of everything from the bar bites if you brought the group. Closed Mondays, open till 2am on weekends when downtown finally wakes up. @paperplanesjc

Haberdasher — 43 W San Salvador St, San Jose. A basement speakeasy that grew out of the old Singlebarrel, now a full craft cocktail den with a deep archive of recipes and a whiskey club for the obsessed. No reservations, so weekends mean a wait, the kind of line that tells you the neighborhood is alive. Come Wednesday through Sunday, closed the first two days of the week. @haberdashersj

Miniboss — 52 E Santa Clara St, San Jose. An arcade bar where the cocktails hold their own next to the Street Fighter cabinets, 90s nostalgia and a photo booth included. Free Play Thursdays turn it into the loudest happy hour downtown, and the $10 after-work menu is your friend. Bring quarters, or don't, and lose to a stranger who becomes a friend by round three. @sjminiboss

Dr — Funk. 29 N San Pedro St, San Jose. A serious rum and tiki house on the San Pedro Square strip, all Trader Vic escapism and fresh-juice cocktails without the kitsch tax. The rum list runs deep enough to have its own club. Grab a booth before a game or a show at the arena a few blocks over, and let the South Pacific do the rest. @dr.funksj

El Jardin — 368 Santana Row, San Jose. Santana Row's tequila and mezcal patio, where Latin flavors meet a cocktail list built for a slow evening under the string lights. Weekend brunch stretches into afternoon agave, and the DJ programming picks up after. It's the rare Row spot that feels like a night out, not a mall stop. @eljardin.sj

Cardiff & Cocktails — 260 E Campbell Ave, Campbell. Downtown Campbell's late-night cocktail bar and dance floor, a house-music institution since 2002 that turns into the best floor in the South Bay after dark. No cover most weeknights, tables for the weekends you want to remember. Dress to dance, and know Campbell's walkable core is why people keep moving here. @cardiffandcocktails

Cash Only — 78 E Santa Clara St, San Jose. Half dive, half cocktail bar, open 2pm to 2am every single day of the year, with free pool early in the week and a whiskey list longer than most menus. The $7 Sazerac is the local's tell. Come for a proper Daiquiri, stay because nobody is rushing you out. @cashonlysanjose

Seven for a San Jose night that moves: Paper Plane, Haberdasher, Miniboss, Dr. Funk, El Jardin, Cardiff, and Cash Only. Speakeasy to arcade to agave to after-hours in Campbell. Which one is your first round?

item.title: San Francisco San Jose Ice Cream and Dessert Shops
item.description: Eight San Jose ice cream and dessert stops worth the sugar high, from Santana Row to Alum Rock to a Willow Glen drive-through turned creamery. Locals guard
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco San Jose Ice Cream and Dessert Shops

Eight San Jose ice cream and dessert stops worth the sugar high, from Santana Row to Alum Rock to a Willow Glen drive-through turned creamery. Locals guard these, tourists drive right past them. Bring napkins and a friend who shares.

Cocola Bakery — 333 Santana Row Suite 1045, San Jose. Open till midnight on weekends. That's either a gift or a trap depending on your bedtime. The fruit tarts and eclairs look like jewelry and taste better, and the patio people-watching on the Row costs nothing. Grab a box for the drive home. @cocolabakery

Smitten Ice Cream — 3055 Olin Avenue, San Jose. They freeze each scoop to order with liquid nitrogen, so yes, there is a little fog show while you wait. Seasonal flavors rotate with whatever is ripe, and the texture comes out impossibly smooth. A few steps from Cocola, so pace yourself on the Row. @smittenicecream

Willow Glen Creamery — 1100 Lincoln Avenue, San Jose. A converted photo drive-through on Lincoln has scooped Midwest-grade dairy since 2002, and the line out front doubles as the advertising. Get the real Wisconsin custard, or a Dole Whip for the dairy-free crowd, then walk it down the Willow Glen strip. Open till 10 most nights. @wgcreamery

Kwality Ice Cream — 1599 Berryessa Road, San Jose. Indian flavors done right: cassata layered like a rainbow, malai kulfi that is dense and slow-cooked, falooda you drink with a spoon nearby. Open Thursday through Sunday, so plan around it. A sweet reason to explore the Berryessa side of town. @kwality_bayarea

Peters' Bakery — 3108 Alum Rock Avenue, San Jose. Baking since 1936, and the Burnt Almond Cake is the one people order for every birthday, wedding, and random Tuesday. Custard filling, toasted almonds, zero pretense. Open Tuesday to Saturday, and do not sleep on the strawberry rings in summer. @peters.bakery

Sagar Sweets — 146 George Street, San Jose. Serving Indian mithai since 1978, from barfi to gulab jamun to ladoo stacked like they mean it, plus fresh jalebi if you time it right. Closed Mondays, open till 8 the rest of the week. The kind of old-school shop that quietly anchors a neighborhood.

Bijan Bakery and Cafe — 170 S Market Street, San Jose. Tucked by the Fairmont downtown, European-style pastries, croissants, and cakes since 1986. Grab a fruit danish and a coffee, then walk it off through the plaza. One location only, so downtown gets to keep this one to itself. @bijanbakery

Euro Delights Bakery — 1816 Tully Road, San Jose. A small Lion Plaza shop known for custom celebration cakes in flavors like mango, taro, pandan, and durian for the brave. Fresh cakes sit in the case daily for anyone who did not plan ahead, which covers most of us. Open weekdays. @eurodelightsbakery

Eight for a San Jose sweet tooth: Santana Row scoops at Cocola and Smitten, Midwest custard at Willow Glen Creamery, Berryessa kulfi at Kwality, that legendary Alum Rock burnt almond cake, downtown mithai and pastries at Sagar and Bijan, and Tully Road cakes at Euro Delights. Which one gets your first stop?

item.title: San Francisco Beer Bars and Taprooms
item.description: Eight San Francisco beer bars and taprooms worth building a night around, from a Lower Haight institution to a Bernal Heights tank room. Think of it as the
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Beer Bars and Taprooms

Eight San Francisco beer bars and taprooms worth building a night around, from a Lower Haight institution to a Bernal Heights tank room. Think of it as the walkable version of a citywide crawl, one neighborhood anchor at a time. Bring a designated driver and an appetite.

Toronado — 547 Haight St, San Francisco. The Lower Haight beer temple that has poured obscure Belgians and hop bombs since 1987, cash-friendly and gloriously grumpy. The tap list changes daily, so trust the chalkboard over whatever you planned. Grab a sausage from Rosamunde next door and post up. @toronadosf

Zeitgeist — 199 Valencia St, San Francisco. A walled beer garden where the picnic tables run long into the fog. Forty-plus taps, tall pours, and a cash policy that keeps the line moving. Claim a bench on a sunny afternoon before the after-work crowd descends. @zeitgeist_sf

Cellarmaker House of Pizza — 3193 Mission St, San Francisco. The Mission outpost of a beloved SF brewery, pairing hazy IPAs and barrel-aged stouts with Detroit-style square pies. New beers drop weekly, so freshness is the whole point here. Reserve ahead on weekends, then split a Classic Pepperoni. @cellarmakerbrewing

Standard Deviant Brewing — 280 14th St, San Francisco. A scrappy Mission taproom that bills itself as the coldest tasting beer in SF and leans into cheeky, self-deprecating service. Clean, true-to-style lagers and ales, plus a rotating list you can nurse all evening. Dog-friendly and low-key, the move on a mellow weeknight. @standarddeviantbrewing

Southern Pacific Brewing — 620 Treat Ave, San Francisco. A cavernous 10,000-square-foot warehouse turned beer hall, all soaring ceilings and industrial steel in the heart of the Mission. House lagers and IPAs pour alongside a solid food menu, with live music some nights. Big enough that you could lose your group on the mezzanine, so pick a landmark table. @southernpacificbrewing

Harmonic Brewing — 7 Warriors Way, San Francisco. Harmonic's Thrive City taproom sits right at Chase Center with a wide patio built for pregame pints and sunny afternoons. Approachable lagers, pale ales, and a full food and drink menu anchor the Mission Bay scene. Time your visit off game nights unless crowds are the goal. @harmonicbrewing

Laughing Monk — 1785 Fulton St, San Francisco. A NoPa brewery and gastropub known for Belgian-inspired ales and vibrant IPAs, now paired with Chef Reina Montenegro's bold, plant-forward Filipino plates. The lumpia and a fresh IPA is a combination you will think about later. Book a table on weekends, this corner fills up. @thelaughingmonksf

Barebottle Brewing — 1525 Cortland Ave, San Francisco. The Bernal Heights mothership, a working brewery and taproom where the fermentation tanks double as decor and the recipes come from homebrew contests. Award-winning hazies, plus wine, coffee, and NA options for the non-beer crowd. Tucked up on Cortland, it rewards the climb. @barebottle

Eight anchors for a San Francisco beer crawl: Toronado, Zeitgeist, Cellarmaker, Standard Deviant, Southern Pacific, Harmonic, Laughing Monk, and Barebottle. Which neighborhood taproom is your regular, and who is missing from this list?

item.title: San Francisco Hot Pot and Shabu
item.description: Eight San Francisco hot pot and shabu rooms where you cook dinner yourself and leave prouder than when you walked in. Fog outside, steam inside, the whole
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Hot Pot and Shabu

Eight San Francisco hot pot and shabu rooms where you cook dinner yourself and leave prouder than when you walked in. Fog outside, steam inside, the whole city misted over while your broth goes to work. From Chinatown to Japantown to the far end of the Sunset, here is where locals dip.

Nabe — 1325 9th Ave, San Francisco. Inner Sunset shabu where the broth is the whole personality and the sake list keeps pace. Organic meat, tidy pots, that foggy-avenue warmth the second you slide into a booth. Open Wednesday through Sunday, so plan the craving around it. @nabe.sf

Hotpot Champ — 801 Kearny St, San Francisco. All-you-can-eat on the Chinatown edge, where the beef and lamb roll out on a literal Ferris wheel and nobody judges a third plate. Bring the friends who order like it is a contest. Kitchen runs past midnight on weekends. @hotpot_champ_sf

Dragon Beaux — 5700 Geary Blvd, San Francisco. The Koi Palace family's Outer Richmond room does dim sum by day, then flips to hot pot at night with live seafood, Wagyu, and geoduck that arrives still forming an opinion of you. Reserve ahead, the lines are a Richmond institution. @dragonbeaux

Fiery Hot Pot and Grill — 2333 Irving St, San Francisco. Outer Sunset spot running smokeless hot pot and Korean BBQ on one table, A5 Wagyu on the menu, so your jacket will not smell like dinner tomorrow. All-you-can-eat, come hungry and a little competitive. @fiery_sf

Matsuyama Shabu House — 1726 Buchanan St, San Francisco. Japantown shabu done the quiet, careful way, thin Wagyu swirled through clean broth with an izakaya lean and a Michelin nod. Closed Tuesdays, packed on weekend nights, so book a table before the Japan Center crowd beats you to it. @matsuyamashabuhousesf

IPOT — 1420 Irving St, San Francisco. A bi-level Inner Sunset favorite since 2015, pairing all-you-can-eat hot pot with Korean BBQ on the same table and eighteen house broths to argue over. Grills and pots going at once, so the indecisive friend finally gets a win. Weekends fill fast. @ipot.food

Boiling Hot Pot — 5512 Geary Blvd, San Francisco. A Richmond all-you-can-eat where you tap four broths into one pot on an iPad and race a ninety-minute clock. Efficient, generous, priced like the neighbors want you back next week. Come early on a Friday, word got out a while ago.

Nan Hot Pot SF — 501 Broadway, San Francisco. Sichuan hot pot on the North Beach and Chinatown seam, mala broth with a numbing kick and a tidy ingredient list that respects a smaller table. Good for two, better for a booth of four after a night out on Broadway. @nanhotpotsf

Eight for steam season across San Francisco: shabu in the Sunset, AYCE off Chinatown, banquet hot pot in the Richmond, Japantown Wagyu, smokeless by the beach, mala on Broadway. Which broth gets you first when the fog rolls in?

item.title: San Francisco South Bay Filipino Restaurants
item.description: Eight South Bay Filipino spots worth the drive, and most sit where you would never think to look. The real kare-kare, crispy pata, and all-day silog live i
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco South Bay Filipino Restaurants

Eight South Bay Filipino spots worth the drive, and most sit where you would never think to look. The real kare-kare, crispy pata, and all-day silog live in Milpitas strip malls, a Sunnyvale side street, and San Jose turo-turo counters, not a polished downtown row. Here is the run, in order.

Kalesa — 1783 N. Milpitas Blvd, Milpitas. Named for the horse-drawn carriage of old Manila, this family kitchen runs the comfort canon straight: kare-kare, crispy pata, sizzling sisig. Come hungry and come as a group, the party trays are sized for a fiesta, not a Tuesday. Closed Tuesdays, so plan around it. @mykalesa

Max's of Manila — 1535 Landess Ave, Milpitas. The Manila fried-chicken institution landed in a plaza that local Filipino families treat as a second dining room. Order the whole fried chicken with the tangy sarsa, add a plate of lumpia, and skip the diet talk for a night. A crowd-pleaser that earned its name over decades. @maxsmilpitas

Ima's Kusina — 1535 Landess Ave Ste 163, Milpitas. Same plaza, a few doors down, and this one leads with heart: ima means mother in Kapampangan, and the kakanin case makes the case. Load up on suman, ube suman, and turon, then pretend you plan to share the box. Homey delicacies and comfort plates under one roof. @imaskusina

Tapsilog Cantina — 1998 Homestead Rd, Santa Clara. Silog is the Filipino breakfast religion: garlic rice, egg, and your pick of meat, served well past noon because mornings are negotiable. The tapa and the longganisa are the moves here, and a vegetarian silog holds its own too. Closed Mondays, breakfast hours that stretch into dinner. @tapsilog_cantina2020

Clarita's Filipino Cuisine — 905 E Duane Ave, Sunnyvale. A small counter-serve room where the steam trays taste like somebody's lola cooked all morning and the owners clock your order by the third visit. Point at the kare-kare, the bistek, the crispy pata, and let them build the plate. Weekday lunch is the sweet spot before the tech crowd files in.

Tindahan Pinoy — 1647 N Capitol Ave, San Jose. Part Filipino grocery, part silog counter out in Berryessa, open early enough to fuel a work morning. The longsilog is the local order, a juicy longganisa over garlic rice, and the dessert case keeps turon, cassava, and bibingka close. Grab pantry staples on the way out. @tpinoy1647

Jam's Kitchen — 2351 McKee Rd Ste A, San Jose. A family-run Alum Rock kitchen plating home-cooked Filipino food the way somebody's mom would, no polish, all comfort. The rotating steam-tray specials reward regulars who ask what came out fresh today. Closed Mondays, a cozy room that fills with neighbors. @jamskitchensanjose

Manila Turo Turo — 3900 Lake Arrowhead Ave, Fremont. Turo-turo means point-point: you scan the cafeteria-style trays, point at what looks good, and walk out full without spending much. Adobo, pinakbet, dinuguan, whatever the kitchen ran that day. Daytime hours, so make it a lunch run.

Eight for a South Bay Filipino crawl: Kalesa, Max's, Ima's Kusina, Tapsilog Cantina, Clarita's, Tindahan Pinoy, Jam's Kitchen, and Manila Turo Turo. Milpitas to Sunnyvale to San Jose to Fremont, no bridge required. Which one is your first stop, the fried chicken or the silog?

item.title: San Francisco South Bay Seafood Restaurants
item.description: Eight South Bay seafood spots worth the drive, and not one is a chain crab bucket. San Jose keeps its best fish quiet, from a downtown room running since 1
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco South Bay Seafood Restaurants

Eight South Bay seafood spots worth the drive, and not one is a chain crab bucket. San Jose keeps its best fish quiet, from a downtown room running since 1985 to strip-mall Cantonese tanks the neighbors guard, with a Milpitas halal kitchen and a Berryessa boil shack in the mix. Skip the freeway crawl to the coast. The good stuff sits closer than you think, and here is where locals go.

Scott's Seafood — 200 S First St Ste 10, San Jose. Downtown's grown-up seafood room since 1985, white tablecloths, a raw bar, and a seafood boil that ignores the calendar. Book it for the anniversary you keep forgetting, or slide in for oysters at Social Hour, 3 to 6. @scottsseafoodsj

EMC Seafood and Raw Bar — 378 Santana Row Ste 1100, San Jose. The uni pasta gets all the Instagram love, but the move is a seafood tower and a full raw bar tucked into Santana Row's shopping bustle. Open Fridays and Saturdays to midnight, so it survives a movie-then-dinner change of plans. @emcseafood

Blue Water Seafood and Crab — 4180 N 1st St Unit 10, San Jose. An East Coast style crab house up in North San Jose, all cracked crab, fish and chips, and oyster shooters with or without the vodka. Open to midnight daily, patio heaters running, and yes, there are burgers for the one friend who fears the sea. @bluewaternorthsj

Dynasty Seafood — 1001 Story Rd, San Jose. Second floor of Grand Century Mall, this is Cantonese banquet seafood done right, live tanks, carts of dim sum, and big round tables built for a loud family Sunday. Go with a crowd so you can order the whole steamed fish and still have room for har gow.

East Lake Chinese Seafood — 2850 Quimby Rd, San Jose. An Evergreen strip-mall room where the seafood comes straight from the tank and weekend dim sum starts at 10:30. No frills, no view, the kind of neighborhood Cantonese kitchen you'd want three blocks from a new place. @eastlakechineseseafood

Darda Seafood — 296 Barber Ct, Milpitas. Halal Chinese seafood with a Northwest China accent, hand-pulled noodles and clay-pot dishes alongside the fish. Tucked in a Milpitas office park where you'd never look. That's exactly why regulars keep the tables full. @dardaseafoodrestaurant

Claw Shack — 1696 Berryessa Rd, San Jose. Viet-Cajun boil in a bag off Berryessa, where you pick your seafood, pick your sauce, pick your heat, then tie on a plastic bib and dig in with both hands. The Shackie's butter over shrimp and garlic noodles is the order. Closed Mondays, cash-friendly, napkins by the fistful. @clawshack

Mariscos Costa Alegre — 855 N 13th St, San Jose. Nayarit style mariscos on the north side, aguachile, ceviche tostadas, and a molcajete of seafood that arrives steaming and dramatic. Casual, cash-friendly, and open for a long lazy weekend lunch. @costaalegresj

Eight for South Bay seafood: Scott's, EMC, Blue Water, Dynasty, East Lake, Darda, Claw Shack, and Costa Alegre. Raw bar to crab house to Cantonese tank to Viet-Cajun boil, all without crossing a bridge. Which one is landing on your Friday list first?

item.title: Bay Area German and Austrian Beer Halls
item.description: Eight Bay Area German and Alpine beer halls where the pretzels are bigger than your forearm and nobody rushes you off the bench. Old-world beer culture run
item.content:encoded:
Bay Area German and Austrian Beer Halls

Eight Bay Area German and Alpine beer halls where the pretzels are bigger than your forearm and nobody rushes you off the bench. Old-world beer culture runs from Hayes Valley to the Oakland waterfront, long communal tables the whole way. Plan the crawl for a cool evening and bring friends. Here is the lineup, one long table at a time.

Suppenkuche — 525 Laguna St, San Francisco. This Hayes Valley anchor has been pouring German drafts at long communal tables since 1993, back when the neighborhood was still transitional. You sit shoulder to shoulder with strangers, order the sausage plate, and leave with new friends whether you planned to or not. Weekends fill fast, so come early. @suppenkuchesf

Schroeder's — 240 Front St, San Francisco. Founded in 1893, this Bavarian beer hall is one of the oldest restaurants in the city, rebuilt on Front Street after the 1906 quake. It went male-only until the 1970s, a detail the current owners like to note over a stein. Grab the communal table in the FiDi and order the schnitzel. A downtown institution worth the walk. @schroederssf

Radhaus — 2 Marina Blvd, San Francisco. Tucked into Fort Mason with a 200 foot ponderosa bar and a clear view of the Golden Gate Bridge, this Alpine beerhall pours world-class bier next to the water. Walkable from the Marina Green, it draws locals and visitors to the same benches. Come for the doppelbock, stay for the sunset over the bridge. @radhaus_sf

Biergarten — 424 Octavia St, San Francisco. Suppenkuche's open-air little sibling one block away, this Hayes Valley courtyard is the move on a sunny afternoon. Order a pretzel with Obatzda and a cold German beer, snag a picnic table, and settle in. Hours shift with the weather since it is all outdoors, so check before you go. Oktoberfest brings an oompah band. @biergarten_sf

Rosamunde Sausage Grill — 2832 Mission St, San Francisco. A German-inspired California biergarten serving the Mission since 1998, this is the local move for currywurst, a rotating wall of craft and German taps, and Tuesday trivia. The space is tight and pub-style, so expect a friendly crowd. Vegan sausages hold their own here too. Cash-and-cold-beer comfort, no fuss. @rosamundesf

Steins — 731 Clement St, San Francisco. Family-owned and women-owned on Clement Street since 2011, this Inner Richmond beer hall runs a dozen European drafts and puts every major match on the big screens. Bavarian benches, flags on the ceiling, and a boot of Hofbrau make it a proper neighborhood hub. Walk-ins always welcome, which the Richmond appreciates. @steins_sf

Speisekammer — 2424 Lincoln Ave, Alameda. Alameda's German anchor since 2002, a Lincoln Avenue room where the schnitzel arrives the size of the plate and the biergarten out back fills the second the sun shows. Order the jaegerschnitzel and a Weihenstephaner, then let the afternoon run long. Regulars treat it like a second dining room, so a weekend reservation saves you a wait. @speisekammer

Brotzeit Lokal — 1000 Embarcadero, Oakland. Bavarian fare on the Oakland waterfront at Brooklyn Basin, where the biergarten looks across the estuary to Alameda and the sunsets do half the work. Come for the pretzel and a liter, stay for weekend games like cornhole and the wiener dog races. Every table here gets a view, a rare thing this side of the bridge. @brotzeitlokal

Eight for the Bay Area beer hall crawl: Suppenkuche, Schroeder's, Radhaus, Biergarten, Rosamunde and Steins in the city, Speisekammer in Alameda and Brotzeit Lokal on the Oakland water. From an 1893 FiDi institution to a waterfront sunset, the long table tradition holds. Which bench are you claiming first?

item.title: San Francisco Burmese Restaurants
item.description: Eight San Francisco Burmese tables worth the Clement Street parking hunt, from a James Beard honored institution to a converted downtown fire house. Tea le
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Burmese Restaurants

Eight San Francisco Burmese tables worth the Clement Street parking hunt, from a James Beard honored institution to a converted downtown fire house. Tea leaf salad is the gateway, then it gets deep.

Burma Superstar — 309 Clement St, San Francisco. The one that put Burmese food on the local map back in 1992, and the line out front still makes the case. Get the tea leaf salad tossed at your table and the samusa soup. They take no reservations, so put your name down and go wander Clement Street until they wave you in. @burmasuperstar

Mandalay — 4348 California St, San Francisco. The oldest Burmese kitchen in the city, open since 1984 and crowned a James Beard America's Classic. The room is unfussy and the regulars hold firm opinions about the sesame beef and the fish noodle soup. Come early, the kitchen keeps its own hours. @mandalayrestaurant_

B Star — 127 Clement St, San Francisco. The little sister up the same Clement strip from Burma Superstar, calmer and easier to walk into on a whim. It roams past Burma into Thai and Chinese comfort food, but the tea leaf salad and coconut rice hold the line. Weekend brunch here is the neighborhood's quiet secret. @bstarbar

Burma Love — 211 Valencia St, San Francisco. Burma Superstar's Mission spinoff, louder and glossier with a full bar for once. Order the pumpkin pork stew, the garlic noodles and a cocktail you cannot get out in the Richmond. Good for the group that argues about where to eat before anyone agrees. @burmalove

Burma Love Downtown — 8 Mint Plaza, San Francisco. The same kitchen tucked into a restored historic fire house off Mint Plaza, a short walk from Union Square. High ceilings, big cocktails and platters built for sharing after a day downtown. Slip in before a show at the nearby theaters. @burmalove

Burmese Kitchen — 3815 Geary Blvd, San Francisco. Once a Tenderloin fixture, it came back from the dead on Geary and the faithful followed west. This is the homestyle end of the spectrum, so go for the mohinga, the pork curry and whatever the specials board is pushing. Quietly one of the best values in the Richmond. @burmesekitchen

Inle Burmese Cuisine — 822 Irving St, San Francisco. Named for the lake back home, it traded Noe Valley for a bigger Inner Sunset room in 2023 and the seats fill fast. The tea leaf salad and mohinga are the tells, and the Thai half of the menu covers your picky friend. Easy stop before or after Golden Gate Park. @inlecuisine

Pagan — 3199 Clement St, San Francisco. Way out at the foggy end of Clement, this Burmese and Thai corner is the name locals drop when they want the flavors without the wait. Ginger salad, tea leaf salad, one good curry, and you will forget the drive out.

Eight for the Burmese map of San Francisco: the 1992 original, the 1984 James Beard classic, two Burma Loves and a foggy Clement sleeper. Which tea leaf salad wins your table?

item.title: San Francisco South Bay Hot Pot
item.description: Eight South Bay hot pot rooms worth skipping the national chains for, from Santa Clara wagyu counters to a Japantown standby, plus two out on the Milpitas
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco South Bay Hot Pot

Eight South Bay hot pot rooms worth skipping the national chains for, from Santa Clara wagyu counters to a Japantown standby, plus two out on the Milpitas and Fremont edge. Cold night, big table, everyone cooks their own. Where the regulars go.

Mikiya Wagyu Shabu House — 3590 Homestead Rd, Santa Clara. The wagyu comes out marbled like a painting and you swish it through the broth about ten seconds before it is done. All you can eat runs three tiers, so the size of the splurge is yours to set. Bring someone who appreciates good beef. @mikiyabayarea

Taichi Pot Shabu Shabu — 2640 Homestead Rd, Santa Clara. Same street as Mikiya, quieter room, individual pots so nobody fights over the spicy side. They handcraft the broths and age the beef, and the after work crowd fills the bar first. Go early or wait. @taichipotshabu

One Pot Shabu Shabu — 19648 Stevens Creek Blvd, Cupertino. Tucked in the Marketplace plaza and running since 2011, back when Cupertino shabu options were thin. Each person gets a pot and a broth, which ends the ordering negotiations. The sesame sauce is why regulars stay loyal. @onepotshabushabu

Revopot — 2934 Aborn Sq, San Jose. The plates ride a conveyor belt past your seat and you grab what looks good. That's either efficient or dangerous depending on your appetite. All you can eat, open late on weekends, easy on the East San Jose crowd. Pace yourself. @revopot_sj

Tasty Pot — 1143 Story Rd Ste 100, San Jose. Taiwanese style, so your pot arrives loaded and you are not building it from an empty broth. They added all you can eat, and the milk tea comes from the same kitchen. A solid weeknight call when you want hot pot without the ceremony. @tastypot.usa

Shabu Time — 171 Jackson St, San Jose. The Japantown pick, individual pots in a room that has fed the neighborhood for years. Certified meats, udon and ramen add ons, and a lunch that moves fast enough for a work break. Walk it off with a loop past the museum after. @shabutimesj

Shabu Shabu Kiwami — 79 S Abbott Ave, Milpitas. The new kid on Abbott, all you can eat with premium cuts and a broth list that rewards the curious. Booths fill on weekends, so put your name down and let the wait build the appetite. Come hungry, leave slow. @shabukiwami

Happiness Hot Pot — 37140 Fremont Blvd, Fremont. Over the Fremont line and worth the drive, a Chongqing room where the beef tallow broth carries real heat. Order the goose intestine if you know it, the house shrimp paste if you are easing in. Bring water and a friend who commits. @happiness_hot_pot2025

Eight for the coldest South Bay nights: Mikiya and Taichi on Homestead, One Pot in Cupertino, Revopot, Tasty Pot and Shabu Time in San Jose, Kiwami in Milpitas, Happiness over in Fremont. Which broth are you starting with?

item.title: San Francisco Marin Burgers
item.description: Eight Marin burgers that locals drive across town for, from a Tiburon dock deck to a Corte Madera park truck. Skip the chains at the mall. Here is the Nort
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Marin Burgers

Eight Marin burgers that locals drive across town for, from a Tiburon dock deck to a Corte Madera park truck. Skip the chains at the mall. Here is the North Bay burger map you keep.

Phyllis' Giant Burgers — 2202 4th St, San Rafael. Four decades in and the line still moves because the griddle never stops. Order the classic with cheese, grab a booth, and let the milkshake carry the conversation. The teriyaki burger sounds wrong and eats right. @phyllisgiantburgers

M&G Burgers — 989 Magnolia Ave, Larkspur. A 1962 counter joint that never chased a trend, and the town loves it for exactly that. Burger, fries, thick shake, no reservation, no fuss. Old-school energy in a downtown that has otherwise gone boutique. @mandg_burgers

Buckeye Roadhouse — 15 Shoreline Hwy, Mill Valley. Open off the 101 since 1937, this is the dressed-up burger with a white-tablecloth backbone. It took Best Burger in the county and did not get quiet about it. Sit at the bar, get the burger and a martini, thank yourself later. @thebuckeyeroadhouse

Sam's Anchor Cafe — 27 Main St, Tiburon. The deck sits right on the water and half the boats tie up to eat. The burger is not reinventing anything. That's the point when the view does the heavy lifting. Ferry over from the city and make a day of it. @sams_cafe

Finnegan's Marin — 877 Grant Ave, Novato. A downtown Irish pub that quietly won Best Burger in Marin and kept the receipt. Open 365 days, patio out back, a pint that arrives cold and correct. The kind of room where the bartender has your order by the third visit. @finnegansmarin

Napa Valley Burger Company — 670 Bridgeway, Sausalito. Gourmet burgers a block off the ferry landing, tourists and locals sharing one patio. Wine-country toppings without the wine-country prices. Grab a window seat and watch the Bridgeway parade go by. @napavalleyburgercompany

Humble Cheeseburger — Town Park at Pixley Ave, Corte Madera. A halal smash-burger truck parked by the post office, and the picnic tables fill fast on a warm Saturday. Crispy edges, potato roll, no attitude. Closed Monday and Tuesday, so plan around it. @humblecheeseburger

Barefoot Cafe — 1900 Sir Francis Drake Blvd, Fairfax. An Italian family cafe hiding a sleeper burger called the Barefoot Special, open from breakfast straight through dinner. Fairfax keeps it funky and this room proves it. Take the patio, order the burger, stay for the ravioli talk. @barefootcafefairfax

Eight for the Marin burger crawl: waterfront decks, a 1962 counter, a park truck, and a pub that keeps winning. Which stop is your Saturday?

item.title: San Francisco Ramen
item.description: Eight San Francisco ramen shops worth the fogged-up windows and the wait, and not one is a mall-food-court chain. The slurp order runs Japantown to the Mis
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco Ramen

Eight San Francisco ramen shops worth the fogged-up windows and the wait, and not one is a mall-food-court chain. The slurp order runs Japantown to the Mission to the Marina, tonkotsu to dashi to a beef-bone bowl almost nobody in town makes. Bring a napkin and a little patience. Save this before the next cold night rolls in off the ocean.

Marufuku Ramen — 1581 Webster St, San Francisco. The Japantown mall hides a Hakata tonkotsu so thick and creamy it clings to the hair-thin noodles like a secret. Put your name down, wander the bookstore upstairs, and drift back when they text you. The wait here is a rite of passage, not a warning. @marufukuramenofficial

Nojo Ramen Tavern — 231 Franklin St, San Francisco. The whole point is chicken, a golden paitan so silky it makes pork broth feel loud. Order a few yakitori skewers while you wait and you have built yourself a little Tokyo-alley dinner in Hayes Valley. Dim, cozy, and made for a rainy Tuesday with nowhere to be. @nojoramen

Mensho Tokyo — 672 Geary St, San Francisco. This is the Michelin-listed one, a Tokyo legend's first US shop, and the line out front tells you the rest. The tori paitan is the move, though the lamb bowl has a cult that shows up at opening on purpose. Go early or make peace with standing on Geary a while. @mensho.usa

Taishoken — 665 Valencia St, San Francisco. The Tokyo shop that invented tsukemen back in 1951 planted its flag on Valencia, so order the dipping noodles, not the standard bowl. Cold chewy noodles, a small cup of intense pork-and-fish broth, and you dunk. It feels like a hack the first time and a habit by the second. @taishoken.sf

Izakaya Sozai — 1500 Irving St, San Francisco. A pint-sized Inner Sunset room where the tonkotsu quietly out-punches shops triple its size. Come for the ramen, stay for the yakitori and a cold Sapporo, and book ahead because the locals guard this table. Foggy-night comfort with a wait list attached. @izakayasozaisf

Ushi Taro Ramen — 343 8th St, San Francisco. The rebel of the group runs on beef instead of pork, a rich gyukotsu broth with slices of brisket where the chashu usually sits. If you have slurped every tonkotsu in the city and want a new page, this SoMa spot is your reset button. Small room, loud flavor. @ushi_taro_ramen

Saiwaii Ramen — 2240 Irving St, San Francisco. Deep in the Outer Sunset fog sits a neighborhood workhorse turning out honest tonkotsu and a spicy garlic bowl the regulars order on repeat. No scene, no gimmicks, portions that quietly end your night. The kind of place that makes a gray avenue feel like home. @saiwaiiramen

Hinodeya Ramen — 3340 Steiner St, San Francisco. Family-style dashi ramen near Chestnut, lighter and cleaner than the tonkotsu crowd, built on bonito and kombu instead of pork fat. The wontons and the sudachi bowl are the tells that someone back there cares. Bright, breezy, and kinder on the walk-in wait. @hinodeya_sf

Eight San Francisco ramen bowls, one map: Marufuku (Japantown tonkotsu), Nojo (Hayes Valley chicken paitan), Mensho (Tenderloin, Michelin), Taishoken (Mission tsukemen), Izakaya Sozai (Inner Sunset), Ushi Taro (SoMa beef broth), Saiwaii (Outer Sunset), Hinodeya (Marina dashi). Save it, pick your fog level, go slurp. Which bowl gets your vote?
